title: Session 12 · Final Project Presentations
text:
Your complete project (R script, dataset, written report) was due via Canvas before midnight Sunday, November 29. No late submissions, no appeals. Presentations happen in class today.
Twelve sessions ago the course opened with a statistical model you couldn’t read; today you present one you built. Everything the semester practiced converges here: a real criminal-justice question, data you cleaned yourself, a model fit and interpreted honestly, and (the part that matters most) saying what it all means in plain language. The written project is already in; today is about standing behind it.

title: Session 12 · Final Project Presentations
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this session you can:

deliver an 8-minute, evidence-backed presentation of your project: question, data, methods, results, and what they mean
answer questions about every line of your code: how it works and why you wrote it that way
interpret your findings for a non-statistician, limitations included, without overclaiming

title: Session 12 · Final Project Presentations
text:
Format

8 minutes + 2 minutes of questions, in the order announced at Session 11. At 8 minutes you’ll be stopped so everyone presents: practice once with a timer
Slides or your rendered report on screen: either works, but you must show your one key visualization
You will walk through your code and explain how and why it works. Being unable to confidently explain your own code will affect your grade: this is the point of the AI policy
Questions from the class and from me
The presentation is 8% of your course grade; the full grading criteria are in the presentation spec

title: Session 12 · Final Project Presentations
text:
What makes a good presentation

Lead with the question, not the code
One clear visualization beats three cluttered ones
Interpret in plain language: what would you tell a police chief, a judge, or a journalist?
Own your limitations: every real analysis has them, and naming them is a strength

Thank you for a great semester. 🎓

title: Session 10 · Multiple Linear Regression
text:
📽️ Slides: Multiple Linear Regression · 🧪 Lab 10: Multiple Regression: Chicago’s 77 Areas, Then 500 Neighborhoods · 📝 Homework 10 + Project Checkpoint 3 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 8’s correlation said that two variables travel together; regression answers the sharper question: how much the outcome changes per unit of a predictor, and with several predictors, how much each matters after accounting for the others. Least squares gets built from scratch on ten students’ study hours, then scaled up to the interactive 3D plane through Chicago’s 77 community areas, where you watch shared variance get reassigned as a second predictor enters. The humility rules ride along: adjusted associations still aren’t causal effects, and area-level patterns still aren’t people-level claims. Checkpoint 3 fits the first regression on your own project data, and if your outcome is a yes/no, Session 11 hands you the right tool.

title: Session 10 · Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

fit and interpret lm() with several predictors, reading each coefficient as “holding the others constant”
explain R², and what happens to a coefficient when a correlated predictor joins the model
run the basic diagnostics: a residuals-vs-fitted plot read honestly, and VIF for multicollinearity
fit the Bayesian version with brm() and report a coefficient with the credible-interval sentence
state what a regression coefficient does, and doesn’t, license you to claim

title: Session 10 · Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Before class

Read: Stanton Ch. 8 (Linear Multiple Regression)
Install one new package before class: install.packages("car"); we use it for multicollinearity checks (VIF). (brms you installed for Project Checkpoint 2, and bayesplot rode along with it; if that test fit failed, flag me down before class.)
Bring your laptop and your final-project dataset: Homework 10 contains Checkpoint 3, the first regression model on your own data

title: Session 10 · Multiple Linear Regression
text:
In class

From Session 8’s correlation to today’s sharper question: not do two variables move together, but how much does the outcome change per unit of a predictor, holding the others constant
Least squares from scratch: three candidate lines through ten students’ study hours and exam scores, a sum-of-squared-residuals ruler to judge them, and lm() finding the one line no other line beats, then the animated best-fit search, and R² (which, with one predictor, is exactly Session 8’s r, squared)
Two predictors = a plane in 3D: the interactive plotly plane you can grab and spin in the browser, regenerated live from code, plus the recorded guided tour
Why “holding constant” earns its keep: ice cream sales “significantly predict” drownings until temperature enters the model and the association evaporates, and an added-variable plot to see the partialing happen
Real-data thread: violent-crime rates across Chicago’s 77 community areas: unemployment alone (slope ~3.3, R² ≈ .71), then vacancy added (unemployment’s slope drops to ~2.1, R² ≈ .82: shared variance reassigned before your eyes), a third predictor that doesn’t earn its keep, and a units lesson (a -0.0006 coefficient that’s actually ~6 fewer violent crimes per 1,000 residents per $10,000 of income)
Diagnostics: the residuals-vs-fitted plot read honestly (ours fans out at high fitted values; we say so), and VIF for multicollinearity
The Bayesian version: your first brm() fit (the compile pause, what the sampler settings and brms default priors mean, and the rule that a credible interval crossing 0 means no credible effect), same formula as lm(), posterior distributions for each coefficient visualized with bayesplot, and the credible-interval sentence the confidence interval never allowed, plus model reporting sentences in both traditions
Standing warnings, now attached to coefficients: adjusted associations are not causal effects, and area-level associations are not people-level claims (the ecological fallacy rides along)
Lab 10: the full workflow yourself: Chicago start to finish, then your own model on the Lab 3 neighborhoods (including the residual plot’s tell that a count outcome is starting to strain the linear model)

Missed class? The demo walkthrough reproduces today’s live demos step by step.

title: Session 9 · Midterm Exam
text:
In-class, monitored exam. You write and troubleshoot real R code. Printed notes and homework allowed: no internet, no AI tools.
The first half of the course is complete: describing data, probability, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing in both traditions, real questions answered with real tests, and correlation. The midterm asks you to show you can use it: an .R script you complete in class, code and interpretation together, drawn only from things we’ve already done. Nothing on it is new; the preparation is re-running your own work until it feels routine.

title: Session 9 · Midterm Exam

explain in a written comment what a p-value, a confidence interval, and a Bayesian probability each mean
read an R error message and troubleshoot your own code with only printed notes at hand

title: Session 9 · Midterm Exam
section: After class: Project Checkpoint 2 (due Sunday, October 18, 11:59 pm)
text:
After class: Project Checkpoint 2 (due Sunday, October 18, 11:59 pm)
No problem set this week. Instead, one short checkpoint on your project dataset, submitted as an .R script via Canvas. It does for your project what Session 8 did for Chicago, and it gets brms ready for Session 10.
In a script with a clearly marked section (for example, # ---- PROJECT CHECKPOINT 2 ----):

Associations. For your outcome and each of your 2 or 3 candidate predictors from Checkpoint 1 (swapping one is fine, with one comment line saying why):

a numeric predictor gets a scatterplot against your outcome plus cor(). Use Spearman (method = "spearman") instead if the plot shows serious skew or wild values, and say why;
a categorical predictor gets a grouped boxplot or a table of group means instead, since r doesn’t apply to categories.

One test. Run cor.test() on the predictor that looks most promising, and report it in one sentence: r, the confidence interval, the p-value, direction, and strength.
A paragraph (as a comment block, roughly 5 to 8 sentences): what each association looks like, and whether the plot makes the number a fair summary; any surprises (a predictor you expected to matter that shows nothing, a sign pointing the “wrong” way, one wild point doing all the work); and which predictors you’ll carry into the regression in Checkpoint 3.
Install brms and run one test model. Session 10 fits your first Bayesian regression, and the first install can take a while. Run this once (the fit takes a minute or two the first time while it compiles; that pause is normal):
install.packages("brms")
library(brms)
test_fit <- brm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars, chains = 1, iter = 500, refresh = 0)
test_fit
If it prints a summary table, you’re ready. If it errors, paste the error into a comment and email me before Session 10, so we can fix it before class rather than during it.

Checkpoint 2 is graded on completion and quality of reasoning, not on whether your correlations turn out strong. If everything is essentially zero, or a variable turns out to be broken, say so plainly: finding that now is the checkpoint working.

Read before Session 10: Stanton Ch. 8 (Multiple Regression)
No class October 27 or November 3. Session 10 is Tuesday, October 20

title: Session 6 · Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
📽️ Slides: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian · 🧪 Lab 6: One Question, Two Tests · 📝 Homework 6 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
This is the signature week of the course: the same research question answered by both of statistics’ great traditions, side by side — the reason we use the Stanton book at all. Session 5’s confidence intervals grow into the Null Hypothesis Significance Test (fine print included), and then Session 3’s Bayes’ theorem returns — pointed at hypotheses instead of diagnoses, answering the question you probably meant to ask. Every method from here to the end of the course runs in both traditions, so this week’s vocabulary is permanent.

title: Session 6 · Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

run prop.test() and bayes_prop_test() on the same question, and state correctly what each output lets you claim
explain in plain language what a p-value is — and name the things it is not
state a prior in plain words, read a posterior, and report a credible interval honestly
find the p-value in prop.test() and t.test() output, and say how big a difference is in real units

title: Session 6 · Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Before class

Read: Stanton Ch. 5 (Bayesian & Frequentist Hypothesis Testing)
Read: Mourtgos, S. M. (2023). “Bayesian Inference in Criminological Research.” Police Forum, 32(1), 7–16 — PDF posted on Canvas. Yes, I assigned my own article; consider it a preview of where your instructor’s sympathies lie, and feel free to argue with it in class
Read: R4DS Ch. 16 — Factors — plus the exercises assigned in Session 5
Nothing new to install: tonight’s Bayesian tool is a course function you load with one source() line

title: Session 6 · Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
In class

From Session 5’s confidence intervals to the Null Hypothesis Significance Test: repeated sampling, a world with no real difference, the verdict machine — and an animation of what the p-value is actually doing
What a p-value is, and the long list of things it is not
The fine print: NHST never scores the alternative hypothesis, and rarely checks the distribution it assumes
Bayes’ theorem, recapped from Session 3 — and the new insight: the p-value lives entirely in the likelihood, and never becomes P(H₀ | data); the two traditions side by side
Optional self-study appendix (end of the deck): why Bayes was long impractical (the intractable denominator) and how MCMC solved it, watched live
Tonight’s real question, in percent: among Chicago’s violent crimes, are domestic ones more likely to end in arrest? (19.7% vs 13.2%)
The recidivism trial, both ways: p = 0.20 from prop.test() vs. a 91% probability the program works from bayes_prop_test() — same data, different questions — with the prior stated in plain words
Back to Chicago with both tools: with thousands of cases the two traditions give nearly the same range; with 100 per group they read very differently
Sample size, animated: p-values dive below .05 for trivial effects as n grows; posteriors just sharpen around the truth. So always say how big the difference is, in real units
Lab 6: one question about the correctional officers, answered twice — prop.test() and bayes_prop_test(), step by step (lab page). You submit your Your Turn script

Missed class? The demo walkthrough reproduces today’s live demos step by step.

title: Session 4 · Sampling Distributions
text:
📽️ Slides: Sampling Distributions · 🧪 Lab 4: Building a Sampling Distribution · 📝 Homework 4 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 3 gave you the rules single random events follow; this week zooms out to what happens when sampling repeats. Draw a thousand samples and the sample means themselves form a distribution — with a predictable shape, a predictable center, and a width you can compute (the standard error). Nothing gets derived: it’s all live simulation, watching the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem appear on screen, including with 30,000 real Chicago incidents. This is the engine under every inference in the rest of the course — Session 5 cashes it in for confidence intervals.

title: Session 4 · Sampling Distributions
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

explain in your own words: law of large numbers, sampling distribution, standard error, central limit theorem
simulate a sampling distribution in R and connect its spread to the SD/√n formula
say why var() and sd() divide by n − 1 (Session 2’s IOU, paid)
build a sampling distribution yourself in R, and keep your scripts and projects organized

title: Session 4 · Sampling Distributions
text:
Before class

Read: Stanton Ch. 3 (Probabilities in the Long Run)
Read: R4DS Ch. 5 — Data tidying — plus the exercises assigned in Session 3
Bring your laptop. The lecture is mine to run: I simulate on screen, you watch and push back. The laptop is for the in-class exercise afterward, where we write the code together.

title: Session 4 · Sampling Distributions
text:
In class

Theoretical vs. empirical probability: coin flips, the law of large numbers, and why “long run” is longer than you think
Simulating CJ probabilities: false-positive drug tests, stop-and-frisk hit rates, and why random ≠ balanced
Sampling from a visible population (population-data.csv): one sample, tail samples, and then a thousand samples — watching the sampling distribution of the mean form on screen
The standard error: simulation vs. the SD/√n formula, and why sample size buys precision at a √n rate
Real-data thread: the central limit theorem with 30,000 real Chicago incidents — repeated samples of case files turn TRUE/FALSE arrest data into a bell curve of sample proportions
Paying Session 2’s IOU: a simulation showing why var() and sd() divide by n − 1
Lab 4 (in-class exercise): build a sampling distribution by hand on 20,000 Alaska crash records — the long run, one sample, five hundred samples, the standard error, and the CLT on a TRUE/FALSE variable, plus scripts-and-projects hygiene

Missed class? The demo walkthrough reproduces today’s live demos step by step.

title: Session 2 · Descriptive Statistics & EDA
text:
📽️ Slides: Descriptive Statistics · 🧪 Lab 2: First Plots with ggplot2 · 📝 Homework 2 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 1 handed you the raw material — variables and their levels of measurement — and swirl got your fingers moving in R. This week you start actually describing data: where a distribution centers, how much it spreads, and what shapes distributions take (including the normal and the Poisson, which turn out to be everywhere in criminal justice). It’s also the week the course’s two threads officially launch: statistics in lecture and homework, data wrangling in lab, beginning with your first real ggplots. Every later topic — probability, inference, regression — rests on being able to describe a distribution honestly, so this vocabulary never leaves.

title: Session 2 · Descriptive Statistics & EDA

Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

define in your own words: mean, median, mode, variance, and standard deviation — and say when the mean misleads
compute and interpret measures of center and spread in R
recognize a distribution’s shape from a histogram — normal, skewed, or Poisson-like counts — and say why shape matters for what comes next
build a histogram, bar chart, and boxplot with ggplot2

title: Syllabus
text:
Academic Bulletin
Descriptive and inferential statistics and the use of computers in criminal justice.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Identify the role of statistics in criminology and criminal justice research.
Distinguish between different types of data and levels of measurement.
Import, clean, transform, and visualize real data in R using modern (tidyverse) tools.
Apply descriptive statistics to summarize and interpret data.
Explain the concepts of probability and distributions as they relate to criminological data.
Conduct and interpret basic statistical tests — from both frequentist and Bayesian perspectives — including t-tests, tests of proportions, correlation, and regression.
Critically evaluate statistical claims in criminal justice policy and research.
Effectively communicate statistical findings in both written and visual formats.

Final Project Information
The final project is the culminating assignment for this course, integrating conceptual understanding with applied statistical skills in R. You will select your own dataset early (you choose it in Homework 7, after the Session 7 workshop tours the data options), and project checkpoints attached to homework in the second half of the semester keep your analysis moving. Session 11 closes with a project code clinic — open Q&A on your own code — before presentations.
Your completed project — R script, output, and written report — is due via Canvas by 11:59 pm on Sunday, November 29, 2026 (the Sunday before presentations day). You will then present your work in class at Session 12 on December 01, 2026.
There will be absolutely no assignments, exams, or final projects accepted after that date and time. None. Add it to your calendar now. Failure to submit any part of the project by that deadline will result in a zero toward your final grade. No appeals will be accepted, so please plan ahead.
You are responsible for ensuring that your final project is submitted successfully and on time, with all required components included: the R script, output, and written report.

text:
Respectful & Appropriate Class Conduct
Public policy processes, including the criminal justice system, inherently center on topics for which individuals hold strong opinions. This course will challenge students to acknowledge and respect perspectives that differ from their own. Respectful behavior is the expectation, norm, and requirement in this class. Arguments and ideas may (and are expected to) be challenged, but personal attacks, disrespectful behavior, and/or hateful attitudes will not be tolerated.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
This Week

Least squares, the line of best fit, and R²
Two predictors: the best-fitting plane, and you’ll spin it with your mouse
“Holding the others constant”: reading coefficients honestly
Diagnostics: the residual plot and VIF
The Bayesian version with brms; reporting both traditions

Learning goals: fit, interpret, and diagnose lm() with several predictors, and say what a coefficient does and doesn’t mean.
Project: Homework 10 contains Checkpoint 3: your first regression on your data.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 8: correlation: r measured how tightly two variables move together; r² was the variance they share
Two humility rules came with it: correlation is not causation, and area-level patterns are not people-level claims (the ecological fallacy)
Today: correlation says that two variables travel together. Regression answers the sharper question: how much, and with several predictors, how much does each matter after accounting for the others?

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The New Question
Correlation is a one-lane road between two variables.
Multiple regression adds more lanes, but all the traffic still arrives at one place: the outcome, \(Y\). Each predictor lane contributes part of how we got there.

The question multiple regression answers:

“How much does Y change when \(X_1\) changes by one unit, holding \(X_2\) constant?”



That phrase, holding constant, is the entire value added today. We’ll earn it slowly.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Model, With One Predictor
\[Y = a + bX + e\]



Piece
Name
Meaning




\(Y\)
outcome
the thing we’re predicting (DV)


\(a\)
intercept
predicted \(Y\) when \(X = 0\)


\(b\)
slope
change in predicted \(Y\) per one-unit change in \(X\)


\(e\)
error
what the line leaves unexplained



The model is a claim: knowing X, here’s my best guess at Y, plus some miss.
The residual is each observation’s miss: actual \(Y\) minus predicted \(Y\).

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Ten Students, Hours and Scores


# seed 1 kept from the 2025 deck: the three
# candidate lines coming up were tuned to this draw
set.seed(1)
students <- tibble(
  hours = 1:10,
  score = 40 + 5 * hours + rnorm(10, 0, 5)
)

ggplot(students, aes(hours, score)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = crju_colors["navy"]) +
  labs(x = "Hours studied", y = "Exam score")









Some line through this cloud is the “best” one. Best by what ruler?

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: Three Candidate Lines

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: The Ruler: Sum of Squared Residuals
text:
The Ruler: Sum of Squared Residuals
For any candidate line, measure every vertical miss, square it (so misses above and below don’t cancel), and add them up:

SSR <- function(a, b) {
  predicted <- a + b * students$hours
  sum((students$score - predicted)^2)
}

SSR(20, 5)      # too low

[1] 4405.871

SSR(50, 3)      # too flat

[1] 584.9933

SSR(37, 5.2)    # roughly right

[1] 196.9529



Smaller total = better line. Least squares = find the line with the smallest total of all.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
lm() Finds the Winner
No trial and error: lm() solves for the one line that minimizes SSR:

fit_hours <- lm(score ~ hours, data = students)
coef(fit_hours)

(Intercept)       hours 
   39.15588     5.27366 

SSR(coef(fit_hours)[1], coef(fit_hours)[2])

[1] 130.9173



Our best hand-picked guess left 197 in squared misses; lm() gets it down to 131, and no other line does better.
Read the slope: each additional hour of studying predicts about 5.3 more points, in this sample.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Watching the Search Land

The line tilts until the SSR stops shrinking, then it’s the least-squares line.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: What the Line Leaves Behind

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: R²: How Much Did We Explain?
text:
R²: How Much Did We Explain?

summary(fit_hours)$r.squared

[1] 0.9460216

cor(students$hours, students$score)^2

[1] 0.9460216



R² = the proportion of the outcome’s variance the model accounts for. Here, hours studied explain ~95% of the spread in scores (it’s simulated data: real life will humble us shortly).
Notice the second line: with one predictor, R² is just Session 8’s correlation, squared. Same quantity, new outfit.
With multiple predictors, R² keeps the same meaning (variance explained by the whole team), but no single correlation owns it anymore.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Model, Full Form
\[Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \cdots + \beta_k X_k + e\]

\(\beta_0\) (intercept): predicted \(Y\) when every \(X\) is zero (often a nonsense scenario; it anchors the model, it doesn’t need to be meaningful)
\(\beta_1 \ldots \beta_k\) (slopes): the effect of each \(X\) holding the others constant
\(e\) (error): what’s still unexplained


Each \(\beta\) is conceptually a partial relationship: how \(X_1\) relates to \(Y\) after removing the overlap with the other predictors. That’s what makes multiple regression more than a stack of correlations.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
From Line to Plane

One predictor: the model is a line through a 2-D cloud
Two predictors: the model is a plane floating in a 3-D cloud, with one slope along each predictor’s axis
The ruler never changes: least squares, which minimizes the total squared vertical distance from every point to the surface
Three or more predictors: a hyperplane in a space we can’t draw. The math shrugs; only our eyes give out.


Two predictors is the last stop where we can actually see the model. So let’s look at it properly.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Best-Fitting Plane, Live






Grab it and spin it.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Guided Tour
Points above the plane are positive residuals; below, negative. For the walkthrough again later: same plane, narrated:

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Remember the Lurker?
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated. Every summer. Reliably.

set.seed(705)
lurk <- tibble(
  temperature    = runif(100, 60, 100),
  icecream_sales = 20 + 5 * temperature + rnorm(100, 0, 30),
  drownings      = -10 + 0.8 * temperature + rnorm(100, 0, 10)
)

ggplot(lurk, aes(icecream_sales, drownings)) +
  geom_point(color = crju_colors["navy"], size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  labs(title = paste0("r = ", round(cor(lurk$icecream_sales, lurk$drownings), 2),
                      ". Ban ice cream?"),
       x = "Ice cream sales", y = "Drownings")

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: Remember the Lurker?

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Model 1: Ice Cream “Predicts” Drownings

lurk_m1 <- lm(drownings ~ icecream_sales, data = lurk)
summary(lurk_m1)$coefficients |> round(4)

               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)     -0.3876     7.5245 -0.0515    0.959
icecream_sales   0.1315     0.0175  7.5165    0.000



The coefficient is positive and the p-value has ten zeros in it
It’s statistically significant. The model says it’s real.
Do we believe it? No, but notice that nothing in this output warns us. The model can only see the variables we gave it.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Model 2: Give the Model the Lurker
text:
Model 2: Give the Model the Lurker

lurk_m2 <- lm(drownings ~ icecream_sales + temperature, data = lurk)
summary(lurk_m2)$coefficients |> round(4)

               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)    -10.0979     6.5333 -1.5456   0.1255
icecream_sales  -0.0339     0.0299 -1.1352   0.2591
temperature      0.9884     0.1553  6.3634   0.0000



Holding temperature constant, ice cream’s coefficient collapses to ~0 (and goes nonsignificant). Temperature was driving both variables the whole time.
This is holding constant doing real work: comparing days with the same temperature, ice cream tells you nothing about drownings.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Side by Side

icecream coef

R²

A “significant” bivariate relationship evaporated once the right third variable entered
Beware the evil lurking third variable. It does not announce itself.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Seeing “Holding Constant”
An added-variable plot shows the relationship between ice cream and drownings after temperature’s contribution is removed from both:

Flat. That flat line is the multiple-regression coefficient for ice cream.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Moral

Multiple regression can hold constant only the variables you measured and included
Every observational model has potential lurkers you didn’t measure, so coefficients are adjusted associations, not causal effects
“Holding constant” is a statistical operation, not a controlled experiment
This is why theory matters: which variables belong in the model is a substantive question, not a statistical one


Keep this loaded. We’re about to fit real Chicago models, and the temptation to talk causally will be enormous.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: Look First. Always.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
One Predictor First

chi_m1 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate, data = areas)
summary(chi_m1)



Each additional percentage point of unemployment is associated with 3.3 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, and unemployment alone accounts for 71% of the between-area variance. Strong, but is unemployment getting credit for other disadvantage it travels with?

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-32.137  -6.340  -2.670   5.843  43.339 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value            Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        -2.7444     2.8629  -0.959               0.341

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Add a Second Predictor: Vacant Housing
text:
Add a Second Predictor: Vacant Housing

chi_m2 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas)
summary(chi_m2)



Both predictors earn significant coefficients, and R² climbs from 0.71 to 0.82.
Watch unemployment’s slope: 3.3 → 2.1. Some of what looked like “unemployment” in the simple model was shared with vacancy. That shrinkage is “holding constant”: the lurker lesson, on real data.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Add a Second Predictor: Vacant Housing
text:
Add a Second Predictor: Vacant Housing


Call:
lm(formula = violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-27.6759  -5.8167  -0.9943   4.5144  26.7266 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value         Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        -9.2679     2.4616  -3.765         0.000332 ***
unemployment_rate   2.1156     0.2620   8.075 0.00000000000935 ***
pct_vacant          1.9352     0.2859   6.769 0.00000000264664 ***

Multiple R-squared:  0.818, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8131

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Reading the Coefficients Out Loud

Intercept (-9.3): predicted rate when both predictors are 0: no Chicago area looks like that; it anchors the plane, nothing more
unemployment_rate (2.12): +1 point of unemployment ↔︎ ~2.1 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, vacancy held fixed
pct_vacant (1.94): +1 point of vacancy ↔︎ ~1.9 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, unemployment held fixed

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
What These Coefficients Are Not

Not causal effects. Adjusted associations between areas, and every lurker we didn’t measure is still at large
Not people-level claims. An unemployed person is not “2.1 crimes more dangerous.” Area-level in, area-level out: Session 8’s ecological fallacy rides along with every coefficient today
Not the full story. The model holds constant only what’s in the model

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Watch the Units
Coefficient size is meaningless until you check the predictor’s units. Median income, in dollars:

coef(lm(violent_rate ~ median_income, data = areas))

  (Intercept) median_income 
68.5585257487 -0.0005221118 

areas |>
  mutate(income_10k = median_income / 10000) |>
  lm(violent_rate ~ income_10k, data = _) |>
  coef()

(Intercept)  income_10k 
  68.558526   -5.221118 



Same model, same fit. But -0.0005 “looks like” nothing; the honest reading is about 5 fewer violent crimes per 1,000 residents per $10,000 of median income. Rescale before you interpret.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Does a Third Predictor Earn Its Keep?
text:
Does a Third Predictor Earn Its Keep?
Add the share of adults without a high-school diploma:

chi_m3 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant + pct_no_hs_diploma,
             data = areas)
summary(chi_m3)$coefficients |> round(3)

                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)         -8.853      2.862  -3.093    0.003
unemployment_rate    2.140      0.276   7.741    0.000
pct_vacant           1.923      0.291   6.613    0.000
pct_no_hs_diploma   -0.039      0.135  -0.290    0.773



Coefficient ≈ 0, p ≈ 0.77: with unemployment and vacancy already in, it adds nothing detectable; adjusted R² (R² with a per-predictor penalty) actually falls: 0.813 → 0.811
More predictors ≠ more truth. Every variable argues its way in: theory first, fit second

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Residual Plot
Regression assumes the misses are patternless. So look at the misses:

chi_diag <- tibble(fitted = fitted(chi_m2), residual = resid(chi_m2))

ggplot(chi_diag, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(color = crju_colors["navy"], size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. fitted values: the all-purpose diagnostic",
       x = "Fitted violent-crime rate", y = "Residual")

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text: The Residual Plot

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Reading Our Residual Plot Honestly

What we want: a patternless horizontal band around zero
What we have: centered on zero with no obvious curve (good: the straight-plane assumption isn’t visibly wrong), but the spread widens at higher fitted values, so the model misses by more in high-violence areas
That fanning (heteroscedasticity) is common with rate outcomes. It doesn’t bias the coefficients, but it makes the SEs less trustworthy at the extremes: worth a sentence when you report
A curve in this plot would be worse news: it would say the model’s shape is wrong, not just its noise

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Multicollinearity: When Predictors Tell the Same Story
text:
Multicollinearity: When Predictors Tell the Same Story
If two predictors move in near-lockstep, the model can’t tell whose coefficient the shared variance belongs to: estimates get wobbly and standard errors balloon.

VIF (variance inflation factor, from the car package) measures how redundant each predictor is with all the others.
Common rules of thumb: VIF > 5, pay attention; VIF > 10, you have a problem.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
VIF on Our Model

vif(chi_m2)

unemployment_rate        pct_vacant 
         1.807177          1.807177 



~1.8: unemployment and vacancy are correlated (r ≈ 0.67), but each still carries plenty of its own information
If VIF were high: drop one predictor, combine them into an index, or accept wide intervals; you cannot p-value your way out

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Two Traditions, One Formula








Approach
What it estimates
The 95% statement




Frequentist
Point estimates and confidence intervals
“If we repeated this study many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true β.”


Bayesian
A full posterior distribution for each β
“Given the data and priors, there’s a 95% probability β lies in this range.”




Same formula, same data, but the Bayesian statement is the one everyone wants to make (remember Session 5’s forbidden sentence? Here it’s allowed).

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Meet brms

brms: Bayesian Regression Models using Stan. It writes the model, compiles it, and samples the posterior
You installed it for Project Checkpoint 2 and ran one test fit. If that test fit failed, flag me down now
bayesplot came along with it: that’s where today’s posterior plots come from







brms compiles models with your computer’s C++ toolchain. Expect the first model of each R session to pause about a minute at “Compiling Stan program…”: that’s normal, not a crash.

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Fitting It: brm()
Identical formula, Bayesian machinery:

chi_bayes <- brm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant,
                 data = areas,
                 chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


Same formula syntax as lm(): this pattern carries through the rest of the course
chains = 2, iter = 2000: two independent samplers, 2,000 steps each (the first half is warm-up) → a full posterior distribution for every coefficient
seed = 705 makes your numbers match mine; refresh = 0 just silences the sampling progress log
Priors: we didn’t state any, so brms used its defaults. Next slide

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: The Posterior, and the Prior We Used
text:
The Posterior, and the Prior We Used

fixef(chi_bayes) |> round(2)

                  Estimate Est.Error   Q2.5 Q97.5
Intercept            -9.25      2.42 -13.93 -4.68
unemployment_rate     2.12      0.27   1.58  2.64
pct_vacant            1.92      0.29   1.36  2.48



Posterior means land almost exactly on the lm() estimates: with decent n and default priors, they should. (Full summary() in today’s lab.)
Default priors: essentially flat on the coefficients, weakly informative on the intercept and spread. “The data do the talking,” but say so: “we used brms default priors” belongs in any write-up
The rule, from here on: a 95% credible interval that crosses 0 → no credible effect; excludes 0 → credible effect

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
The Posteriors, Seen

mcmc_areas(chi_bayes, pars = c("b_unemployment_rate", "b_pct_vacant"),
           prob = 0.95) +
  labs(title = "Posterior distributions: predictors of violent-crime rate",
       subtitle = "Shaded = central 95% credible interval: both sit clear of zero")

title: Multiple Linear Regression
text:
Saying It in Each Tradition
Frequentist:

“Holding vacancy constant, each percentage point of unemployment was associated with 2.1 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents (b = 2.12, 95% CI [1.6, 2.6], p < .001).”

Bayesian:

“Given the data and priors, there is a 95% probability the unemployment coefficient lies between 1.6 and 2.6: zero is not a credible value.”

Both are area-level, adjusted associations: neither sentence licenses “unemployment causes violence.”

title: Multiple Linear Regression
section: Your Turn (5 minutes, with a neighbor)
text:
Your Turn (5 minutes, with a neighbor)
The fitted model:
\[\widehat{\text{violent rate}} = -9.3 + 2.12\,(\text{unemployment}) + 1.94\,(\text{vacancy})\]

Predict the rate for an area with 10% unemployment, 10% vacancy, then 23% and 25% (roughly Englewood). Which prediction does the residual plot say to trust more?
Write one defensible sentence interpreting the vacancy coefficient. Swap and audit: does it say holding unemployment constant? Any smuggled causal verbs (“drives,” “increases”)? Fix what you catch.

Homework 10: cleaning data for regression (you’ll meet some 999s), regression on the cleaned file, plus Project Checkpoint 3: the first regression model on your project data (posted on the Session 10 page)

title: Applied Workshop: Real Questions, Real Tests
text:
This Week
Topic: no new statistics. Tonight we use what you already have.

Four real questions from four corners of criminal justice: reentry, pretrial release, neighborhoods, police use of force
Every one answered with tools from Sessions 5 and 6: count(), prop.test(), bayes_prop_test(), t.test()
Then: what data is out there, so you can choose your final-project dataset this week

Learning goal: given a two-group question on a dataset you have never seen, pick the test, run it, and say what it means (and what it does not).

title: Applied Workshop: Real Questions, Real Tests
text:
How Today Works


Lecture
Four worked examples, one recipe, and a picture of what each test measures

Lab 7
Two more, and you write the code

What’s out there
A menu of real datasets to explore this week

Everything I run tonight is written up in the demo walkthrough, animations included.

title: Applied Workshop: Real Questions, Real Tests
text:
The Recipe
Every question tonight, the same four steps:

Question. Name the two groups and the outcome
Count or describe. count() for yes/no; group averages for a number
Test. Frequentist always; Bayesian too when the outcome is yes/no
Say it. The honest sentence · how big, in real units · one thing this test cannot tell you

title: Applied Workshop: Real Questions, Real Tests
text:
Which Test?








The outcome is…
Example
Test




yes/no
arrested again? searched? released?
prop.test() and bayes_prop_test()


a number
age, income, number of prior arrests
t.test(outcome ~ group, data = )




That table covers every question in tonight’s lecture and lab, and a surprising share of what gets published in criminal justice journals.

title: Applied Workshop: Real Questions, Real Tests
text:
The Study

432 men released from Maryland state prisons in the 1970s, followed for one year
Half were randomly assigned to receive financial aid after release; half were not
Outcome: arrested again within the year (1 = yes)
One row = one released man


Question: did the aid group get re-arrested less often? Two groups, yes/no outcome: prop.test() and bayes_prop_test().

title: Applied Workshop: Real Questions, Real Tests
text:
Count

rossi |> count(fin, arrest)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  fin   arrest     n
  <chr>  <dbl> <int>
1 no         0   150
2 no         1    66
3 yes        0   168
4 yes        1    48



Aid (fin = yes): 48 re-arrested out of 48 + 168 = 216 (22.2%)
No aid: 66 out of 66 + 150 = 216 (30.6%)

Aid first all the way through, so every difference reads Aid minus No aid.

title: Applied Workshop: Real Questions, Real Tests
text:
Test: prop.test()

prop.test(x = c(48, 66), n = c(216, 216))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

X-squared = 3.4439, df = 1, p-value = 0.06349

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
This Week
Topic: The logic of inference, using confidence intervals

What statistical inference actually is (and isn’t)
Point estimates and why they’re not enough
Confidence intervals: building them, reading them, and — hardest of all — saying what they mean out loud without lying

Learning goals: explain in your own words what a 95% confidence interval does and does not mean; compute CIs for a proportion and a difference in means from real data.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
How Today Works


The lecture — concepts
Stanton Ch. 4 → confidence intervals: building them, and saying them out loud honestly

The in-class exercise — code
You write it, together, one idea at a time: a point estimate, an interval around it, and an honest sentence.

Everything I run today is written up in the demo walkthrough, so nothing on screen is something you have to capture in real time.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 3: probability — the rules randomness follows
Session 4: sampling distributions — take many samples, and the sample statistics themselves form a distribution with predictable behavior
Today: we cash that in. If we know how sample statistics behave, we can attach an honest statement of uncertainty to a single sample’s estimate.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Does “Inference” Mean?
Inference: a reasoning process that begins with some information and leads to some conclusion.
Inductive inference: reasons from specific cases to the more general — a cat jumps from a tree and lands on its feet; you infer something about cats generally.
Statistical inference: dealing systematically with situations where we have uncertain or incomplete information. Conclusions drawn inductively from samples are never fixed or firm.







You cannot PROVE anything from samples or by using statistical inference.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: If We Can’t Prove Anything, What Are We Doing?
text:
If We Can’t Prove Anything, What Are We Doing?
We collect data and analyze it with inferential statistics to build up a weight of evidence that influences our certainty about one conclusion or another.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: Let’s Look at the Classic Example
text:
Let’s Look at the Classic Example

1854 — cholera breaks out in Soho, London
The debate: bad air (“miasma”) or contaminated water?
John Snow couldn’t test every household in London — that’s the whole population
So he mapped the sample of evidence he could get: deaths, and where people got their water

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Why This Is Statistical Inference

Why wasn’t Snow just describing the map?
What bigger claim was he making about the whole city — and about cholera itself?

That jump — from the data you have to the world you don’t — is what we mean by inference.

Review from previous weeks — why do we sample?
We almost never have access to the totality of the population data. At its best, a sample is representative of a population.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: A Rare Luxury: We Know the Truth
text:
A Rare Luxury: We Know the Truth
Our Chicago file holds ~30,000 incidents from 2025. Today, pretend the file is the whole population — then we can check our inferences against the truth.

crimes |> summarize(pop_arrest_rate = mean(arrest), n = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  pop_arrest_rate     n
            <dbl> <int>
1           0.161 30000


The “true” citywide arrest proportion is 16.1%. Lock that in — in real research you never get to see this number.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: Now Act Like a Researcher: Draw One Sample
text:
Now Act Like a Researcher: Draw One Sample
A researcher can rarely afford all 30,000 case files. Suppose we pull a random sample of 250 incidents:

sample_250 <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = 250)

sample_250 |> summarize(sample_arrest_rate = mean(arrest))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  sample_arrest_rate
               <dbl>
1              0.148



This is a point estimate — the sample’s best single guess at the population value.
14.8% vs the true 16.1%. Close-ish. But how good is this estimate? How certain are we?

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Caution! Samples Fluctuate
Draw a fresh sample of 250 and the estimate moves. Do it 1,000 times:

many_estimates <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) {
  crimes |> slice_sample(n = 250) |> summarize(p = mean(arrest)) |> pull(p)
})

ggplot(tibble(p = many_estimates), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = crju_colors["blue"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(crimes$arrest),
             color = crju_colors["garnet"], linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "1,000 sample estimates of the arrest rate (n = 250 each)",
       subtitle = "Garnet line = the true population value",
       x = "Sample arrest proportion", y = "Number of samples")

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text: Caution! Samples Fluctuate

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
What the Fluctuation Tells Us

quantile(many_estimates, c(0.025, 0.975))   # what is this telling us?

 2.5% 97.5% 
0.120 0.208 



95% of sample estimates landed between about 12% and 21% — that’s the sampling distribution from Session 4, live
Any single sample’s estimate could easily be a couple points off the truth
So reporting “14.8%” alone is overconfident — we owe our reader a range that reflects the fluctuation
Problem: this required 1,000 samples and a known population. A real researcher has one sample. Now what?

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Our First Inferential Tool
The confidence interval turns one sample into an honest range, using what Session 4 taught us about how sample statistics behave:
\[\text{estimate} \; \pm \; \underbrace{1.96 \times SE}_{\text{margin of error}}\]

SE (standard error) = the standard deviation of the sampling distribution, estimated from the one sample you have
1.96 comes from the normal distribution: ±1.96 SDs covers the middle 95%

Bigger samples → smaller SE → narrower interval.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: R Does This For Us: prop.test()
text:
R Does This For Us: prop.test()

prop.test(sum(sample_250$arrest), n = 250)


    1-sample proportions test with continuity correction

data:  sum(sample_250$arrest) out of 250, null probability 0.5
X-squared = 122.5, df = 1, p-value < 0.00000000000000022
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1075899 0.1995409
sample estimates:
    p 
0.148 



Our one sample of 250 says: point estimate 14.8%, 95% CI 10.8% to 20.0%. The true value (16.1%) is inside — this time. But “95% confident” of what, exactly?

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text: The Classic Picture, Seen

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Just Happened

Each of the 100 samples produced a different interval — the interval is a random quantity, the population value is fixed
97 of our 100 intervals captured the true arrest rate; 3 missed (the garnet ones)
In the long run, the 95% procedure captures the truth in ~95% of replications — that long-run capture rate is the entire meaning of “95% confident”
The researchers who drew the garnet samples did nothing wrong — and their data give no warning that theirs are the unlucky intervals

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
In Practice
If we reran our whole study many times — drawing a new sample each time and constructing a new confidence interval each time — in 95% of those replications the interval would contain the true population value.






IMPORTANT:

Our 95% CI does not necessarily contain the true population value
Our 95% CI is not a statement about the probability that this particular interval is correct
It is a long-run prediction based on numerous replications





WTF?!? Yes. Everyone reacts this way. So let’s run the whole thing again, slower.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: You Are One of Those Researchers
text:
You Are One of Those Researchers

You only ever get one stick, and nothing in your data tells you its color. The 95% belongs to the procedure, not to your interval.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Saying It Out Loud
✅ Defensible:

“We estimate the citywide arrest rate at 14.8% (95% CI: 10.8% to 20.0%). Values in this range are consistent with our data.”


“The method we used captures the true value 95% of the time.”

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: Saying It Out Loud: What Not to Say
text:
Saying It Out Loud: What Not to Say
❌ Not defensible:

“There is a 95% probability the true arrest rate is between 10.8% and 20.0%.” (The truth is fixed — it’s either in there or it isn’t.)


“95% of arrest rates fall in this interval.” (The CI is about the population parameter, not individual observations.)

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: The Sentence You Wanted to Say
text:
The Sentence You Wanted to Say

“There’s a 95% probability the truth is in this interval” is forbidden only under frequentist rules: probability attaches to the procedure, never to the parameter
Attaching probability to a claim itself is exactly what Session 3’s Bayes’ theorem does — and the license costs a stated prior
Next week we compute an interval you can say that sentence about: the credible interval
If the forbidden sentence felt like the natural reading all along — your intuitions were Bayesian. You’re in good company

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Buys Precision
Same procedure, four sample sizes, one draw each:

width_tbl <- map(c(100, 250, 1000, 4000), \(n) {
  s  <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = n)
  ci <- prop.test(sum(s$arrest), n = n)$conf.int
  tibble(n = n, estimate = mean(s$arrest),
         lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2], width = ci[2] - ci[1])
}) |>
  list_rbind()

width_tbl



# A tibble: 4 × 5
      n estimate     lo    hi  width
  <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1   100    0.12  0.0663 0.204 0.138 
2   250    0.184 0.139  0.239 0.0998
3  1000    0.165 0.143  0.190 0.0470
4  4000    0.167 0.155  0.179 0.0234



Quadrupling n roughly halves the width — precision grows with \(\sqrt{n}\), so it gets expensive fast.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: A Real Question: Do Violent Crimes Happen Later in the Day?
text:
A Real Question: Do Violent Crimes Happen Later in the Day?
Street lore says violence is a nighttime phenomenon. Property crime, the daytime hustle. Our data:

vp <- crimes |>
  filter(crime_category %in% c("Violent", "Property")) |>
  mutate(crime_category = factor(crime_category, levels = c("Violent", "Property")))

vp |> summarize(mean_hour = mean(hour), sd_hour = sd(hour), n = n(), .by = crime_category)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  crime_category mean_hour sd_hour     n
  <fct>              <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
1 Violent             12.8    6.87  9148
2 Property            12.5    6.63 10371



Two point estimates: violent crimes average about 12:48 pm, property crimes about 12:33 pm. Is that 15-minute gap real, or sample fluctuation?

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: One Extra Line: Who Comes First
text:
One Extra Line: Who Comes First
mutate(crime_category = factor(crime_category, levels = c("Violent", "Property")))

R’s default order is alphabetical: Property before Violent, so every “difference” it reported would come out as Property minus Violent, the reverse of how we asked the question
factor(levels = ...) tells R which group comes first. From here on, every subtraction reads Violent minus Property
That one line is what next week’s R4DS chapter (Factors) is about

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Let’s Look at It Visually

ggplot(vp, aes(crime_category, hour, fill = crime_category)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(crju_colors[c("garnet", "blue")])) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24),
                     labels = c("midnight", "6 am", "noon", "6 pm", "midnight")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Time of day")


The boxes nearly coincide — the eye can’t settle this one. We need inference.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Resample the Difference
Same trick as before — resample each group, compute the difference in means, repeat:

set.seed(705)
violent_hours  <- vp$hour[vp$crime_category == "Violent"]
property_hours <- vp$hour[vp$crime_category == "Property"]

boot_violent  <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(violent_hours,  replace = TRUE)))
boot_property <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(property_hours, replace = TRUE)))
mean_diffs    <- boot_violent - boot_property

quantile(mean_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975)) * 60   # in minutes: Violent minus Property

     2.5%     97.5% 
 3.709722 26.345208

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: What “Does Not Cross Zero” Looks Like
text:
What “Does Not Cross Zero” Looks Like

Every plausible value of the difference is on the “later” side. “No difference” is not on the list.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: The Two-Sample t-Test Gives the CI Directly
text:
The Two-Sample t-Test Gives the CI Directly

t.test(hour ~ crime_category, data = vp)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  hour by crime_category
t = 2.6061, df = 19021, p-value = 0.009164
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Violent and group Property is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.06263688 0.44272107
sample estimates:
 mean in group Violent mean in group Property 
              12.79602               12.54334 


Two lines matter: 95 percent confidence interval, and the two mean in group lines that tell you which minus which. Violent is listed first because we told R so.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Reading That Output Honestly

The 95% CI for the difference (Violent minus Property) runs from 0.06 to 0.44 hours: about 4 to 27 minutes later. It excludes zero, so the data are consistent with violent crimes genuinely averaging later
The resampling picture said the same thing. t.test() is a formula for the interval we just simulated, no loop required

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
Reading That Output Honestly, Continued

But look at the magnitude: somewhere between about 4 and 27 minutes. Detectable ≠ dramatic.
With ~19,500 incidents, we can detect tiny differences. The CI hands you both facts at once: direction (probably real) and size (small). Never report the first without the second.
This is your vaccination against next week’s topic — a “significant” result can be substantively trivial

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
section: And When It Does Cross Zero
text:
And When It Does Cross Zero
Same city, a question the data cannot settle: within violent crimes, do the ones that end in an arrest happen at a different time of day?

Zero is one of the plausible answers, so this sample cannot even tell you the direction. Next week this contrast gets a name.

title: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals
text:
R Agrees

t.test(hour ~ arrest, data = violent)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  hour by arrest
t = -1.2287, df = 1941.3, p-value = 0.2193
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Arrest and group No arrest is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.6653724  0.1527959
sample estimates:
   mean in group Arrest mean in group No arrest 
               12.58047                12.83676 


The interval runs from about 40 minutes earlier to 9 minutes later, zero inside. Arrested violent crimes might happen a little earlier, a little later, or at the same time; this sample cannot say which.

This Week
Topic: Essentials of probability

Outcome tables — toast drops in place of coin tosses
The binomial distribution; generating random data
Contingency tables: marginal, joint, and conditional probability
A first pass at Bayes’ theorem and base rates

Learning goals: reason with outcome and contingency tables; generate random distributions in R; reverse a conditional with Bayes’ theorem.
Today’s rule: don’t take a probability claim on faith — simulate it and watch it happen.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Two Threads, One Course


Statistics thread — lecture + homework
Stanton Ch. 2 → probability, conditional thinking, and a first pass at Bayes’ theorem

Wrangling thread — lab
R4DS Ch. 3–4 → the dplyr verbs: filter(), arrange(), mutate(), summarize(), count()

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Probability = Long-Run Proportion
Claim: a fair coin lands heads with probability 0.5. Don’t trust me — flip some coins:

flips <- sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10, replace = TRUE)
flips

 [1] "heads" "heads" "heads" "tails" "tails" "tails" "heads" "tails" "heads"
[10] "heads"

mean(flips == "heads")

[1] 0.6




# six more batches of ten flips each:
replicate(6, mean(sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10, replace = TRUE) == "heads"))

[1] 0.6 0.1 0.5 0.6 0.6 0.7


Ten flips is not the long run — batches of 10 bounce around, and none is entitled to land exactly on 0.5.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Our Simulation Verbs, In Words
You just met the two verbs that power every simulation this semester:

sample() — run one random event (flip the coins, drop the toast)
replicate(k, expr) — repeat the whole recipe k times and collect the answers
One run = a trial; many runs = the long run
Later today, rbinom() compresses “flip six coins and count the heads” into a single call



A plain-language reference for all the course’s simulation verbs lives on the Resources page.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
The Long Run, Seen

lln <- tibble(flip = sample(c(1, 0), size = 100000, replace = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(n_flips = row_number(),
         running_prop = cummean(flip))

ggplot(lln, aes(n_flips, running_prop)) +
  geom_line(color = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Number of flips (log scale)", y = "Running proportion of heads")


Wobbly early, pinned to 0.5 eventually. A probability is the value the long-run proportion settles on. Every probability “fact” today gets this treatment.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text: The Long Run, Seen

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Real Stakes: P(Arrest) in Chicago
Our anchor data: 30,000 real Chicago incidents from 2025. Each incident either ended in an arrest or didn’t — 30,000 recorded trials.

mean(crimes$arrest)

[1] 0.1608


Pick a 2025 incident at random and the probability it ended in arrest is about 0.16 — arrest is the exception, not the rule.
(arrest is TRUE/FALSE; mean() of a logical is the proportion of TRUEs. You’ll use this trick constantly.)

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: The Long Run Works on Real Data Too
text:
The Long Run Works on Real Data Too
Read case files one at a time, tracking the running arrest proportion:

running <- tibble(arrest = sample(crimes$arrest, size = 5000)) |>
  mutate(n_cases = row_number(),
         running_prop = cummean(arrest))

ggplot(running, aes(n_cases, running_prop)) +
  geom_line(color = crju_colors["navy"]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Case files read (log scale)", y = "Running proportion arrested")


The first few dozen cases can wander far from 0.16. Thousands pin it down. Small samples lie; long runs don’t.

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: A Reality Show About Dropped Toast
text:
A Reality Show About Dropped Toast
Imagine a restaurant where the waiters always drop the food. Each order = six pieces of toast; each piece lands topping-down or topping-up.

One piece of toast falling = one event
One dropped order of six = one trial

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
The Toast Data: 100 Dropped Orders
Here’s data from 100 trials:

toast <- tibble(
  jelly_down = 0:6,
  trials     = c(4, 9, 20, 34, 21, 11, 1)
)
toast

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  jelly_down trials
       <int>  <dbl>
1          0      4
2          1      9
3          2     20
4          3     34
5          4     21
6          5     11
7          6      1

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Proportions ≈ Probabilities

toast |> mutate(prob = trials / sum(trials))

# A tibble: 7 × 3
  jelly_down trials  prob
       <int>  <dbl> <dbl>
1          0      4  0.04
2          1      9  0.09
3          2     20  0.2 
4          3     34  0.34
5          4     21  0.21
6          5     11  0.11
7          6      1  0.01



Rule #1: probabilities across all outcomes sum to 1:

toast |> summarize(total_prob = sum(trials / sum(trials)))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  total_prob
       <dbl>
1          1

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Simulate Your Own Toast Drops

drops <- rbinom(n = 100, size = 6, prob = 0.5)
# rbinom() generates random trials of the "binomial distribution"
# n = 100 gives the number of trials
# size = 6 asks for six pieces of toast in each trial
# prob = 0.5 says there's an even (50:50) chance of jelly-down or jelly-up

tibble(jelly_down = drops) |> count(jelly_down)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  jelly_down     n
       <int> <int>
1          0     1
2          1     8
3          2    23
4          3    32
5          4    22
6          5    13
7          6     1


Compare to the reality-show table — same shape, without filming a single waiter.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Run It Again — It Changes

two_runs <- tibble(
  run = rep(c("Run 1", "Run 2"), each = 100),
  jelly_down = c(rbinom(100, size = 6, prob = 0.5),
                 rbinom(100, size = 6, prob = 0.5))
)
ggplot(two_runs, aes(jelly_down)) +
  geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  facet_wrap(~run) +
  labs(x = "Jelly-down count (out of 6)", y = "Trials")


Same process, different picture — sampling variability. 100 trials is still a shortish run. Try running it yourself!

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Cumulative Probabilities
“What’s the probability of 3 or fewer jelly-down?” Add up the outcomes as you go:

cum_toast <- tibble(jelly_down = rbinom(n = 100000, size = 6, prob = 0.5)) |>
  count(jelly_down) |>
  mutate(prob = n / sum(n),
         cum_prob = cumsum(prob))
ggplot(cum_toast, aes(jelly_down, cum_prob)) +
  geom_col(fill = crju_colors["navy"]) +
  labs(x = "Jelly-down count", y = "P(this count or fewer)")


Each bar = probability of that count or fewer. The last bar is always 1 — rule #1 again.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text: Cumulative Probabilities

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Linked Outcomes
Now each falling piece of toast has two classifications: how it lands (down/up) and its topping (jelly/butter). Ten dropped pieces:

toast10 <- tribble(
  ~topping, ~landed, ~n,
  "Jelly",  "Down",  2,
  "Jelly",  "Up",    1,
  "Butter", "Down",  3,
  "Butter", "Up",    4
)
toast10 |> pivot_wider(names_from = landed, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  topping  Down    Up
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 Jelly       2     1
2 Butter      3     4


A contingency table: rows = one classification, columns = the other, cells = counts of events with both.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Marginal Totals Answer Questions

Total toast-drop events? How many landed down? Up?
More likely to land down or up?
Which topping is more common, butter or jelly?


toast10 |> summarize(n = sum(n), .by = landed)    # column margins


The row/column sums live in the margins of the table — hence marginal probabilities.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Marginal Totals Answer Questions

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  landed     n
  <chr>  <dbl>
1 Down       5
2 Up         5

toast10 |> summarize(n = sum(n), .by = topping)   # row margins

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  topping     n
  <chr>   <dbl>
1 Jelly       3
2 Butter      7

sum(toast10$n)                                    # grand total

[1] 10

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: Super Challenge: Does the Topping Matter?
text:
Super Challenge: Does the Topping Matter?
Jelly landed down 2/3 of the time (0.67); butter 3/7 (0.43). Is jelly really doomed — or is 10 pieces of toast just a short run? Simulate a world where topping makes no difference:

sim_gap <- function() {
  p_jelly  <- rbinom(1, size = 3, prob = 0.5) / 3   # 3 jelly pieces, fair
  p_butter <- rbinom(1, size = 7, prob = 0.5) / 7   # 7 butter pieces, fair
  abs(p_jelly - p_butter)
}
gaps <- replicate(10000, sim_gap())
mean(gaps >= 2/3 - 3/7)   # how often does pure chance produce our gap?

[1] 0.611

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Super Challenge: The Verdict
Even with no real difference, chance alone produces a gap at least this big well over half the time. Ten drops can’t answer the question.
(This simulate-a-boring-world move is the seed of hypothesis testing — coming in Session 6.)

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
A Real Contingency Table
Same structure, real stakes — crime category × arrest, 30,000 Chicago incidents:

crimes |>
  count(crime_category, arrest) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arrest, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category `FALSE` `TRUE`
  <chr>            <int>  <int>
1 Other             7867   2614
2 Property          9615    756
3 Violent           7694   1454


count() gets the cell counts; pivot_wider() lays them out as the table. This is today’s lab skill set doing probability work.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Joint Probabilities, For Real
Joint — divide every cell by the grand total:

crimes |>
  count(crime_category, arrest) |>
  mutate(p = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  crime_category arrest     n      p
  <chr>          <lgl>  <int>  <dbl>
1 Other          FALSE   7867 0.262 
2 Other          TRUE    2614 0.0871
3 Property       FALSE   9615 0.320 
4 Property       TRUE     756 0.0252
5 Violent        FALSE   7694 0.256 
6 Violent        TRUE    1454 0.0485


P(Property and arrest) ≈ 0.025 — a joint probability.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Marginal Probabilities, For Real
Marginal — collapse one classification:

crimes |> count(crime_category) |> mutate(p = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category     n     p
  <chr>          <int> <dbl>
1 Other          10481 0.349
2 Property       10371 0.346
3 Violent         9148 0.305


P(Property) ≈ 0.35 — a marginal probability, next to the joint P(Property and arrest) ≈ 0.025 from the last slide.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
The Restaurant Work Schedule
Back at the toast restaurant — hours worked by four servers:

hours <- tribble(
  ~day,        ~Anne, ~Bill, ~Calvin, ~Devon,
  "Monday",        6,     0,       5,      8,
  "Tuesday",       0,     6,       6,      0,
  "Wednesday",     8,     5,       0,      8,
  "Thursday",      4,     6,       5,      8,
  "Friday",        8,     8,       5,      8,
  "Saturday",      8,    10,       8,      8,
  "Sunday",        0,     3,       6,      0
)
hours_long <- hours |> pivot_longer(-day, names_to = "server", values_to = "hours")

Two interesting questions:

You sit down and Bill is your server. What day is it most likely to be?
You know it’s Monday. Who is most likely to be your server?

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Converting to Proportions
Every cell divided by the grand total (147 hours) — the joint probabilities:

hours_long |>
  mutate(p = hours / sum(hours)) |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = day, names_from = server, values_from = p)

# A tibble: 7 × 5
  day         Anne   Bill Calvin  Devon
  <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Monday    0.0408 0      0.0340 0.0544
2 Tuesday   0      0.0408 0.0408 0     
3 Wednesday 0.0544 0.0340 0      0.0544
4 Thursday  0.0272 0.0408 0.0340 0.0544
5 Friday    0.0544 0.0544 0.0340 0.0544
6 Saturday  0.0544 0.0680 0.0544 0.0544
7 Sunday    0      0.0204 0.0408 0     


But question 1 isn’t about the whole table — Bill being your server rules out every other column.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Question 2: It’s Monday — Who’s Serving?
Same move, conditioning the other way:

hours_long |>
  filter(day == "Monday") |>
  mutate(p_server_given_monday = hours / sum(hours))

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  day    server hours p_server_given_monday
  <chr>  <chr>  <dbl>                 <dbl>
1 Monday Anne       6                 0.316
2 Monday Bill       0                 0    
3 Monday Calvin     5                 0.263
4 Monday Devon      8                 0.421


Devon (0.42). Note the asymmetry: P(Saturday | Bill) and P(Bill | Saturday) are different questions with different answers. The direction of conditioning matters — a lot. Bayes’ theorem, in a few minutes, is the formula for flipping it.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Conditioning = filter(), Then Proportion
In real data, conditional probability is just subset, then take the mean:

crimes |>
  summarize(p_arrest = mean(arrest), n = n(), .by = crime_category)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category p_arrest     n
  <chr>             <dbl> <int>
1 Violent          0.159   9148
2 Other            0.249  10481
3 Property         0.0729 10371


P(arrest | Property) ≈ 0.07; P(arrest | Other) ≈ 0.25. Knowing the crime category changes the arrest probability — the two variables are dependent.

title: Reasoning with Probability
Reasoning with Probability
text:
When Conditioning Changes Nothing: Independence

mean(crimes$arrest)

[1] 0.1608

crimes |>
  summarize(p_arrest = mean(arrest), n = n(), .by = domestic)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  domestic p_arrest     n
  <lgl>       <dbl> <int>
1 FALSE       0.161 24194
2 TRUE        0.160  5806


P(arrest | domestic) and P(arrest | not domestic) are essentially identical to the overall P(arrest) — in this sample, knowing an incident was domestic tells you almost nothing about arrest.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Independence, Defined
Definition: A and B are independent when P(A | B) = P(A). Conditioning that moves the number = dependence; conditioning that doesn’t = independence.

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: The Question We Keep Almost Asking
text:
The Question We Keep Almost Asking

The restaurant taught us direction matters: P(Saturday | Bill) ≠ P(Bill | Saturday)
The narcotics trap was the same lesson with teeth: P(arrest | narcotics) ≈ .97 is not P(narcotics | arrest)
Real life keeps handing you one conditional — test accuracy, match rates, hit rates — and asking you for the other one
There is a formula for flipping the direction — legally

title: Reasoning with Probability
Reasoning with Probability
text:
Bayesian Updating, Watched Live
Start moderately confident a coin is fair — a prior belief centered on “fair” — then flip it 100 times and update after every flip:

This morning we watched a coin’s long-run proportion converge. Same coin, new question: what do we believe about it, updated flip by flip? Beliefs are provisional, quantified, and revised by evidence — that is the entire philosophy in one gif.

title: Reasoning with Probability
section: The Dreaded Adamsitis Strain of Ianfluenza
text:
The Dreaded Adamsitis Strain of Ianfluenza
A screening problem (any resemblance to a frequent co-author is coincidental):

Prevalence 1% — 10 cases per 1,000 people
Sensitivity .90 — catches 90% of true cases
Specificity .95 — clears 95% of the healthy

Two questions that sound identical — and are not:

\(P(\text{test says} + \mid \text{actually sick})\) — what the brochure advertises
\(P(\text{actually sick} \mid \text{test says} +)\) — what you want in the exam room

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Count It Out: 1,000 People




Test says +
Test says −
Total




Sick (1%)
9 caught
1 missed
10


Healthy
~50 false alarms
~941 cleared
990


Total
~59
~942
1,000



Look closely — this is a contingency table, and P(sick | +) is the same move as P(day | Bill): shrink to the “test says +” column, re-proportion.

\[
P(\text{sick} \mid +) \;=\; \frac{9}{9 + 50} \;\approx\; 15\%
\]
The test is “90% accurate” — and a positive result still means you are probably fine.

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Priors Matter

Read the test result the intuitive way — “the test is 90% accurate, so I’m 90% sick” — and you have silently treated \(P(\text{data} \mid H)\) as \(P(H \mid \text{data})\)
The base rate (the prior: 1%) is what separates 90% from 15%. Ignoring it makes the test look far more powerful than it really is
Criminal justice runs on rare events: false confessions, officer-involved shootings, risk-assessment flags, gunshot-residue matches. Base-rate neglect is not a party trick here — it convicts people

title: Reasoning with Probability
text:
Hold This Thought Until Session 6

Today planted two seeds: the Super Challenge (simulate the boring world, see if chance explains your gap) and Bayes’ theorem (update beliefs by evidence)
Those are the two great traditions of statistical inference — frequentist and Bayesian
Session 6 runs both, side by side, on one real Chicago question
Until then: every conditional probability you meet, ask which direction is this?

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
The Situation
Over three months, 40 bank robberies strike across a city’s five zones: North, South, East, West, and Downtown.

No clear pattern. No suspects. No leads.
The robber hits banks, disappears, and resurfaces days later in a different part of the city.
Detectives are stumped. The media is escalating. Public concern is growing.
Then someone makes a call to the PD’s new crime analyst team:



“Can you help us predict where they’ll hit next?”

title: Statistics is Awesome!
section: What Does the Data Look Like?
text:
What Does the Data Look Like?
40 bank robberies across 5 city zones over several months:







Variable
Meaning




robbery_id
Robbery sequence


date
When the robbery occurred


zone
Which part of the city was hit


day_of_year
Numeric version of the date (for modeling time)


lat & lon
Spatial location (for mapping)


prior_robberies_in_zone
How many robberies already happened in that zone?

title: Statistics is Awesome!

Before We Model, We Look
Very little information is available: no suspect descriptions, no MO patterns: just when and where.
Can we use this simple dataset to build a predictive model with statistics?

But before we even build a model, we can use basic plots to spot patterns.
Good data analysts always visualize before they model.

Outcome: future_hit = 1 if another robbery occurs in the same zone within the next 10 days; otherwise 0

title: Statistics is Awesome!
section: You Already Think Like a Bayesian
text:
You Already Think Like a Bayesian
Look at what you just did with the robbery case:

You started with a vague hunch spread across five zones: statisticians call that a prior
Each new robbery was evidence that reshaped the hunch
The model’s “predicted risk by zone” is an updated belief, given the data
Sending officers to the West Zone = deciding under quantified uncertainty
The formal name is Bayesian updating. The formula arrives in Session 3; the full machinery in Session 6: side by side with the other great tradition, the frequentist one

text:
Types of Data
Qualitative (categorical)

Describe groups or labels (zone, sex, race)
Text / interviews

Quantitative (numerical)

Measurable amounts (age, prior robberies)
Discrete = whole counts (number of robberies)

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Levels of Measurement








Level
Definition
Examples




Nominal
Categories without order
Race, sex, zone


Ordinal
Ordered categories, unequal gaps
Likert scales


Interval
Meaningful differences, no true zero
Temperature (°C)


Ratio
Meaningful differences and true zero
Robbery counts, age

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Why Does the Level Matter?

Your variable’s scale determines the math you’re allowed to do
It also determines the plot you should make
Using the wrong scale leads to wrong conclusions

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Scale Determines the Math: Nominal

# WRONG: the "mean zone" is meaningless
rob$zone |> as.numeric() |> mean()

[1] 3.17




# RIGHT: counts and percentages
rob |>
  count(zone) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  zone         n   pct
  <fct>    <int> <dbl>
1 Downtown    32  16  
2 East        28  14  
3 North       59  29.5
4 South       36  18  
5 West        45  22.5

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Scale Determines the Math: Ordinal

# Summarize a Likert item (ordinal): median & IQR
rob |>
  summarize(med = median(risk_likert), iqr = IQR(risk_likert))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
    med   iqr
  <dbl> <dbl>
1     4     3

# Association with a numeric variable: Spearman (rank-based)
cor(rob$risk_likert, rob$prior_robberies_in_zone, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.001707403

title: Statistics is Awesome!
text:
Interval vs. Ratio

mean(rob$temp_c)             # ~20 °C

[1] 20.07643

mean(rob$temp_c * 1.8 + 32)  # same temperatures in °F

[1] 68.13757


Temperature has no true zero: 0 °C is just where water freezes.

“30 °C is 10 °C warmer than 20 °C” ✔ (differences are fine)
“20 °C is twice as hot as 10 °C” ✘ (ratios are meaningless)



mean(rob$age)

[1] 40.605


Age has a true zero: a 40-year-old is twice as old as a 20-year-old. Differences and ratios both work.
