title: Homework 10 · Cleaning Data for Regression + Project Checkpoint 3
text:
Instructions: complete the following exercises in a single .R script file. Your script must run top-to-bottom when I execute it, with answers to interpretive questions in #comments. Submit your .R file via Canvas for credit.
As you begin working with your final-project data, you will quickly discover that most of your time is spent cleaning the data: getting it into a shape where a model will even run, and where the numbers it returns mean what you think they mean. That’s not a detour from analysis; it is analysis. This homework makes the point the honest way: you’ll clean a dirty file, then watch what regression does before and after you cleaned it.
Do not shortcut Part 1. Every minute you spend on these verbs now is an hour saved on your final project. (If any verb feels shaky, the reference chapter is R4DS Ch. 3, Data transformation, the same toolkit from Labs 3 to 6.)

title: Homework 10 · Cleaning Data for Regression + Project Checkpoint 3
text:
Setup
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)
library(car)

officers <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/officers.csv")
glimpse(officers)
The file holds survey records for 200 correctional officers (simulated, but realistically messy): facility, shift, tenure, monthly overtime hours, hours of sleep, and a burnout score that is supposed to run 0 to 100. Your eventual model: burnout ~ overtime_hours_mo + sleep_hours.

title: Homework 10 · Cleaning Data for Regression + Project Checkpoint 3
section: Part 1: Find the Dirt, Fix the Dirt
text:
Part 1: Find the Dirt, Fix the Dirt

First pass. Run summary() on the data (or on the numeric columns). In a comment: identify two impossible values hiding in variables your model needs. (Hint: check each variable’s minimum and maximum against what the variable is.)
Categorical hygiene. Run count(officers, shift). In a comment: what went wrong in data entry? Fix it with mutate() + str_to_title(), then re-run count() to confirm exactly three shifts remain, and report the three counts.
Sentinels to NA. The burnout instrument’s codebook says 999 = “declined to answer.” That is a code, not a score: left as a number, it will poison every mean, SD, and slope downstream. Convert it: mutate(burnout = na_if(burnout, 999)). Then deal with the impossible overtime value the same general way (negative hours cannot happen; make it NA; if_else() is one route). In a comment: how many NAs does each of your two repaired variables now contain?
Build the analysis file. Create officers_clean by dropping the rows with NA on any model variable: drop_na(burnout, overtime_hours_mo, sleep_hours). In a comment: how many rows did you lose, and out of how many?
Grouped summary practice. On officers_clean, compute the mean burnout score and the number of officers per facility (summarize() with .by = facility), and arrange() the result in descending order. In a comment: which facility reports the highest average burnout, and is the gap between facilities large relative to burnout’s SD?

title: Homework 10 · Cleaning Data for Regression + Project Checkpoint 3
section: Part 2: Regression, Before and After Cleaning
text:
Part 2: Regression, Before and After Cleaning

Fit the dirty model. On the original officers data, fit lm(burnout ~ overtime_hours_mo + sleep_hours). Look at summary(), then make the residuals-vs-fitted plot from Lab 10. In a comment: what in the plot (and in the residual standard error) screams that something is wrong? Remember the outcome is supposed to live between 0 and 100.
Fit the clean model. Same formula on officers_clean. In a comment: compare the residual standard error across the two fits, and explain why a handful of 999s did that much damage. (Think about what least squares does to a residual of ~900 when it squares it.)
Interpret the clean model honestly. Look at the coefficients and confint(), and run vif(). In comments:

One holding-constant sentence per predictor, including the direction and size of each estimated coefficient.
Neither predictor reaches conventional significance in this sample. Write the honest version of that finding in one sentence: what the data do and don’t show about overtime, sleep, and burnout here. (“We found no reliable association…” is a legitimate scientific result, not a failure. You will need this sentence again in your career, probably often.)
What does the VIF tell you about these two predictors?

The Bayesian check. Fit the clean model with brms:
burnout_bayes <- brm(burnout ~ overtime_hours_mo + sleep_hours,
                     data = officers_clean,
                     chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)
summary(burnout_bayes)
In a comment: do the 95% credible intervals include 0? Write one Bayesian sentence about the sleep coefficient, and say whether the two traditions agree here.

title: Homework 10 · Cleaning Data for Regression + Project Checkpoint 3
text:
Part 3: Project Checkpoint 3






This section uses YOUR final-project dataset. Checkpoint 3 of 4: you described your variables in Checkpoint 1 (Homework 8) and explored the correlations among them in Checkpoint 2 (midterm week); now you fit the first regression model of your project. Like the others, it is graded on completion and quality of reasoning, not on whether the model comes out significant, and not on polish. A model that comes out null, weird, or broken, noticed and discussed, is a successful checkpoint.



In a clearly marked section at the end of your .R script (e.g., # ---- PROJECT CHECKPOINT 3 ----):

Fit a first regression model: your outcome regressed on 2 to 3 predictors (the ones your Checkpoint 2 exploration made most promising).

If your outcome is continuous (or close to it), use lm(): this is your tool.
If your outcome is binary (yes/no, arrest/no arrest, recidivated/didn’t), say so in a comment: the right tool is logistic regression, which is exactly what Session 11 covers. For now, fit the linear model anyway as a rough first pass (with a binary outcome its coefficients read approximately as changes in the probability of a “yes”), and label it clearly as a placeholder you’ll replace after Session 11.

Report and interpret the coefficients: one plain-language, holding-constant sentence per predictor, with units, plus one sentence on R² (or note that R² will make more sense post-logistic if your outcome is binary).
One diagnostic check: a residuals-vs-fitted plot or vif() (VIF only makes sense with 2+ predictors; running both earns no extra credit but will earn my respect). One comment on what it shows.
Write a short paragraph (comment block, roughly 5 to 8 sentences): what does this first model say about your research question? Which coefficient is most interesting, and is its direction what you predicted in Checkpoint 1? Name one lurking variable your model cannot hold constant because your dataset doesn’t measure it. And if anything looks broken (a nonsense coefficient, an outcome that clearly isn’t continuous, residuals doing something alarming), say so plainly and come see me. Catching it now is the checkpoint working.

title: Homework 7 · Explore Two Datasets, Choose One
text:
Instructions: complete the following in a single .R script and submit it via Canvas. Answer every prompt marked (comment) in a comment (#) in your script. I will run your script, so every line has to be either code or start with #.
This week you choose the dataset for your final project. Explore two options first, then commit to one. The options, with the one line that loads each, are on the Final-Project Data Options page. You may use any dataset on that page, including the reentry, pretrial, police stops, shootings, and risk-assessment data we worked in Session 7, as long as your question goes beyond what we did in class. If you found a dataset somewhere else, clear it with me first. The course datasets are not eligible: that includes the Chicago data from Session 7’s Example 3, plus crash, officers, prisoners, neighborhoods, cities, and reentry-wide.
Start your script with:

title: Homework 7 · Explore Two Datasets, Choose One
text:
Part 1: Explore Two Datasets
Do all five steps for each of your two datasets, under a clear header (# ---- Dataset 1: ... ----).

Load it. The read_csv() line from the data options page (or, for a dataset you found, the line that reads it; no setwd() and no paths to your own computer).
Look at it. Run glimpse() on it.
What is one row? (comment) One row = one what? (A person? An arrest? A stop? A state?) And how many rows are there?

title: Homework 7 · Explore Two Datasets, Choose One

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Instructions: complete the following exercises in a single .R script file. Include comments explaining your code and answers to any interpretive questions. Submit your .R file via Canvas for credit.
This homework uses the Alaska traffic-crash data from Lab 4 — 20,000 real-world-style crash incidents. Our research question: do crashes involving an intoxicated driver injure more people than crashes that don’t? Every step below is one you ran in Lab 5, pointed at a new question.
Start your script with:

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
section: Part 1: Import and Name the Groups
text:
Part 1: Import and Name the Groups

Run glimpse(crashes). The column intox_any is 1 when the driver was intoxicated and 0 when not.
Copy this line into your script and run it. It labels each crash in words, so every later result reads “Intoxicated” and “Sober” instead of 1 and 0:
crashes <- crashes |> mutate(intox = if_else(intox_any == 1, "Intoxicated", "Sober"))
Count the two groups with crashes |> count(intox). In a comment: how many crashes are in each group? You will type these two numbers into prop.test() in Part 5.

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 2: Point Estimates and Spread

Get the mean and standard deviation of injuries for each group in one table:
crashes |>
  summarize(mean_injuries = mean(injuries), sd_injuries = sd(injuries), n = n(), .by = intox) |>
  arrange(intox)
In a comment: write down each mean. Which group has the higher average injury count? Remember what these numbers are — point estimates, not the final word.
In a comment: compare the two standard deviations. Which group’s injury counts vary more?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 3: Visualize

Make a boxplot of injuries for the two groups:
ggplot(crashes, aes(x = intox, y = injuries)) +
  geom_boxplot()
In a comment: interpret the plot. Injury counts are small whole numbers, so the boxes look blocky — can you see a difference between the groups, or do you need inference to settle it?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 4: The Interval, with t.test()

Run the two-sample t-test, exactly as in Lab 5:
t.test(injuries ~ intox, data = crashes)
In a comment: copy down the 95% confidence interval. Does it include 0? Then do the direction check from lab: the output lists Intoxicated first, so the interval is Intoxicated minus Sober. Confirm that its sign agrees with the two group means at the bottom of the output.
In a comment: say what the interval means in words, the way we did in class: about how many more (or fewer) injuries per crash, and does the data settle the direction?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Part 5: A Proportion, for Practice

Compute a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all crashes that involve an intoxicated driver. Type the two numbers from your Part 1 count into prop.test(): how many intoxicated, out of how many crashes.
In a comment: report the interval in one defensible sentence — one that would survive the “Saying It Out Loud” slide from class.

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
Wrap-Up Questions (answer in comments)

How does the confidence interval help us make an inference about the population of Alaska crashes, when we only ever see a sample?
What would happen to the width of the CI if we doubled the sample size? Why?
How does this example compare to John Snow’s inference about the cholera pumps?

title: Homework 5 · Confidence Intervals in Practice
text:
R4DS Exercises (required)
From your R4DS reading for Session 6 — Ch. 16, Factors. No new packages: the gss_cat survey data ships with the tidyverse. All four exercises are about one idea from today: the order of the groups is a choice you make, not something R knows.
Work these in the same .R script, under a # ---- R4DS ---- header.

16.3.1 #2 — what is the most common relig in this survey? The most common partyid? (count() and arrange() will do it.)
16.3.1 #1 — make the default bar chart of rincome. What makes it hard to read? How could you improve it? (Hint: the two problems are the overlapping labels and the order of the levels. aes(y = rincome) fixes the first one.)
16.4.1 #2 — for each of the six factor columns in gss_cat (marital, race, rincome, partyid, relig, denom), is the order of the levels arbitrary or principled? One comment line each. count() the column, or run levels() on it, to see the order.
16.5.1 #2 — collapse rincome into a small set of categories. Start from this, which runs as-is:
gss_cat |>
  mutate(rincome2 = fct_collapse(rincome,
    "Unknown"       = c("No answer", "Don't know", "Refused", "Not applicable"),
    "Under $10,000" = c("Lt $1000", "$1000 to 2999", "$3000 to 3999", "$4000 to 4999",
                        "$5000 to 5999", "$6000 to 6999", "$7000 to 7999", "$8000 to 9999")
  )) |>
  count(rincome2)
Then add the four remaining bands ("$10000 - 14999", "$15000 - 19999", "$20000 - 24999", "$25000 or more") into one or two groups of your choosing, and run count() again.

Chapter 16 has more exercises than these. Skip them; these four are the ones worth your time.

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Instructions: complete the following exercises in a single .R script file. Include comments explaining your code and answers to any interpretive questions. Submit your .R file via Canvas for credit.
Parts 1–3 use the built-in mtcars dataset (type mtcars in the console — it’s always available, no loading needed).

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 1: Contingency Tables

Create a contingency table of mtcars showing the number of cars by number of cylinders (cyl) and number of gears (gear). Use either the classic table(mtcars$cyl, mtcars$gear) or the tidyverse route from Lab 3:
library(tidyverse)
mtcars |>
  count(cyl, gear) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = gear, values_from = n)
How many cars have 4 cylinders and 4 gears?
What is the probability that a randomly selected car (out of all 32) has both 4 gears and 6 cylinders? (This is a joint probability — divide the cell count by the grand total, not by a row or column total.)
What is the probability that a randomly selected car has 6 cylinders? (A marginal probability.)

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 2: Conditional Probability

What is the conditional probability that a car has 6 cylinders given that it has 4 gears? Compute it in R (not by eye) — e.g., filter() to the condition and take a proportion, or divide the right counts.
Interpretation (in a comment): your answers to Q3 and Q5 use the same cell of the table but give different numbers. Explain in one or two sentences why — what changed between the two questions?

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 3: Visualizing Distributions

Create a bar plot showing the distribution of cylinders.
Create a bar plot showing the distribution of gears.
Create a grouped bar plot of the number of cars by cyl and gear. You may use ggplot (geom_bar(position = "dodge") — remember to make the grouping variable a factor) or base R’s barplot(..., beside = TRUE) — your choice.

title: Homework 3 · Probability and Conditional Thinking
text:
Part 4: R4DS Exercises (required)
From your R4DS reading for Session 4 — Ch. 5, Data tidying. No new packages; table1–table3 ship with the tidyverse.
Work these in the same .R script, under a # ---- R4DS ---- header.

5.2.1 #1 — for table1, table2, and table3: what is one row, and what is one column? (Answer in comments.)
5.2.1 #2 — sketch the steps you’d take to compute a rate. You are not expected to write working code yet; name the moves in comments.
Ch. 5 has only this one exercise block — the pivot_longer()/pivot_wider() sections have no exercises at all, so these two are the whole set.

title: Final Project
text: The final project integrates conceptual understanding with applied statistical skills in R. You will identify a research question, analyze a real criminal justice dataset, and interpret your findings using the tools from this course: building it incrementally across the second half of the semester rather than in a December scramble.

title: Final Project
text:
1. Purpose
Demonstrate your ability to apply statistical reasoning and R coding skills to a real-world criminal justice dataset: identify a research question, analyze data, and interpret findings using the concepts learned throughout the course.

title: Final Project
text:
2. Project components
Your submission must include all of the following:

R script (.R): fully runnable code that produces your results
Your dataset: submitted so I can reproduce your analysis
Output: tables, figures, and statistical output from R, as applicable, incorporated in your written report
Written report (.docx): a short report (3 to 5 pages) explaining your research question, dataset, methods, results, and interpretation

title: Final Project
text:
3. Steps and expectations
Step 1: Find a dataset. Select a dataset related to criminal justice (policing, courts, corrections, crime, public opinion, etc.) that can be imported into R (CSV, Excel, or an R dataset). It must include enough numeric variables for regression analysis. Start with the Final-Project Data Options: any dataset there is eligible, including the ones we work in Session 7, as long as your question goes beyond what we did in class. A dataset from somewhere else is welcome once I have cleared it; the course practice datasets are not eligible. (Formal selection criteria are part of the Session 7 assignment.)
Step 2: Define your research question. Keep it focused and testable. Examples: “Are violent crime rates associated with police staffing levels?” or “Do education and income predict victimization (or arrests)?”
Step 3: Apply statistical tools from class. Use descriptive statistics, visualizations, and measures of association. You must include a linear regression or logistic regression for credit. Your final model must be reported in both traditions: the frequentist fit (lm()/glm()) and the Bayesian fit (brm(); default priors are fine, but say so), with at least one sentence comparing what each tells you (e.g., the CI vs. the credible interval, or what the posterior lets you say that the p-value doesn’t). This is the both-traditions course; the capstone shows you can drive both. Supporting analyses (descriptives, correlations) may be run in whichever tradition you prefer.
Step 4: Write and submit your report. Organize clearly: Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion. Interpret results in plain language.

title: Final Project
text:
4. Grading criteria
The project is 30% of your course grade: the written report, script, and output are 22%, and the in-class presentation is 8%.

The written report & code (22% of course grade)










Criterion
Weight
Excellent
Adequate
Needs work




Quality of analysis
7%
Right tools for the question; final model in both traditions with sound model choices; assumptions/diagnostics addressed
Correct core analysis; both traditions present but one is perfunctory; minor tool misfits
Wrong tool for the question, a missing tradition, or mechanical errors that change conclusions


Interpretation & honesty
6%
Every claim matches the output; magnitude interpreted in real units; limitations (incl. null or weak results) owned plainly
Mostly accurate; occasional overclaiming or a p-value/posterior misreading; limitations thin
“Significant” treated as “important”; causal language from observational data; results oversold


Organization & writing
4%
Clear Introduction → Methods → Results → Discussion; labeled figures/tables referenced in text; graduate-level prose
Structure present but uneven; figures unlabeled or orphaned
Hard to follow; output pasted without narrative


Completeness & reproducibility
5%
Script runs top to bottom on the submitted data; all four components present; seed set where results are sampled
Runs with minor fixes; a component thin but present
Script errors out, data missing, or a required component absent





The presentation (8% of course grade)
Format: 8 minutes + 2 minutes of questions. Presentation order is announced at the Session 11 code clinic. You may present slides or your rendered report on screen: either is fine, but you must show your one key visualization and be ready to walk through any line of your code on request (see the AI policy; not being able to explain your own code will cost you well beyond the presentation points).








Criterion

What earns it

A listener knows within a minute what you asked, of what data, and why anyone should care

Findings stated accurately with magnitudes; at least one limitation named without prompting; questions handled honestly (including “I don’t know”)
