title: The Chicago Anchor Dataset
section: Important caveats — we will return to these all semester
text:
Important caveats — we will return to these all semester

Reported crime only. These data reflect crimes reported to and recorded by CPD — not all crime that occurred. Reporting rates differ across offense types and communities.
An arrest is not a conviction, and arrest_rate reflects incident clearance patterns, not “guilt rates.”
The ACS measures are survey estimates with sampling error, larger for smaller areas.
Aggregate (community-level) associations do not license conclusions about individuals — we’ll name this properly (the ecological fallacy) when we get to correlation.

title: The Chicago Anchor Dataset
text:
Provenance
Snapshot pulled July 2026; build script archived in the course repository (R/build-anchor-dataset.R) so the dataset is exactly reproducible. Sources: Chicago Data Portal, Crimes 2001–present (dataset ijzp-q8t2) and CMAP Community Data Snapshots 2026 (CCA table).

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
text: What this page is. The Session 1 lecture demos, written down step by step. Every chunk below is self-contained — copy any of them into your own R session and they run as-is. Use this page to catch up after a missed class, or to re-run what happened on screen at your own pace.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
text:
What you’ll build

Your first R commands: arithmetic, vectors, and the functions you’ll use all semester
Logical indexing — asking a vector a question and keeping only the rows that say yes
Factors, R’s container for categorical data
The “scale determines the math” demos: why a mean zone is nonsense, and why °C and age play by different rules
The 2×2 of plots that match each level of measurement
A five-verb dplyr tour, and a first look at the real Chicago data we’ll use all semester

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
text:
Setup
Everything below needs the tidyverse, plus patchwork for one plot-arranging trick near the end (install.packages("patchwork") once, if you don’t have it):

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(705)

crimes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-crimes-2025.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
section: The case study: catching a bank robber
text:
The case study: catching a bank robber
Session 1 opened with a serial offender hitting 40 banks across a city’s five zones, and a police department with nothing to go on but when and where each robbery happened. A crime analyst turned that thin dataset into a logistic regression predicting which zone would be hit next; the model pointed to the West Zone, units were deployed there, and the robber was arrested days later approaching a bank. The animated timeline, map, and deployment visuals are built with tools from later in the course — watch them in the Session 1 slides; by Session 12 you’ll be able to build the model yourself.
One more thing worth naming: you already reasoned like a Bayesian while watching that story. You started with a vague hunch spread across five zones (a prior), treated each new robbery as evidence that reshaped the hunch, read the model’s risk-by-zone output as an updated belief given the data, and then made a deployment decision under quantified uncertainty. That whole loop has a formal name — Bayesian updating. The formula shows up in Session 3, and the full machinery in Session 6, side by side with the other great tradition, the frequentist one.
The rest of this page is the part of Session 1 you can run right now: your first R commands, and the levels-of-measurement demos.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
section: 1 · Arithmetic, assignment, and your first functions
text:
1 · Arithmetic, assignment, and your first functions
R is a calculator first:

3 + 5

[1] 8


The arrow <- assigns a value to a name. 1:10 builds the vector 1, 2, 3, …, 10, and functions like sum(), mean(), and sd() eat whole vectors at once:

x <- 1:10
sum(x); mean(x); sd(x)

[1] 55


[1] 5.5


[1] 3.02765


Every function has a help page — get in the habit of pulling them up constantly:

?mean

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
section: 2 · Logical indexing — ask the data a question
text:
2 · Logical indexing — ask the data a question
Comparing a vector to a value asks the question element by element:

x > 5

 [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE


Put that question inside square brackets and R keeps only the values that answered TRUE:

x[x > 5]

[1]  6  7  8  9 10


This one move — build a logical test, use it to subset — is the ancestor of every filter() you’ll ever write.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
text:
3 · Characters and factors
Text lives in character vectors; categories that will be analyzed belong in factors, which know their full set of possible levels:

student_names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol")
is.character(student_names)

[1] TRUE

f <- factor(c("red", "blue", "red"))
f

[1] red  blue red 
Levels: blue red


Notice the printout: a factor reports its Levels — the categories that exist, whether or not each one appears in this particular vector.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
text:
4 · Scale determines the math
Session 1’s central claim: a variable’s level of measurement (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio) determines what math is allowed. To demonstrate, simulate a small robbery-style dataset with one variable at each level:

set.seed(58)   # same seed as the lecture, so these numbers match the slides
rob <- tibble(
  zone = factor(sample(c("North", "South", "East", "West", "Downtown"), 200, TRUE)),
  prior_robberies_in_zone = rpois(200, 3),    # discrete count (ratio)
  risk_likert = sample(1:7, 200, TRUE),       # ordinal
  temp_c = rnorm(200, 20, 5),                 # interval
  age = pmax(18, round(rnorm(200, 40, 12))),  # ratio
  caught = factor(rbinom(200, 1, 0.35), labels = c("No", "Yes"))
)

Nominal: the “mean zone” is meaningless
R will happily convert factor levels to their underlying codes and average them. That doesn’t make the answer mean anything:

# WRONG: the "mean zone" is meaningless
rob$zone |> as.numeric() |> mean()

[1] 3.17


3.17 of… what? Zone 3.17 doesn’t exist — the numbers are just labels in disguise. The right math for nominal data is counts and percentages:

# RIGHT: counts and percentages
rob |>
  count(zone) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  zone         n   pct
  <fct>    <int> <dbl>
1 Downtown    32  16  
2 East        28  14  
3 North       59  29.5
4 South       36  18  
5 West        45  22.5


Ordinal: order yes, arithmetic no
A 1–7 risk rating is ordered, but the gaps between points aren’t guaranteed equal — so summarize with the median and IQR, and measure association with a rank-based (Spearman) correlation:

rob |>
  summarize(med = median(risk_likert), iqr = IQR(risk_likert))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
    med   iqr
  <dbl> <dbl>
1     4     3

cor(rob$risk_likert, rob$prior_robberies_in_zone, method = "spearman")

[1] 0.001707403


(That correlation is essentially zero — as it should be, since we simulated these two variables independently. A good sanity check.)
Interval vs. ratio: the true-zero test
Temperature in °C is interval: differences are meaningful, but there’s no true zero — 0 °C is just where water freezes. Watch what unit conversion does to the mean:

mean(rob$temp_c)             # about 20 °C

[1] 20.07643

mean(rob$temp_c * 1.8 + 32)  # the same temperatures, in °F

[1] 68.13757


Same warmth, different number. “30 °C is 10 °C warmer than 20 °C” is fine; “20 °C is twice as hot as 10 °C” is meaningless — the ratio depends on which scale you happen to be using.

mean(rob$age)

[1] 40.605


Age is ratio: it has a true zero, so a 40-year-old really is twice as old as a 20-year-old. Differences and ratios both work.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
text:
5 · Plots that match the scale
The same logic governs graphics. One plot per level of measurement, arranged in a 2×2 with patchwork (p1 + p2 puts plots side by side; / stacks rows):

p1 <- ggplot(rob, aes(zone)) + geom_bar(fill = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "Nominal: bar chart", x = NULL)
p2 <- ggplot(rob, aes(factor(risk_likert, levels = 1:7))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "navy") +
  labs(title = "Ordinal: ordered bars", x = "Risk (1–7)")
p3 <- ggplot(rob, aes(age)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Continuous (ratio): histogram")
p4 <- ggplot(rob, aes(prior_robberies_in_zone)) + geom_bar(fill = "goldenrod") +
  labs(title = "Discrete counts: bars", x = "Prior robberies")

(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)







Categories get bars; continuous measurements get histograms; discrete counts get one bar per whole number. If you ever catch yourself histogramming a nominal variable, stop and check the scale.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
section: 6 · Five dplyr verbs you’ll use every week
text:
6 · Five dplyr verbs you’ll use every week
The tidyverse works on tibbles (modern data frames). The |> symbol is the pipe: x |> f() means f(x) — “take x, then do f.” (Older code, including the Stanton book, writes it %>%; they work the same for everything we do.)

cars_data <- as_tibble(mtcars, rownames = "model")
head(cars_data, 4)

# A tibble: 4 × 12
  model          mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb
  <chr>        <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Mazda RX4     21       6   160   110  3.9   2.62  16.5     0     1     4     4
2 Mazda RX4 W…  21       6   160   110  3.9   2.88  17.0     0     1     4     4
3 Datsun 710    22.8     4   108    93  3.85  2.32  18.6     1     1     4     1
4 Hornet 4 Dr…  21.4     6   258   110  3.08  3.22  19.4     1     0     3     1


select() picks columns; filter() picks rows:

cars_data |> select(model, mpg, cyl, hp) |> head(4)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  model            mpg   cyl    hp
  <chr>          <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Mazda RX4       21       6   110
2 Mazda RX4 Wag   21       6   110
3 Datsun 710      22.8     4    93
4 Hornet 4 Drive  21.4     6   110

cars_data |> filter(cyl == 6) |> head(4)

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
section: 7 · Coming attractions: real data, all semester
text:
7 · Coming attractions: real data, all semester
Starting in Session 2, the running example is real: a 30,000-incident sample of every crime reported in Chicago in 2025 (already loaded in Setup). Here’s the count-and-bar-chart pattern from this session, applied to it:

crimes |>
  count(primary_type, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(primary_type, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "Ten most common reported crimes, Chicago 2025",
       subtitle = "30,000-incident sample · Chicago Police Department data portal",
       x = "Incidents", y = NULL)







Theft tops the list at about 7,000 incidents. And note what kind of variable primary_type is — nominal — which is exactly why this is a bar chart and not a histogram.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 1
text:
Try a variation

Build a vector of seven ages with c(). Compute the mean and SD, subset the values over 30, then use ?seq to figure out how to generate seq(0, 1, by = 0.2).
Using the built-in mpg data (type mpg in the console — ggplot2 ships it), find the top-3 models by hwy and the average cty by class. (Hints: arrange(desc(...)), slice_head(), summarize(..., .by = ...).)

In the Chicago chunk, swap primary_type for location_description. Where does crime actually happen in Chicago?
The ordinal trap: run educ <- rep(1:5, each = 50) and income <- rep(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 1000), each = 50), then cor(educ, income). Pearson’s r looks impressive — why is it misleading here? (Hint: are the education codes equally spaced in any real sense?)

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
text: What this page is. The Session 3 lecture demos, written down step by step. Every chunk below is self-contained — copy any of them into your own R session and they run as-is. Use this page to catch up after a missed class, or to re-run what happened on screen at your own pace.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
text:
What you’ll build

A demonstration that a probability is a long-run proportion — on coins, then on 30,000 real Chicago incidents
The binomial distribution, discovered by simulation before you ever see dbinom()

Contingency tables: joint, marginal, and conditional probability on real data
The conditioning move — shrink the world, re-proportion — run in both directions
Bayes’ theorem as a counting exercise, and a simulation that proves the surprising answer

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
text:
Setup
Everything below needs only the tidyverse and the course’s anchor dataset:

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(705)

crimes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-crimes-2025.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
section: 1 · A probability is a long-run proportion
text:
1 · A probability is a long-run proportion
The claim: a fair coin lands heads with probability 0.5. Don’t take it on faith — flip:

flips <- sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10, replace = TRUE)
flips

 [1] "heads" "heads" "heads" "tails" "tails" "tails" "heads" "tails" "heads"
[10] "heads"

mean(flips == "heads")

[1] 0.6


Ten flips bounce around. replicate() repeats the whole recipe — here, six more batches of ten:

replicate(6, mean(sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10, replace = TRUE) == "heads"))

[1] 0.6 0.1 0.5 0.6 0.6 0.7


None of the batches is entitled to land exactly on 0.5. Now watch what happens as the run gets long:

lln <- tibble(flip = sample(c(1, 0), size = 100000, replace = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(n_flips = row_number(),
         running_prop = cummean(flip))

ggplot(lln, aes(n_flips, running_prop)) +
  geom_line(color = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "The long run pins the proportion to 0.5",
       x = "Number of flips (log scale)", y = "Running proportion of heads")







Wobbly early, pinned eventually. A probability is the value the long-run proportion settles on.
The same thing, on real data
Each of the 30,000 Chicago incidents either ended in arrest or didn’t — 30,000 recorded trials:

mean(crimes$arrest)

[1] 0.1608


(arrest is TRUE/FALSE; mean() of a logical is the proportion of TRUEs — you’ll use this trick constantly.) And the long run works here too — read case files one at a time, tracking the running proportion:

running <- tibble(arrest = sample(crimes$arrest, size = 5000)) |>
  mutate(n_cases = row_number(),
         running_prop = cummean(arrest))

ggplot(running, aes(n_cases, running_prop)) +
  geom_line(color = "navy") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Small samples lie; long runs don't",
       x = "Case files read (log scale)", y = "Running proportion arrested")

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
text:
2 · The binomial, discovered by simulation
Session 3’s toast restaurant: each dropped order is six pieces of toast, each landing topping-down or topping-up. rbinom() compresses “drop six pieces and count the downs” into one call — here are 100 dropped orders:

drops <- rbinom(n = 100, size = 6, prob = 0.5)
tibble(jelly_down = drops) |> count(jelly_down)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  jelly_down     n
       <int> <int>
1          0     1
2          1     8
3          2    23
4          3    32
5          4    22
6          5    13
7          6     1


Run it again and the counts change — that’s sampling variability, and 100 trials is a shortish run. So make the run long, and compare against the theoretical binomial probabilities:

tibble(jelly_down = rbinom(n = 100000, size = 6, prob = 0.5)) |>
  count(jelly_down) |>
  mutate(
    simulated   = n / sum(n),
    theoretical = dbinom(jelly_down, size = 6, prob = 0.5)
  )

# A tibble: 7 × 4
  jelly_down     n simulated theoretical
       <int> <int>     <dbl>       <dbl>
1          0  1543    0.0154      0.0156
2          1  9645    0.0964      0.0937
3          2 23336    0.233       0.234 
4          3 31036    0.310       0.312 
5          4 23365    0.234       0.234 
6          5  9425    0.0942      0.0937
7          6  1650    0.0165      0.0156


At 100,000 trials the two columns agree to within a few thousandths. Theory is the long run; simulation is how we watch the long run.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
text:
3 · Contingency tables on real data
Two classifications per incident — crime category and arrest — cross-counted:

crimes |>
  count(crime_category, arrest) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = arrest, values_from = n)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category `FALSE` `TRUE`
  <chr>            <int>  <int>
1 Other             7867   2614
2 Property          9615    756
3 Violent           7694   1454


Joint probability: divide every cell by the grand total.

crimes |>
  count(crime_category, arrest) |>
  mutate(p = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  crime_category arrest     n      p
  <chr>          <lgl>  <int>  <dbl>
1 Other          FALSE   7867 0.262 
2 Other          TRUE    2614 0.0871
3 Property       FALSE   9615 0.320 
4 Property       TRUE     756 0.0252
5 Violent        FALSE   7694 0.256 
6 Violent        TRUE    1454 0.0485


Marginal probability: collapse one classification.

crimes |> count(crime_category) |> mutate(p = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category     n     p
  <chr>          <int> <dbl>
1 Other          10481 0.349
2 Property       10371 0.346
3 Violent         9148 0.305

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
text:
4 · Conditioning: shrink the world, re-proportion
The lecture’s restaurant work schedule, computed live. The question “Bill is your server — what day is it?” rules out every other server, so: isolate Bill’s column, re-scale it to sum to 1.

hours <- tribble(
  ~day,        ~Anne, ~Bill, ~Calvin, ~Devon,
  "Monday",        6,     0,       5,      8,
  "Tuesday",       0,     6,       6,      0,
  "Wednesday",     8,     5,       0,      8,
  "Thursday",      4,     6,       5,      8,
  "Friday",        8,     8,       5,      8,
  "Saturday",      8,    10,       8,      8,
  "Sunday",        0,     3,       6,      0
)
hours_long <- hours |> pivot_longer(-day, names_to = "server", values_to = "hours")

hours_long |>
  filter(server == "Bill") |>
  mutate(p_day_given_bill = hours / sum(hours)) |>
  arrange(desc(p_day_given_bill))

# A tibble: 7 × 4
  day       server hours p_day_given_bill
  <chr>     <chr>  <dbl>            <dbl>
1 Saturday  Bill      10           0.263 
2 Friday    Bill       8           0.211 
3 Tuesday   Bill       6           0.158 
4 Thursday  Bill       6           0.158 
5 Wednesday Bill       5           0.132 
6 Sunday    Bill       3           0.0789
7 Monday    Bill       0           0     


Same move, other direction — “it’s Monday; who’s serving?”:

hours_long |>
  filter(day == "Monday") |>
  mutate(p_server_given_monday = hours / sum(hours))

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  day    server hours p_server_given_monday
  <chr>  <chr>  <dbl>                 <dbl>
1 Monday Anne       6                 0.316
2 Monday Bill       0                 0    
3 Monday Calvin     5                 0.263
4 Monday Devon      8                 0.421


Note the asymmetry: P(Saturday | Bill) and P(Bill | Saturday) are different questions with different answers. Hold that thought — it’s the whole reason Bayes’ theorem exists.
On real data, conditioning is just subset, then mean


crimes |>
  summarize(p_arrest = mean(arrest), n = n(), .by = crime_category)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  crime_category p_arrest     n
  <chr>             <dbl> <int>
1 Violent          0.159   9148
2 Other            0.249  10481
3 Property         0.0729 10371


Knowing the category moves the arrest probability → the variables are dependent. And the famous trap:

crimes |>
  filter(primary_type == "NARCOTICS") |>
  summarize(p_arrest = mean(arrest), n = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  p_arrest     n
     <dbl> <int>
1    0.971   919


Is Chicago spectacular at solving drug crimes? No — a narcotics record usually exists because someone was arrested. Conditional probabilities describe the data-generating process, not just the world.
Independence is what it looks like when conditioning doesn’t move the number:

mean(crimes$arrest)

[1] 0.1608

crimes |>
  summarize(p_arrest = mean(arrest), n = n(), .by = domestic)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  domestic p_arrest     n
  <lgl>       <dbl> <int>
1 FALSE       0.161 24194
2 TRUE        0.160  5806

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
section: 5 · Bayes’ theorem: count it out, then simulate it
text:
5 · Bayes’ theorem: count it out, then simulate it
The Ianfluenza screening problem: prevalence 1%, sensitivity .90, specificity .95. The brochure advertises P(test + | sick) = .90. You, in the exam room, want the reversed conditional: P(sick | test +). Count 1,000 people:

tribble(
  ~status,    ~test_pos, ~test_neg, ~total,
  "Sick",             9,         1,     10,
  "Healthy",         50,       940,    990,
  "Total",           59,       941,   1000
)

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  status  test_pos test_neg total
  <chr>      <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 Sick           9        1    10
2 Healthy       50      940   990
3 Total         59      941  1000

9 / (9 + 50)   # P(sick | test +)

[1] 0.1525424


About 15% — because the false alarms from the huge healthy pool swamp the true positives. If that seems impossible, apply Session 3’s rule: don’t take a probability claim on faith — simulate it and watch it happen.

sim <- tibble(
  sick = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), size = 100000, replace = TRUE,
                prob = c(0.01, 0.99))
) |>
  mutate(
    test_pos = if_else(
      sick,
      sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), size = 100000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.90, 0.10)),
      sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), size = 100000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.95))
    )
  )

sim |>
  filter(test_pos) |>
  summarize(p_sick_given_pos = mean(sick), n_positive = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  p_sick_given_pos n_positive
             <dbl>      <int>
1            0.158       5869


100,000 simulated patients, filter to the positives, take the mean — the long run lands right on the counting-table answer. The base rate is never optional.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 3
text:
Try a variation

In the long-run arrest plot, change size = 5000 to size = 200. How wrong can the early running proportion be?
Re-run the binomial convergence with prob = 0.7 (a biased toast-dropper). Which outcome becomes most common?
In the screening simulation, raise the prevalence from 0.01 to 0.20 (a high-risk clinic). What happens to P(sick | +)? (This is the entire “priors matter” lesson in one edit.)

Find a primary_type where P(arrest | type) is lower than the overall arrest rate. What might that say about how those records enter the data?

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text: What this page is. The Session 5 lecture demos, written down step by step. Every chunk below is self-contained — copy any of them into your own R session and they run as-is. Use this page to catch up after a missed class, or to re-run what happened on screen at your own pace.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
What you’ll build

John Snow’s 1854 cholera inference, recomputed from his original data — the classic example of reasoning from a sample to the world
A demonstration that point estimates fluctuate: 1,000 samples from a population whose truth we secretly know
A 95% confidence interval from prop.test(), and the 100-intervals plot — the picture that shows what “95% confident” actually means
Sentences you can and cannot say when reporting an interval
How sample size buys precision, and a CI for a two-group difference with t.test() — including what it looks like when an interval does, and does not, cross zero

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
Setup
Three packages today: the tidyverse; HistData, which ships John Snow’s original cholera data (Snow.deaths and Snow.pumps); and patchwork, which puts two plots side by side:

library(tidyverse)
library(HistData)    # install.packages("HistData")   — once, if you don't have it
library(patchwork)   # install.packages("patchwork")  — once, if you don't have it
set.seed(705)

crimes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-crimes-2025.csv",
                   show_col_types = FALSE)

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
1 · Inference, in 1854
Cholera breaks out in Soho, London. The debate: bad air (“miasma”) or contaminated water? John Snow couldn’t test every household in London — that’s the whole population. So he mapped the sample of evidence he could get: deaths, and where people drew their water.
We can rerun his reasoning. For each of the 578 recorded deaths, find the nearest pump. Two verbs arrive ahead of schedule here — crossing() builds every death–pump pair, and left_join() looks up each point’s coordinates. Joins get their full treatment in next week’s lab; today, read them as “pair up, then look up” and focus on the logic:

deaths <- as_tibble(Snow.deaths)
pumps  <- as_tibble(Snow.pumps)

pairs <- crossing(case = deaths$case, pump = pumps$pump) |>
  left_join(deaths |> select(case, dx = x, dy = y), by = "case") |>
  left_join(pumps  |> select(pump, label, px = x, py = y), by = "pump") |>
  mutate(dist = sqrt((dx - px)^2 + (dy - py)^2))

nearest <- pairs |>
  slice_min(dist, n = 1, by = case)

nearest |>
  count(label, name = "deaths_nearest") |>
  arrange(desc(deaths_nearest))

# A tibble: 12 × 2
   label          deaths_nearest
   <chr>                   <int>
 1 Broad St                  359
 2 So Soho                    64
 3 Crown Chapel               61
 4 Briddle St                 27
 5 Oxford St #2               24
 6 Warwick                    16
 7 Oxford St #1               12
 8 Gt Marlborough              6
 9 Vigo St                     4
10 Coventry St                 2
11 Dean St                     2
12 Castle St E                 1


One pump — Broad St — is the nearest pump for 359 of the 578 deaths. Seen on the map:

broad <- pumps |> filter(label == "Broad St")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = deaths, aes(x, y), color = "firebrick", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = pumps, aes(x, y), color = "navy", size = 3, shape = 17) +
  # the Broad St pump gets a gold triangle instead of a label, so nothing covers the deaths
  geom_point(data = broad, aes(x, y), fill = "gold", color = "navy", size = 5, shape = 24) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Cholera deaths cluster around a single pump",
       subtitle = "Red dots = deaths · navy triangles = water pumps · gold = the Broad St pump",
       x = NULL, y = NULL)







Snow wasn’t just describing this map — he was making a bigger claim about the whole city, and about cholera itself. That jump — from the data you have to the world you don’t — is what we mean by inference. And the fine print from lecture: you cannot PROVE anything from samples. We collect data and analyze it to build up a weight of evidence that shifts our certainty toward one conclusion or another.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
section: 2 · A rare luxury: we know the truth
text:
2 · A rare luxury: we know the truth
Our Chicago file holds ~30,000 incidents from 2025. Today, pretend the file is the whole population — then we can check every inference against the truth:

crimes |> summarize(pop_arrest_rate = mean(arrest), n = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  pop_arrest_rate     n
            <dbl> <int>
1           0.161 30000


The “true” citywide arrest proportion is 16.1%. Lock that in — in real research you never get to see this number.
Now act like a researcher who can only afford to pull 250 case files:

sample_250 <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = 250)

sample_250 |> summarize(sample_arrest_rate = mean(arrest))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  sample_arrest_rate
               <dbl>
1              0.148


This is a point estimate — the sample’s best single guess at the population value. About 14.8% versus the true 16.1%. Close-ish. But how good is this estimate? How certain are we?

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
3 · Caution! Samples fluctuate
Draw a fresh sample of 250 and the estimate moves. Do it 1,000 times:

many_estimates <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) {
  crimes |> slice_sample(n = 250) |> summarize(p = mean(arrest)) |> pull(p)
})

ggplot(tibble(p = many_estimates), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "1,000 sample estimates of the arrest rate (n = 250 each)",
       subtitle = "Red line = the true population value",
       x = "Sample arrest proportion", y = "Number of samples")







That’s Session 4’s sampling distribution, live. Where did the middle 95% of estimates land?

quantile(many_estimates, c(0.025, 0.975))

 2.5% 97.5% 
0.120 0.208 


Roughly 12% to 21% — any single sample’s estimate could easily be a couple points off the truth. So reporting “14.8%” alone is overconfident; we owe our reader a range that reflects the fluctuation. Problem: this exercise required 1,000 samples and a known population. A real researcher has one sample. Now what?

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
4 · The confidence interval
The confidence interval turns one sample into an honest range, using what Session 4 taught us about how sample statistics behave:
\[\text{estimate} \; \pm \; \underbrace{1.96 \times SE}_{\text{margin of error}}\]
The SE (standard error) is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution, estimated from the one sample you have; 1.96 comes from the normal distribution — ±1.96 SDs covers the middle 95%. R does the whole thing for us:

prop.test(sum(sample_250$arrest), n = 250)


    1-sample proportions test with continuity correction

data:  sum(sample_250$arrest) out of 250, null probability 0.5
X-squared = 122.5, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1075899 0.1995409
sample estimates:
    p 
0.148 


Our one sample of 250 says: point estimate 14.8%, 95% CI 10.8% to 20.0%. The true value (16.1%) is inside — this time. But “95% confident” of what, exactly?

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
5 · The classic picture: 100 samples, 100 intervals
Draw 100 samples; build a 95% CI from each. (map() runs the procedure 100 times and list_rbind() stacks the 100 one-row results into one tibble — Session 3’s replicate(), tibble-flavored; see the simulation verbs reference.)

ci_100 <- map(1:100, \(i) {
  s  <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = 250)
  ci <- prop.test(sum(s$arrest), n = 250)$conf.int
  tibble(sample = i, estimate = mean(s$arrest), lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2])
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(captured = lo <= mean(crimes$arrest) & mean(crimes$arrest) <= hi)

sum(ci_100$captured)   # how many of the 100 intervals caught the truth?

[1] 97



ggplot(ci_100, aes(sample, estimate, color = captured)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), color = "grey30", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = 0.7, size = 0.25) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "grey65", "FALSE" = "firebrick")) +
  labs(title = paste0("100 samples, 100 confidence intervals — ",
                      sum(ci_100$captured), " capture the truth"),
       subtitle = "Horizontal line = true population arrest rate; red = intervals that missed",
       x = "Sample number", y = "Arrest proportion", color = "Captured?")







In plain language: each vertical bar is one research team’s interval, the truth never moves, and about 95 of 100 intervals catch it. Each sample produced a different interval — the interval is a random quantity; the population value is fixed. In our run, 97 of 100 captured the truth. The teams who drew the red samples did nothing wrong — and their data give no warning that theirs are the unlucky intervals.
That long-run capture rate is the entire meaning of “95% confident”: if we reran the whole study many times, in 95% of those replications the interval would contain the true value. Three things follow:

Our 95% CI does not necessarily contain the true population value
Our 95% CI is not a statement about the probability that this particular interval is correct
It is a long-run prediction based on numerous replications

(Everyone reacts to this with some version of “WTF?!?” — so run it again, slower.)
Run it again: 100 new researchers
New samples, new intervals. This time look at them first without the truth line, the way each of the 100 researchers would:

set.seed(1854)   # a local seed, so this figure is the same every time it renders
ci_100b <- map(1:100, \(i) {
  s  <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = 250)
  ci <- prop.test(sum(s$arrest), n = 250)$conf.int
  tibble(sample = i, estimate = mean(s$arrest), lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2])
}) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(captured = lo <= mean(crimes$arrest) & mean(crimes$arrest) <= hi)

y_lims <- range(c(ci_100b$lo, ci_100b$hi))

ggplot(ci_100b, aes(sample, estimate)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.7, size = 0.25) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = y_lims) +
  labs(title = "100 new researchers, 100 new intervals: what each of them sees",
       subtitle = "No truth line yet. From inside any one study, every interval looks equally trustworthy",
       x = "Researcher", y = "Arrest proportion")







Now drop the truth in:

ggplot(ci_100b, aes(sample, estimate, color = captured)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), color = "grey30", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = 0.7, size = 0.25) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "grey65", "FALSE" = "firebrick")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = y_lims) +
  labs(title = paste0(sum(ci_100b$captured),
                      " of 100 caught it this time; the intervals moved, the truth did not"),
       subtitle = "Horizontal line = true population arrest rate; red = intervals that missed",
       x = "Researcher", y = "Arrest proportion", color = "Captured?")







The intervals moved; the truth did not; again about 95 of 100 caught it. Finally, pick two of those researchers — the first whose interval caught the truth and the first whose interval missed — and look at what each of them had in front of them (patchwork’s + puts the two plots side by side):

i_hit  <- which(ci_100b$captured)[1]
i_miss <- which(!ci_100b$captured)[1]
two <- ci_100b |>
  filter(sample %in% c(i_hit, i_miss)) |>
  mutate(who = paste0("Researcher ", sample))

left <- ggplot(two, aes(who, estimate)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), color = "grey40", linewidth = 1, size = 0.6) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = y_lims) +
  labs(title = "What the researchers see", x = NULL, y = "Arrest proportion")

right <- ggplot(two, aes(who, estimate, color = captured)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), color = "grey30", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = 1, size = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "grey65", "FALSE" = "firebrick")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = y_lims) +
  labs(title = "What only we can see", x = NULL, y = NULL)

left + right







You only ever get one stick, and nothing in your data tells you its color. That is why the 95% belongs to the procedure, not to your interval.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
6 · Saying it out loud
Defensible sentences:

“We estimate the citywide arrest rate at 14.8% (95% CI: 10.8% to 20.0%). Values in this range are consistent with our data.”


“The method we used captures the true value 95% of the time.”

Not defensible:

“There is a 95% probability the true arrest rate is between 10.8% and 20.0%.” — the truth is fixed; it’s either in there or it isn’t.


“95% of arrest rates fall in this interval.” — the CI is about the population parameter, not individual observations.

The forbidden first sentence is forbidden only under frequentist rules, where probability attaches to the procedure, never to the parameter. Attaching probability to a claim itself is exactly what Session 3’s Bayes’ theorem does — and next session we compute an interval you can say that sentence about: the credible interval. If the forbidden sentence felt like the natural reading all along, your intuitions were Bayesian. You’re in good company.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
7 · Sample size buys precision
Same procedure, four sample sizes, one draw each:

width_tbl <- map(c(100, 250, 1000, 4000), \(n) {
  s  <- crimes |> slice_sample(n = n)
  ci <- prop.test(sum(s$arrest), n = n)$conf.int
  tibble(n = n, estimate = mean(s$arrest),
         lo = ci[1], hi = ci[2], width = ci[2] - ci[1])
}) |>
  list_rbind()

width_tbl

# A tibble: 4 × 5
      n estimate     lo    hi  width
  <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1   100    0.12  0.0663 0.204 0.138 
2   250    0.184 0.139  0.239 0.0998
3  1000    0.165 0.143  0.190 0.0470
4  4000    0.167 0.155  0.179 0.0234


Quadrupling n roughly halves the width — precision grows with \(\sqrt{n}\), so it gets expensive fast. The same table as a picture:

ggplot(width_tbl, aes(factor(n), estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), color = "grey30", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), color = "navy", linewidth = 1, size = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(y = hi, label = sprintf("width %.3f", width)), vjust = -0.7, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.2))) +
  labs(title = "Same procedure, four sample sizes: the interval tightens as n grows",
       subtitle = "Horizontal line = the true arrest rate",
       x = "Sample size", y = "Arrest proportion")

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
section: 8 · Comparing two groups: do violent crimes happen later in the day?
text:
8 · Comparing two groups: do violent crimes happen later in the day?
Street lore says violence is a nighttime phenomenon; property crime, the daytime hustle. Our data:

vp <- crimes |>
  filter(crime_category %in% c("Violent", "Property")) |>
  mutate(crime_category = factor(crime_category, levels = c("Violent", "Property")))

vp |> summarize(mean_hour = mean(hour), sd_hour = sd(hour), n = n(), .by = crime_category)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  crime_category mean_hour sd_hour     n
  <fct>              <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
1 Violent             12.8    6.87  9148
2 Property            12.5    6.63 10371


One line we did not need before: factor(levels = ...) tells R which group comes first, so every subtraction below reads Violent minus Property. (R’s default is alphabetical, which would have put Property first and flipped every sign.) Two point estimates: violent crimes average about 12:48 pm (12.80 hours after midnight), property crimes about 12:33 pm (12.54). Is that 15-minute gap real, or sample fluctuation?

ggplot(vp, aes(crime_category, hour, fill = crime_category)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("firebrick", "steelblue")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24),
                     labels = c("midnight", "6 am", "noon", "6 pm", "midnight")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Time of day")







The boxes nearly coincide — the eye can’t settle this one. So resample: pull a bootstrap sample from each group (sample() with replace = TRUE draws a full-size resample), take each group’s mean, and difference them, 1,000 times:

set.seed(705)
violent_hours  <- vp$hour[vp$crime_category == "Violent"]
property_hours <- vp$hour[vp$crime_category == "Property"]

boot_violent  <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(violent_hours,  replace = TRUE)))
boot_property <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(property_hours, replace = TRUE)))
mean_diffs    <- boot_violent - boot_property

quantile(mean_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975)) * 60   # in minutes: Violent minus Property

     2.5%     97.5% 
 3.709722 26.345208 


The middle 95% of resampled differences (Violent minus Property) runs from about 4 to 26 minutes — all above zero. Here is what that looks like, and what “the interval does not cross zero” means. Two small helpers first: clock() turns hours-after-midnight into a clock time, and two_panel() draws the same pair of pictures for any two groups, so both examples below are built the same way:

clock <- function(h) {
  m  <- round(h * 60)
  hh <- (m %/% 60) %% 24
  mm <- m %% 60
  sprintf("%d:%02d %s", ifelse(hh %% 12 == 0, 12, hh %% 12), mm, ifelse(hh < 12, "am", "pm"))
}

two_panel <- function(boot_a, boot_b, name_a, name_b) {
  groups <- tibble(group = factor(rep(c(name_a, name_b), each = length(boot_a)),
                                  levels = c(name_a, name_b)),
                   mean_hour = c(boot_a, boot_b))
  diffs <- tibble(diff_min = (boot_a - boot_b) * 60)
  q <- quantile(diffs$diff_min, c(0.025, 0.975))

  left <- ggplot(groups, aes(mean_hour, fill = group)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.6, color = NA) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("firebrick", "steelblue")) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = clock) +
    labs(title = "1,000 resampled means per group", x = "Mean time of day", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")

  right <- ggplot(diffs, aes(diff_min, fill = between(diff_min, q[1], q[2]))) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 40, color = "white") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
    expand_limits(x = 0) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "navy", "FALSE" = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
    labs(title = paste0(name_a, " minus ", name_b),
         subtitle = paste0("Middle 95%: ", round(q[1]), " to ", round(q[2]), " minutes"),
         x = "Minutes", y = NULL)
  left + right
}


two_panel(boot_violent, boot_property, "Violent", "Property")







Left: the two bootstrap distributions of the group means barely overlap. Right: the distribution of their difference, in minutes, with the middle 95% shaded. The zero line sits outside the shading: every plausible value of the difference is on the “later” side, and “no difference” is not on the list. That is what “the interval does not cross zero” looks like.
The two-sample t-test gives the same interval directly, no loop required:

t.test(hour ~ crime_category, data = vp)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  hour by crime_category
t = 2.6061, df = 19021, p-value = 0.009164
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Violent and group Property is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.06263688 0.44272107
sample estimates:
 mean in group Violent mean in group Property 
              12.79602               12.54334 


Two lines matter: 95 percent confidence interval, and the two mean in group lines that tell you which minus which. Violent is listed first because we told R so.
Reading it honestly: the 95% CI for the difference (Violent minus Property) runs from 0.06 to 0.44 hours, about 4 to 27 minutes later — it excludes zero, so the data are consistent with violent crimes genuinely averaging later. But look at the magnitude: somewhere between about 4 and 27 minutes. Detectable ≠ dramatic. With ~19,500 incidents we can detect tiny differences; the CI hands you both facts at once — direction (probably real) and size (small). Never report the first without the second. This is your vaccination against next session’s topic: a “significant” result can be substantively trivial.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
section: 9 · And when it does cross zero
text:
9 · And when it does cross zero
Same city, a question the data cannot settle: within violent crimes, do the ones that end in an arrest happen at a different time of day? Same recipe, new groups:

set.seed(705)
violent <- crimes |>
  filter(crime_category == "Violent") |>
  mutate(arrest = factor(if_else(arrest, "Arrest", "No arrest"), levels = c("Arrest", "No arrest")))

arrest_hours   <- violent$hour[violent$arrest == "Arrest"]
noarrest_hours <- violent$hour[violent$arrest == "No arrest"]
boot_arrest    <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(arrest_hours,   replace = TRUE)))
boot_noarrest  <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(noarrest_hours, replace = TRUE)))


two_panel(boot_arrest, boot_noarrest, "Arrest", "No arrest")







Now the two bells overlap heavily, and the shaded middle 95% of the difference straddles zero. Zero is one of the plausible answers, so this sample cannot even tell you the direction. R agrees:

t.test(hour ~ arrest, data = violent)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  hour by arrest
t = -1.2287, df = 1941.3, p-value = 0.2193
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Arrest and group No arrest is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.6653724  0.1527959
sample estimates:
   mean in group Arrest mean in group No arrest 
               12.58047                12.83676 


The interval runs from about 40 minutes earlier to 9 minutes later, zero inside. Next session this contrast gets a name: the violent-versus-property difference is statistically significant, the arrest-versus-no-arrest difference is not — and you have now seen what the name is pointing at.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 5
text:
Try a variation

Compute a 95% CI for the proportion of incidents flagged as domestic: run crimes |> count(domestic), then type the TRUE count and 30,000 into prop.test(). Then write one defensible sentence reporting it — and audit yourself: did you claim a probability about this interval?
Add conf.level = 0.80 to a prop.test() call. Does the interval get wider or narrower — and what did you trade to get it?
In the 100-intervals simulation, change n = 250 to n = 1000 in both places. What changes: the capture rate, or the widths?
Remove the Broad Street pump before the slice_min() step (filter(pump != 7) on the pairs). Which pump inherits the deaths — and why should that make you more confident in Snow’s inference, not less?

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 7
text: What this page is. The Session 7 lecture, written down step by step. Every chunk below is self-contained: copy any of them into your own R session and it runs as-is. Use this page to catch up after a missed class, or to re-run the examples at your own pace.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 7
text:
What you’ll build
Four answers to four real questions, each with the same recipe:


Question. Name the two groups and the outcome. A yes/no outcome means prop.test() and bayes_prop_test(); a number means t.test().
Count or describe.
Test.

Say it. The honest sentence, how big in real units, and one thing the test cannot tell you.

The questions: did financial aid at release lower re-arrest? Were employed arrestees released more often? How much lower is income in Chicago’s high-violence areas? Was body camera footage reported more often in fatal police shootings after 2020?
Each example also has the “Where is zero?” explorer from class: four ways to see what the test is measuring, built from that example’s own numbers. Pick one of the four buttons, then press Play (or Step to go one at a time). Every one asks the same question: the gap between the two groups is uncertain, so where could it really be, and is zero (no difference) one of the places?


Rerun the study: run the same study again and again; each rerun’s gap drops onto the number line. The middle 95% of reruns is the confidence interval.

Arrows between groups: pick a plausible value for each group; the arrow between them is the gap. Arrows pointing the other way cross zero.

Is zero plausible?: imagine a world where the two groups are truly the same. Luck alone would still spread studies like ours around zero; 95% of them land in the green. Then drop our actual result on it: inside the green means zero is plausible, far outside means it is ruled out.

More-data dial: keep the gap, change the amount of data, and watch the interval shrink or grow around it.

Chicago and the body-camera example also have a descriptive animation from class (Chicago’s areas splitting into two groups, and camera footage year by year). Their code is folded away (click “Code” to see it); you do not need to write code like that.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 7
text:
Setup
The tidyverse, the course’s Bayesian function, and four datasets. Two of them are new to you and live on the course site; one is our Chicago anchor data; one comes straight from the Washington Post. plotly draws the two descriptive animations; if you want to run those chunks yourself, install it once with install.packages("plotly").

library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)   # only for the animations
source("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/R/bayes.R")   # gives you bayes_prop_test()
set.seed(705)

rossi   <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/rossi.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE)
arrests <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/toronto-arrests.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE)
areas   <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE)
shootings <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/washingtonpost/data-police-shootings/master/v2/fatal-police-shootings-data.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)

More about each dataset, and four more like them, is on the Final-Project Data Options page.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 7
section: 1 · Reentry: does money at release keep people out of jail?
text:
1 · Reentry: does money at release keep people out of jail?
432 men released from Maryland state prisons in the 1970s were followed for one year. Half were randomly assigned to receive financial aid (fin). The outcome is arrest: 1 if arrested again within the year. One row is one man.

rossi |> count(fin, arrest)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  fin   arrest     n
  <chr>  <dbl> <int>
1 no         0   150
2 no         1    66
3 yes        0   168
4 yes        1    48


Aid: 48 re-arrested out of 48 + 168 = 216 (22.2%). No aid: 66 out of 66 + 150 = 216 (30.6%). Aid goes first, so every difference reads Aid minus No aid.

prop.test(x = c(48, 66), n = c(216, 216))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(48, 66) out of c(216, 216)
X-squared = 3.4439, df = 1, p-value = 0.06349
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.170713151  0.004046484
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.2222222 0.3055556 


The interval runs from about 17 points lower to 0.4 points higher, and p = 0.063. Zero is just inside, so: fail to reject the null. A funder who reads only that line cuts the program.
Now ask the other question:

bayes_prop_test(x = c(48, 66), n = c(216, 216))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  48 of 216 (22.2%)
data, group 2:  66 of 216 (30.6%)
prior:          know-nothing (1 yes, 1 no), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  22.5%         17.2% to 28.2%
group 2                  30.7%         24.8% to 37.0%
difference (1 minus 2)   -8.2 points   -16.5 to 0.0 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: 0.03 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  0.97 


Where is zero? Start with Rerun the study, then try Is zero plausible?: our gap of -8.3 lands just inside the green of the no-difference world, which is exactly why p = 0.063.

Say it. Given these data, there is about a 97% probability that men who got aid were re-arrested at a lower rate. About 22 of every 100 men with aid were re-arrested, against about 31 of every 100 without: roughly 8 fewer re-arrests per 100 people released. What this cannot tell you: whether the effect lasts past a year, or would hold today. “Not significant” is not “no effect.”

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 7
section: 2 · Pretrial release: does a job get you released?
text:
2 · Pretrial release: does a job get you released?
5,226 Toronto arrests for possessing small amounts of marijuana, 1997 to 2002. released is whether the person was released with a summons instead of held for a bail hearing. The group is employed. One row is one arrest.

arrests |> count(employed, released)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  employed released     n
  <chr>    <chr>    <int>
1 No       No         349
2 No       Yes        766
3 Yes      No         543
4 Yes      Yes       3568


Employed: 3,568 released out of 3,568 + 543 = 4,111 (86.8%). Not employed: 766 out of 766 + 349 = 1,115 (68.7%).

prop.test(x = c(3568, 766), n = c(4111, 1115))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(3568, 766) out of c(4111, 1115)
X-squared = 201.54, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1512300 0.2106097
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.8679153 0.6869955 



bayes_prop_test(x = c(3568, 766), n = c(4111, 1115))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  3,568 of 4,111 (86.8%)
data, group 2:  766 of 1,115 (68.7%)
prior:          know-nothing (1 yes, 1 no), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  86.8%         85.7% to 87.8%
group 2                  68.7%         65.9% to 71.4%
difference (1 minus 2)   18.1 points   15.2 to 21.0 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: more than 0.99 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  less than 0.01 


About 15 to 21 points more often for the employed, by either test, and more than a 99% probability the employed rate is higher. But the two groups differ in other ways. checks counts how many of six police databases (prior arrests, convictions, parole, and so on) had the person’s name:

arrests |> summarize(avg_checks = mean(checks), people = n(), .by = employed)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  employed avg_checks people
  <chr>         <dbl>  <int>
1 Yes            1.44   4111
2 No             2.35   1115


People without a job had more of a record, and a record is a reason to hold someone. So compare like with like: keep only people with no record at all, and ask again.

arrests |> filter(checks == 0) |> count(employed, released)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  employed released     n
  <chr>    <chr>    <int>
1 No       No          35
2 No       Yes        166
3 Yes      No         124
4 Yes      Yes       1526

prop.test(x = c(1526, 166), n = c(1650, 201))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(1526, 166) out of c(1650, 201)
X-squared = 21.112, df = 1, p-value = 4.333e-06
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.04224058 0.15571509
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.9248485 0.8258706 

bayes_prop_test(x = c(1526, 166), n = c(1650, 201))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  1,526 of 1,650 (92.5%)
data, group 2:  166 of 201 (82.6%)
prior:          know-nothing (1 yes, 1 no), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  92.4%         91.1% to 93.7%
group 2                  82.3%         76.7% to 87.2%
difference (1 minus 2)   10.2 points   5.1 to 15.8 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: more than 0.99 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  less than 0.01 


Where is zero? Start with Arrows between groups, then switch between Everyone and No record only: with only 201 people in the not-employed group, its curve gets wider, and so does the gap’s pile, but it never reaches zero.

Say it. Among people with clean records, the employed were released about 10 points more often (92.5% vs 82.6%; interval about 4 to 16 points, credible interval 5.1 to 15.8 points, more than a 99% probability the employed rate is higher). The gap shrank from 18 points to 10 when we compared like with like, but it did not disappear. What this cannot tell you: whether some other difference (age, citizenship, where the arrest happened) explains the rest.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 7
text:
3 · Neighborhoods: violence and income
Chicago’s 77 community areas. high_violence marks the 38 areas whose violent-crime rate is above the city’s median. The outcome is median_income, a number in dollars, so the test is t.test(). One row is one area, not one person. First, name the groups and put High violence first:

areas <- areas |>
  mutate(violence = factor(if_else(high_violence, "High violence", "Other areas"),
                           levels = c("High violence", "Other areas")))

areas |>
  summarize(avg_income = mean(median_income), areas = n(), .by = violence) |>
  arrange(violence)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  violence      avg_income areas
  <fct>              <dbl> <int>
1 High violence     54355.    38
2 Other areas       90088.    39


See it. Each dot is one community area:

Codeset.seed(705)
jit <- runif(nrow(areas), -0.18, 0.18)
stage_labels <- c("All 77 areas", "Split by violence", "The two averages")
chi_pts <- map_dfr(1:3, \(s) areas |>
  mutate(x = if (s == 1) 1.5 + jit else if_else(violence == "High violence", 1, 2) + jit,
         stage = stage_labels[s])) |>
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = stage_labels),
         hover = paste0(community, "<br>$", format(round(median_income), big.mark = ",")))
chi_means <- areas |>
  summarize(avg = mean(median_income), .by = violence)
chi_means <- map_dfr(1:3, \(s) chi_means |>
  mutate(x = if (s < 3) -1 else if_else(violence == "High violence", 1, 2),
         stage = stage_labels[s])) |>
  mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = stage_labels),
         txt = paste0("Average<br>$", format(round(avg), big.mark = ",")))
chi_gap <- tibble(stage = factor(stage_labels, levels = stage_labels),
                  x = c(-1, -1, 1.5), y = 175000, txt = "Gap: about $35,700")

plot_ly(height = 470) |>
  add_markers(data = chi_pts, x = ~x, y = ~median_income, frame = ~stage, ids = ~community,
              color = ~violence, colors = c("firebrick", "steelblue"),
              marker = list(size = 10, opacity = 0.8), text = ~hover, hoverinfo = "text") |>
  add_markers(data = chi_means, x = ~x, y = ~avg, frame = ~stage, ids = ~violence,
              marker = list(symbol = "line-ew-open", size = 60, color = "navy",
                            line = list(width = 4, color = "navy")),
              showlegend = FALSE, hoverinfo = "none") |>
  add_text(data = chi_means, x = ~x + 0.33, y = ~avg, text = ~txt, frame = ~stage,
           textfont = list(size = 14, color = "navy"), showlegend = FALSE, hoverinfo = "none") |>
  add_text(data = chi_gap, x = ~x, y = ~y, text = ~txt, frame = ~stage,
           textfont = list(size = 18, color = "navy"), showlegend = FALSE, hoverinfo = "none") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "", range = c(0.4, 2.6), tickvals = c(1, 2),
                      ticktext = c("High violence", "Other areas")),
         yaxis = list(title = "Median household income", tickprefix = "$", range = c(0, 190000)),
         legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 1800, transition = 900, redraw = FALSE) |>
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "")) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)






t.test(median_income ~ violence, data = areas)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  median_income by violence
t = -6.3561, df = 74.959, p-value = 1.458e-08
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group High violence and group Other areas is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -46932.44 -24533.58
sample estimates:
mean in group High violence   mean in group Other areas 
                   54354.63                    90087.64 


Where is zero? Start with Arrows between groups: the two curves are where each group’s true average income could be, and the arrows between them never come close to pointing the other way.

Say it. High-violence areas minus other areas: about $25,000 to $47,000 lower median household income ($54,355 vs $90,088 on average), p = 0.00000001. The unit is dollars because the column is dollars. What this cannot tell you: which way it runs (does poverty breed violence, or does violence drive income out?), and anything about individual people. Each row is an area.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 7
section: 4 · Use of force: body cameras over time
text:
4 · Use of force: body cameras over time
The Washington Post’s database of every person shot and killed by on-duty police in the U.S., 2015 to 2024. body_camera is TRUE when news or police reports said a camera recorded the incident. One row is one person killed. Group: before and after 2020.

shootings <- shootings |>
  mutate(period = if_else(year(date) >= 2020, "2020 to 2024", "2015 to 2019"))

shootings |> count(period, body_camera)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  period       body_camera     n
  <chr>        <lgl>       <int>
1 2015 to 2019 FALSE        4329
2 2015 to 2019 TRUE          594
3 2020 to 2024 FALSE        4302
4 2020 to 2024 TRUE         1205


2020 to 2024: 1,205 of 1,205 + 4,302 = 5,507 (21.9%). 2015 to 2019: 594 of 594 + 4,329 = 4,923 (12.1%).
Year by year first, because two five-year averages can hide a lot:

Codeyearly <- shootings |>
  mutate(year = year(date)) |>
  summarize(pct = 100 * mean(body_camera), .by = c(year, period)) |>
  arrange(year)
yr_labels <- c(as.character(2015:2024), "The two periods")
bwc_anim <- map_dfr(seq_along(yr_labels), \(s) yearly |>
  mutate(shown = if_else(s <= 10 & year > 2014 + s, 0, pct), step = yr_labels[s])) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = yr_labels),
         txt = if_else(shown > 0, paste0(round(shown), "%"), ""))
per <- shootings |> summarize(pct = 100 * mean(body_camera), .by = period)
bwc_lines <- map_dfr(seq_along(yr_labels), \(s) per |>
  mutate(x = if (s < 11) 2010 else if_else(period == "2015 to 2019", 2017, 2022),
         step = yr_labels[s])) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = yr_labels),
         ytxt = if_else(period == "2015 to 2019", 19.5, 35),
         txt = paste0(period, ": ", round(pct, 1), "%"))

plot_ly(height = 470) |>
  add_bars(data = bwc_anim, x = ~year, y = ~shown, frame = ~step, color = ~period,
           colors = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), text = ~txt, textposition = "outside",
           hoverinfo = "none") |>
  add_markers(data = bwc_lines, x = ~x, y = ~pct, frame = ~step, ids = ~period,
              marker = list(symbol = "line-ew-open", size = 200, color = "navy",
                            line = list(width = 4, color = "navy")),
              showlegend = FALSE, hoverinfo = "none") |>
  add_text(data = bwc_lines, x = ~x, y = ~ytxt, text = ~txt, frame = ~step,
           textfont = list(size = 15, color = "navy"), showlegend = FALSE, hoverinfo = "none") |>
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "", range = c(2014.4, 2024.6), dtick = 1),
         yaxis = list(title = "Body camera reported (%)", range = c(0, 38)),
         legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.08)) |>
  animation_opts(frame = 900, transition = 400, redraw = FALSE) |>
  animation_slider(currentvalue = list(prefix = "")) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)





The rise is real but not smooth: 2023 hit 30%, and 2024 fell back to 20%. Comparing two five-year periods averages over those bumps; that is a choice, and an honest write-up says so. Now both tests on the two periods:

prop.test(x = c(1205, 594), n = c(5507, 4923))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(1205, 594) out of c(5507, 4923)
X-squared = 174.76, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.08374831 0.11256026
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.2188124 0.1206581 

bayes_prop_test(x = c(1205, 594), n = c(5507, 4923))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  1,205 of 5,507 (21.9%)
data, group 2:  594 of 4,923 (12.1%)
prior:          know-nothing (1 yes, 1 no), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  21.9%         20.8% to 23.0%
group 2                  12.1%         11.2% to 13.0%
difference (1 minus 2)   9.8 points    8.4 to 11.2 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: more than 0.99 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  less than 0.01 


Where is zero? Start with the More-data dial: even with a quarter of the data, the interval stays well clear of zero. With 10,430 cases, a gap this size could not hide.

Say it. About 12 in 100 fatal shootings had known camera footage before 2020, and about 22 in 100 after (8 to 11 points higher, by either test). Close to doubling, and still fewer than 1 in 4. What this cannot tell you: whether cameras changed anything about the shootings, or how many cameras existed but went unreported. With 10,430 cases, the p-value was never in doubt. The size is the whole story.
