title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
text: What this page is. The Session 10 lecture demos, written down step by step. Run the setup chunk once, then work top to bottom: every demo reproduces exactly what happened on screen. Use this page to catch up after a missed class, or to re-run the lecture at your own pace.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
text:
What you’ll build

A hand-rolled ruler for “best line” (SSR()), tested on three candidate lines, the proof that lm() beats every hand-picked guess, and the check that one-predictor R² is just Session 8’s correlation, squared
The best-fitting plane for two predictors (static slices here: the slides have the spinnable 3D version)
The ice-cream/drownings lurker: a “significant” coefficient that evaporates when the third variable enters
A real two-predictor model of violent crime across Chicago’s 77 community areas: read honestly, then diagnosed (residual plot, VIF)
The same model in brms: posterior distributions, and the reporting sentence each tradition licenses

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
text:
Setup

library(tidyverse)
library(bayesplot)
library(brms)
library(car)
set.seed(705)

areas <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv",
                  show_col_types = FALSE)







Two non-tidyverse packages today: car (for VIF; install.packages("car") if you don’t have it) and brms, which you installed for Project Checkpoint 2 (bayesplot came along free with it). If your Checkpoint 2 test fit failed, sort that out before Section 5. brms compiles models with your computer’s C++ toolchain, so the first brm() of an R session pauses at Compiling Stan program... for about a minute before sampling starts. That’s normal, not a crash.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
section: 1 · Least squares: build the ruler by hand
text:
1 · Least squares: build the ruler by hand
Ten students, hours studied and exam scores. Some line through this cloud is the “best” one, but best by what ruler? Start with three candidates. (Seed 1 is kept from the lecture so every number matches the slides.)

set.seed(1)
students <- tibble(
  hours = 1:10,
  score = 40 + 5 * hours + rnorm(10, 0, 5)
)

candidates <- tibble(
  a = c(20, 50, 37),
  b = c(5, 3, 5.2),
  line = c("a = 20, b = 5", "a = 50, b = 3", "a = 37, b = 5.2")
)

ggplot(students, aes(hours, score)) +
  geom_abline(data = candidates, aes(intercept = a, slope = b, color = line),
              linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 4, color = "navy") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("firebrick", "seagreen", "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "Hours studied", y = "Exam score", color = NULL,
       title = "Which line is best? We need a ruler, not a vibe.")







The ruler: for any candidate line, measure every vertical miss, square it (so misses above and below don’t cancel), and add them up. That total is the sum of squared residuals:

SSR <- function(a, b) {
  predicted <- a + b * students$hours
  sum((students$score - predicted)^2)
}

SSR(20, 5)      # too low

[1] 4405.871

SSR(50, 3)      # too flat

[1] 584.9933

SSR(37, 5.2)    # roughly right

[1] 196.9529


Smaller total = better line. Least squares = find the line with the smallest total of all. No trial and error required: lm() solves for it directly:

fit_hours <- lm(score ~ hours, data = students)
coef(fit_hours)

(Intercept)       hours 
   39.15588     5.27366 

SSR(coef(fit_hours)[1], coef(fit_hours)[2])

[1] 130.9173


Our best hand-picked guess left about 197 in squared misses; lm() gets it down to about 131, and no other line does better. Read the slope: each additional hour of studying predicts about 5.3 more points, in this sample. The vertical gap between each point and the winning line is that student’s residual: the miss the model owns. (The slides animate the search: the line tilts until the SSR stops shrinking.) So how much did the winning line explain? That’s R²:

summary(fit_hours)$r.squared

[1] 0.9460216

cor(students$hours, students$score)^2

[1] 0.9460216


R² is the proportion of the outcome’s variance the model accounts for: here about 95% (it’s simulated data; real life humbles us below). And notice the second line: with one predictor, R² is just Session 8’s correlation, squared. With multiple predictors, R² keeps the same meaning (variance explained by the whole team), but no single correlation owns it anymore.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
section: 2 · Two predictors: from line to plane
text:
2 · Two predictors: from line to plane
With one predictor the model is a line through a 2-D cloud. With two, it’s a plane floating in a 3-D cloud, with one slope along each predictor’s axis, chosen by the same ruler: minimize the total squared vertical distance from every point to the surface. Simulate data where we know the truth (intercept 10, slopes 2 and 3) and check that lm() finds it:

set.seed(42)   # kept from the lecture: same cloud as the slides
plane_data <- tibble(
  x1 = runif(100, 0, 10),
  x2 = runif(100, 0, 10),
  y  = 10 + 2 * x1 + 3 * x2 + rnorm(100, 0, 2)
)

plane_fit <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = plane_data)
coef(plane_fit) |> round(2)

(Intercept)          x1          x2 
       9.80        1.98        3.02 


Close to (10, 2, 3): least squares recovered the plane. A flat page can’t spin a 3-D plot, but slicing the plane says the same thing: hold x2 fixed at a few values and plot predicted y against x1:

slices <- expand_grid(x1 = seq(0, 10, length.out = 50), x2 = c(2, 5, 8))
slices$predicted <- predict(plane_fit, newdata = slices)

ggplot(slices, aes(x1, predicted, color = factor(x2))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "navy", "firebrick")) +
  labs(title = "The plane, sliced: the x1 slope is the same at every fixed x2",
       subtitle = "Parallel lines are what 'holding x2 constant' looks like",
       x = "x1", y = "Predicted y", color = "x2 held at")







Every slice climbs at slope ≈ 2 (the x1 coefficient); jumping between slices is the x2 coefficient’s job. For the grab-and-spin 3-D version (points, plane, and residuals), open the Session 10 slides (“The Best-Fitting Plane, Live”).

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
text:
3 · The lurking third variable
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated. Every summer. Reliably. Build the world where temperature secretly drives both:

set.seed(705)
lurk <- tibble(
  temperature    = runif(100, 60, 100),
  icecream_sales = 20 + 5 * temperature + rnorm(100, 0, 30),
  drownings      = -10 + 0.8 * temperature + rnorm(100, 0, 10)
)

ggplot(lurk, aes(icecream_sales, drownings)) +
  geom_point(color = "navy", size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "r = 0.6. Ban ice cream?",
       x = "Ice cream sales", y = "Drownings")







Model 1 fits what the scatterplot suggests: ice cream “predicts” drownings:

lurk_m1 <- lm(drownings ~ icecream_sales, data = lurk)
summary(lurk_m1)$coefficients |> round(4)

               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)     -0.3876     7.5245 -0.0515    0.959
icecream_sales   0.1315     0.0175  7.5165    0.000


The coefficient is positive and the p-value has ten zeros in it. Statistically significant; the model says it’s real. Do we believe it? No, but notice that nothing in this output warns us. The model can only see the variables we gave it. So give it the lurker:

lurk_m2 <- lm(drownings ~ icecream_sales + temperature, data = lurk)
summary(lurk_m2)$coefficients |> round(4)

               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)    -10.0979     6.5333 -1.5456   0.1255
icecream_sales  -0.0339     0.0299 -1.1352   0.2591
temperature      0.9884     0.1553  6.3634   0.0000


Holding temperature constant, ice cream’s coefficient collapses from 0.13 to about -0.03 and goes nonsignificant (p ≈ 0.26), while R² jumps from 0.37 to 0.55. Temperature was driving both variables the whole time. This is holding constant doing real work: comparing days with the same temperature, ice cream tells you nothing about drownings. An added-variable plot (from car) shows exactly that: the relationship between ice cream and drownings after temperature’s contribution is removed from both:

avPlots(lurk_m2, terms = ~ icecream_sales,
        main = "Ice cream vs. drownings, with temperature partialed out")







Flat. That flat line is the multiple-regression coefficient for ice cream. The moral: multiple regression holds constant only the variables you measured and included. Every observational model has potential lurkers you didn’t measure, so coefficients are adjusted associations, not causal effects. Keep that loaded; the Chicago models below will tempt you to talk causally.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
section: 4 · Real data: violence across Chicago’s 77 areas
text:
4 · Real data: violence across Chicago’s 77 areas
You plotted violent-crime rate against unemployment across the 77 community areas in Session 8: a strong upward cloud, each dot an area, not a person (say it with me: ecological). Look at that scatter again first if it isn’t fresh, then fit one predictor:

chi_m1 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate, data = areas)
summary(chi_m1)


Call:
lm(formula = violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate, data = areas)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-32.137  -6.340  -2.670   5.843  43.339 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        -2.7444     2.8629  -0.959    0.341    
unemployment_rate   3.3007     0.2463  13.400   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12.27 on 75 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.7054,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.7014 
F-statistic: 179.5 on 1 and 75 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Each additional percentage point of unemployment is associated with 3.3 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, and unemployment alone accounts for about 70% of the between-area variance. Strong, but is unemployment getting credit for other disadvantage it travels with? Add vacant housing:

chi_m2 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas)
summary(chi_m2)


Call:
lm(formula = violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, data = areas)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-27.6759  -5.8167  -0.9943   4.5144  26.7266 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)        -9.2679     2.4616  -3.765 0.000332 ***
unemployment_rate   2.1156     0.2620   8.075 9.35e-12 ***
pct_vacant          1.9352     0.2859   6.769 2.65e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 9.708 on 74 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.818, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8131 
F-statistic: 166.3 on 2 and 74 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Both predictors earn significant coefficients, and R² climbs from 0.70 to 0.82. But watch unemployment’s slope: 3.3 → 2.1. Some of what looked like “unemployment” in the simple model was shared with vacancy. That shrinkage is “holding constant”: the lurker lesson, on real data. Reading the coefficients out loud:


Intercept (-9.3): predicted rate when both predictors are 0: no Chicago area looks like that; it anchors the plane, nothing more

unemployment_rate (2.12): +1 point of unemployment ↔︎ about 2.1 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, vacancy held fixed


pct_vacant (1.94): +1 point of vacancy ↔︎ about 1.9 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents, unemployment held fixed


And what they are not: not causal effects (these are adjusted associations between areas, with every unmeasured lurker still at large); not people-level claims (an unemployed person is not “2.1 crimes more dangerous”; Session 8’s ecological fallacy rides along with every coefficient today); and not the full story (the model holds constant only what’s in the model).
Watch the units
Coefficient size is meaningless until you check the predictor’s units. Median income, in dollars:

coef(lm(violent_rate ~ median_income, data = areas))

  (Intercept) median_income 
68.5585257487 -0.0005221118 

areas |>
  mutate(income_10k = median_income / 10000) |>
  lm(violent_rate ~ income_10k, data = _) |>
  coef()

(Intercept)  income_10k 
  68.558526   -5.221118 


Same model, same fit. But -0.0005 “looks like” nothing; the honest reading is about 5 fewer violent crimes per 1,000 residents per $10,000 of median income. Rescale before you interpret.
Does a third predictor earn its keep?

chi_m3 <- lm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant + pct_no_hs_diploma,
             data = areas)
summary(chi_m3)$coefficients |> round(3)

                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)         -8.853      2.862  -3.093    0.003
unemployment_rate    2.140      0.276   7.741    0.000
pct_vacant           1.923      0.291   6.613    0.000
pct_no_hs_diploma   -0.039      0.135  -0.290    0.773


Coefficient ≈ 0, p ≈ 0.77: with unemployment and vacancy already in, the diploma share adds nothing detectable. And adjusted R² (R² with a per-predictor penalty) actually falls, 0.813 → 0.811 (compare summary(chi_m2)$adj.r.squared with summary(chi_m3)$adj.r.squared). More predictors ≠ more truth. Every variable argues its way in: theory first, fit second.
Diagnostics: the residual plot and VIF
Regression assumes the misses are patternless. So look at the misses:

tibble(fitted = fitted(chi_m2), residual = resid(chi_m2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(color = "navy", size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. fitted values: the all-purpose diagnostic",
       x = "Fitted violent-crime rate", y = "Residual")







Read it honestly. What we want: a patternless horizontal band around zero. What we have: centered on zero with no obvious curve (good: the straight-plane assumption isn’t visibly wrong), but the spread widens at higher fitted values, so the model misses by more in high-violence areas. That fanning (heteroscedasticity) is common with rate outcomes; it doesn’t bias the coefficients, but it makes the standard errors less trustworthy at the extremes: worth a sentence when you report. A curve in this plot would be worse news: it would say the model’s shape is wrong, not just its noise.
Multicollinearity is the other standard check: if two predictors move in near-lockstep, the model can’t tell whose coefficient the shared variance belongs to; estimates get wobbly and standard errors balloon. VIF measures how redundant each predictor is with the others (rules of thumb: > 5, pay attention; > 10, you have a problem):

vif(chi_m2)

unemployment_rate        pct_vacant 
         1.807177          1.807177 


About 1.8: unemployment and vacancy are correlated (r ≈ 0.67), but each still carries plenty of its own information. If VIF were high: drop one predictor, combine them into an index, or accept wide intervals; you cannot p-value your way out.

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
text:
5 · The Bayesian version
Identical formula, Bayesian machinery. brm(), from the brms package (Bayesian Regression Models using Stan), takes the same formula as lm() and returns a full posterior distribution for every coefficient instead of a single estimate. The sampler settings are the ones you’ll use for the rest of the course: chains = 2, iter = 2000 runs two independent samplers for 2,000 steps each (the first half is warm-up); seed = 705 makes your numbers match these; refresh = 0 just silences the sampling progress log. (This is the chunk with the compile pause. Go refill your coffee.)

chi_bayes <- brm(violent_rate ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant,
                 data = areas,
                 chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


fixef(chi_bayes) |> round(2)

                  Estimate Est.Error   Q2.5 Q97.5
Intercept            -9.25      2.42 -13.93 -4.68
unemployment_rate     2.12      0.27   1.58  2.64
pct_vacant            1.92      0.29   1.36  2.48


Posterior means land almost exactly on the least-squares estimates, and with a decent n they should. The prior we just used: we didn’t state one, so brms fell back on its defaults, essentially flat on the coefficients and weakly informative on the intercept and spread. Flat priors mean “the data do the talking,” which is fine here, but say so: “we used brms default priors” belongs in any write-up that reports a posterior. One sentence in your methods (“brms default priors, 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705”) covers it.
The interpretation rule for every brm() coefficient from here on: if its 95% credible interval crosses 0, zero remains a credible value, so there is no credible effect; if it excludes 0, the effect is credible. Below the posterior plot: the sentence each tradition licenses.

mcmc_areas(chi_bayes, pars = c("b_unemployment_rate", "b_pct_vacant"),
           prob = 0.95) +
  labs(title = "Posterior distributions: predictors of violent-crime rate",
       subtitle = "Shaded = central 95% credible interval: both sit clear of zero")








Frequentist: “Holding vacancy constant, each percentage point of unemployment was associated with about 2.1 more violent crimes per 1,000 residents (b = 2.12, 95% CI [1.59, 2.64], p < .001).”
Bayesian: “Given the data and priors, there is a 95% probability the unemployment coefficient lies between ≈ 1.6 and ≈ 2.6: zero is not a credible value.”

Both are area-level, adjusted associations: neither sentence licenses “unemployment causes violence.”

title: Demo Walkthrough · Session 10
text:
Try a variation

Beat the machine: using SSR(), hunt by hand for an (a, b) pair that gets below 131. (Spoiler: you can tie lm() to more decimal places, but never beat it.)
In the lurker simulation, give ice cream a real effect: change the drownings line to -10 + 0.8 * temperature + 0.05 * icecream_sales + rnorm(100, 0, 10). Does lurk_m2 find it?
In the third-predictor test, swap pct_no_hs_diploma for a predictor of your choice (pct_renter? median_rent?). Does anything earn its keep next to unemployment and vacancy: by its coefficient and by adjusted R²?
Run predict(chi_m2, newdata = tibble(unemployment_rate = 23, pct_vacant = 25)), roughly Englewood, and then again with 10 and 10. Which prediction does the residual plot say to trust more, and why?

title: Final Project Exemplar
text: Read me first. This page is a full final project, written to score “Excellent” on every row of the grading rubric — with 📋 rubric notes in the margins explaining why each part earns its points. It uses the course’s Alaska crash dataset, which — like all course datasets — is not eligible for your own project (you choose your own in Homework 7, starting from the data options). So study the shape, not the content. The complete script is downloadable: final-project-exemplar-script.R.

title: Final Project Exemplar
text:
1 · Introduction
Impaired driving is one of the oldest targets of traffic enforcement, but enforcement resources are finite: patrols concentrate on nights and weekends on the assumption that this is when impaired driving does its damage. This project asks two questions of 20,000 simulated Alaska crash records: (1) are intoxication-involved crashes more likely to injure at least one person, and (2) is that extra risk concentrated at night or on weekends — as the patrol-scheduling assumption implies?
The answer matters practically. If intoxication raises injury risk whenever it occurs, then enforcement rationales built purely around Friday night may miss weekday-afternoon impairment — a pattern DUI court data have long hinted at.
📋 Rubric note (The question, motivated): two sentences in, a reader knows the question, the data, and why anyone should care. No statistics yet — motivation first.

title: Final Project Exemplar
text:
2 · Data and methods

library(tidyverse)
crashes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/crash-ak.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE)

The dataset holds one row per crash (n = 20,000) with the number of people injured, an intoxication flag (intox_any: alcohol or drugs recorded for a driver), a timestamp, and crash characteristics. Three variables are derived for analysis:

crashes <- crashes |>
  mutate(
    any_injury = injuries > 0,                          # outcome: was anyone hurt?
    hour       = lubridate::hour(time),
    night      = hour >= 20 | hour < 4,                 # 8 pm – 4 am
    weekend    = lubridate::wday(lubridate::mdy(date)) %in% c(1, 7)
  )

Outcome. any_injury is binary (someone was hurt / no one was hurt), so the final model is a logistic regression; both the frequentist fit (glm) and the Bayesian fit (brm, default priors, 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705) are reported, per the course requirement. driver_age is included as a control.
📋 Rubric note (Quality of analysis): the outcome’s type drives the model choice, and the sentence says so. The derivations are shown, not hidden — a reader can re-create every variable.

title: Final Project Exemplar
text:
3 · Results
Descriptives

crashes |>
  summarize(
    crashes        = n(),
    p_any_injury   = mean(any_injury),
    mean_injuries  = mean(injuries),
    .by = intox_any
  ) |>
  arrange(intox_any)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  intox_any crashes p_any_injury mean_injuries
      <dbl>   <int>        <dbl>         <dbl>
1         0   18455        0.466         0.743
2         1    1545        0.625         1.13 


About 8% of crashes involve an intoxicated driver. Injury is common in both groups — roughly 48% of sober-driver crashes injure someone — but intoxication-involved crashes injure someone about 64% of the time, and average more injured people per crash (≈1.1 vs ≈0.7).
The key visualization

crashes |>
  mutate(
    intox   = if_else(intox_any == 1, "Intoxication involved", "No intoxication"),
    period  = case_when(
      night & weekend  ~ "Weekend night",
      night            ~ "Weekday night",
      weekend          ~ "Weekend day",
      .default         = "Weekday day"
    )
  ) |>
  summarize(p_injury = mean(any_injury), n = n(), .by = c(intox, period)) |>
  ggplot(aes(period, p_injury, fill = intox)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("firebrick", "grey55")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Intoxication raises injury risk at every time of week",
    subtitle = "Share of crashes injuring at least one person, Alaska crash data (n = 20,000)",
    x = NULL, y = "Crashes with any injury", fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







The gap between the red and grey bars — roughly 15 percentage points — is strikingly flat across the four time windows. Whatever intoxication does to injury risk, it does not appear to save it up for Saturday night.
📋 Rubric note (The key visualization): one figure carries the whole finding, the caption says what the plot shows (not what the author hoped), and the y-axis is honest (percentages, baseline visible).
The final model — both traditions
Frequentist:

m_freq <- glm(any_injury ~ intox_any + night + weekend + driver_age,
              data = crashes, family = binomial)

broom::tidy(m_freq) |>
  mutate(odds_ratio = exp(estimate)) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

# A tibble: 5 × 6
  term        estimate std.error statistic p.value odds_ratio
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>      <dbl>
1 (Intercept)   -0.139     0.044    -3.19    0.001      0.87 
2 intox_any      0.649     0.055    11.9     0          1.91 
3 nightTRUE      0.008     0.03      0.254   0.8        1.01 
4 weekendTRUE   -0.011     0.032    -0.349   0.727      0.989
5 driver_age     0         0.001     0.051   0.96       1    



round(exp(confint(m_freq)), 3)

            2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept) 0.799  0.948
intox_any   1.720  2.131
nightTRUE   0.950  1.069
weekendTRUE 0.929  1.052
driver_age  0.998  1.002


Bayesian twin (same formula; brms default priors — flat on coefficients, weakly informative on the intercept — 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705):

library(brms)
set.seed(705)
m_bayes <- brm(any_injury ~ intox_any + night + weekend + driver_age,
               data = crashes, family = bernoulli(),
               chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


round(exp(fixef(m_bayes)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)

            Estimate  Q2.5 Q97.5
Intercept      0.870 0.800 0.950
intox_any      1.915 1.728 2.122
nightTRUE      1.008 0.951 1.066
weekendTRUE    0.990 0.931 1.057
driver_age     1.000 0.998 1.002


Reading the two fits together. Both traditions tell the same story. Holding time-of-week and driver age constant, intoxication roughly doubles the odds of an injury crash (frequentist OR ≈ 1.9, 95% CI ≈ [1.7, 2.1]; Bayesian posterior OR ≈ 1.9, 95% credible interval ≈ [1.7, 2.1], excluding 1 decisively). The Bayesian fit licenses the sentence the frequentist one doesn’t: given the data and priors, there is a 95% probability the true odds ratio lies in that interval — the confidence interval, by contrast, is a statement about the procedure, not this interval. With 20,000 crashes the two traditions converge numerically; the difference here is what we’re allowed to say, not the numbers.
In concrete terms: for a 35-year-old driver on a weekday afternoon, the model puts the probability of an injury crash near 47% without intoxication and near 62% with it.
And the honest nulls: night (OR ≈ 1.01), weekend (OR ≈ 0.99), and driver_age (OR ≈ 1.00) all sit almost exactly at 1, with intervals straddling it in both traditions. In these data, when a crash happens tells us essentially nothing about injury risk once intoxication is accounted for — and there is no evidence the intoxication effect needs nights or weekends to operate.
📋 Rubric note (Interpretation & honesty): the null predictors are reported with the same prominence as the significant one, magnitudes are in real units (probabilities, not log-odds), and the both-traditions comparison sentence names the actual philosophical difference instead of hand-waving.

title: Final Project Exemplar
text:
4 · Discussion and limitations
What was found. Intoxication-involved crashes are substantially more likely to injure someone — an effect visible in the raw percentages, robust to adjustment, and essentially identical in the frequentist and Bayesian fits. The patrol-scheduling assumption fared worse: injury risk shows no independent night or weekend pattern, and the intoxication penalty is as present on a Tuesday afternoon as on a Saturday night.
Three sentences for a police chief. Crashes involving an impaired driver are about twice as likely to hurt somebody, whatever the day or hour. The extra risk does not concentrate on weekend nights — it travels with the impaired driver. If the goal is fewer injuries, impairment enforcement is a seven-day job, not a Friday-night one.
Limitations. These are simulated training data; real Alaska crash records would bring reporting artifacts (minor no-injury crashes underreported, intoxication recorded more diligently when someone is hurt — which could inflate the association). The unit is the crash, not the driver: nothing here says which driver was injured. The model is deliberately simple; interactions (e.g., intoxication × road condition) were beyond the course’s scope, and severity was excluded because it is partially defined by injuries — putting it in would be circular. Finally, this is an observational association: no crash was randomly assigned an impaired driver, and the causal reading — however plausible — rests on the adjustment being adequate, which three covariates cannot guarantee.
📋 Rubric note (Interpretation & honesty, again): limitations are specific to this analysis — the mechanical “correlation isn’t causation” sentence appears only alongside named, checkable concerns (reporting bias direction, circularity of severity, unit-of-analysis).

title: Homework 6 · Bayesian and Frequentist Inference
section: Part 3: Both Tests on Real Data
text:
Part 3: Both Tests on Real Data
Back to the Alaska crash data from Homework 5. Last week you compared how many people were injured. This week’s question is yes/no: are crashes with an intoxicated driver more likely to hurt someone at all?

Start your script with the same setup as Homework 5, plus the one new line from Lab 6:
library(tidyverse)
source("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/R/bayes.R")

crashes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/crash-ak.csv") |>
  mutate(intox = if_else(intox_any == 1, "Intoxicated", "Sober"),
         anyone_hurt = injuries > 0)
anyone_hurt is TRUE when at least one person was injured (the same line from Lab 4).
Count: crashes |> count(intox, anyone_hurt). In a comment: write the four numbers you need — how many intoxicated-driver crashes hurt someone, out of how many, and the same for sober-driver crashes — and compute the two rates. Intoxicated goes first all the way through, so every difference reads Intoxicated minus Sober.
Run the frequentist test with your four numbers:
prop.test(x = c(__, __), n = c(__, __))
In a comment: report the 95% confidence interval for the difference in percentage points, and the p-value. Do you reject the null? (If R prints the p-value with an e- in it, say in words what that means.)
Run the Bayesian test with the same four numbers in bayes_prop_test(). In a comment: report the 95% credible interval for the difference, and write the one sentence this output lets you say that the prop.test() output does not.
In a comment: compare the two intervals from steps 3 and 4. How close are they? Using what we saw in class about sample size, explain why.
A rarer outcome. Add fatal = fatalities > 0 to crashes with mutate(), count intox by fatal, and run both tests again. In a comment: report both intervals. The gap here is only a few percentage points, and the p-value is still tiny. What does that tell you about what a p-value does and does not measure?
A small study, with a prior. (Pretend numbers.) A county pilots a DUI court. Of 60 participants, 18 are re-arrested for DUI within two years; of 60 similar people who went through regular court, 27 are. Before the pilot, the county’s best information was that about 45% of people like these are re-arrested, and they trust that about as much as having seen 20 cases: prior = c(9, 11).
Run prop.test() and then bayes_prop_test() with that prior, DUI court first. In a comment: report the p-value, and report the probability that the DUI court’s re-arrest rate is lower. Then answer: if you were advising the county on whether to keep funding the court, which result would you put in front of them, and what would you be careful to say about it?
How big, in real units. Go back to step 3. In a comment: state the size of the difference in plain words a legislator would understand (no p-values, no intervals), and say whether you think a gap that size is big enough to matter, and why.

This is the last of the four project checkpoints. Checkpoint 1 described your variables, Checkpoint 2 measured their associations, Checkpoint 3 fit a first model. Checkpoint 4 is the real thing: the model you intend to defend at presentations. It is graded on completion and quality of reasoning, not on whether your results are exciting. In a clearly marked section at the end of your .R script (e.g., # ---- PROJECT CHECKPOINT 4 ----):

Fit your final model, in both traditions. The frequentist fit (lm() for a continuous outcome, glm(family = binomial) for a binary one) and the Bayesian fit (brm() with the same formula; default priors are fine, standard settings: chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0; expect the compile pause). Both fits must match your Part 2 equation. (This is the final-project requirement; see Step 3. Checkpoint 4 is where you get it running with a week of slack.)
Interpret the key coefficients in comments, on the right scale:

Linear: the change in your outcome per one-unit change in each predictor, holding the others constant, with units.
Logistic: exponentiate. Odds ratios per one-unit change, holding the others constant, and at least one predicted probability for a concrete, meaningful case, as we did in class.
Include the uncertainty from both fits (the 95% CI and the 95% credible interval), plus one sentence comparing them: do the two traditions agree here, and what does the posterior let you say that the p-value doesn’t?

Produce ONE table or figure you plan to show at presentations. A tidy coefficient table, a plot of predicted values or probabilities, a well-labeled scatterplot with your fitted line: your choice, but it must be presentation-ready: real variable names, labeled axes or columns, a title. Not raw console output.
Write the three sentences you’d say about it to a non-statistician. As a comment block. Imagine a police chief, a judge, or a city council member: no “log-odds,” no “p < .05,” no Greek letters. What did you find, how sure are you, and why should they care? These three sentences are the spine of your Session 12 presentation: write them now and presentation prep gets much easier.

If anything above breaks (the model won’t run, a coefficient makes no sense, the output contradicts Checkpoint 3), say so in your comments, and if it surfaced by clinic day, bring it to class. Finding that out now, with a week before the full project is due, is precisely what this checkpoint is for.

title: Lab 2 · First Plots with ggplot2
text:
Walkthrough
A histogram — the shape of a numeric variable
Today’s lecture was about summarizing numeric variables. A histogram is the picture version:

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Age distribution of incarcerated persons",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Count")







Anatomy of every ggplot: data (prisoners), aesthetics (aes(x = age) — which variables map to which visual channels), and geometry (geom_histogram() — how to draw them).
How does the picture relate to the numbers?

prisoners |>
  summarize(mean_age = mean(age), median_age = median(age), sd_age = sd(age))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_age median_age sd_age
     <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>
1     34.5         34   10.2








What’s the |> symbol?





That’s the pipe — it feeds whatever is on its left into the function on its right, so you can read code top-to-bottom as “take the data, then do this, then do that.” R4DS uses it everywhere. In older code (and in the Stanton book) you’ll see %>% instead — for our purposes they’re interchangeable.



A bar chart — counts of a categorical variable

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = offense_type)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Offense types", x = NULL, y = "Count")







A boxplot — a distribution split by groups

The five-number-summary as a picture, one box per offense type:

ggplot(prisoners, aes(x = offense_type, y = sentence_years)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90") +
  labs(title = "Sentence length by offense type",
       x = NULL, y = "Sentence (years)")







The box is the middle 50% (median = the line inside); the dots are outliers — the same “one 30-year sentence” problem from lecture, visible instantly.

title: Lab 4 · Building a Sampling Distribution
text:
Goal: see, with your own hands, the three ideas from today’s lecture — the long run settles down, a sample mean is a moving target, and the standard error is how much it moves. Nothing here needs a new package or a new verb. It is sample(), mean(), and one repeat command.
How labs work: run the Setup chunk as-is, follow the Walkthrough along with me, then complete the Your Turn tasks in your own script. The Exit Ticket gets submitted to Canvas before you leave.

title: Lab 4 · Building a Sampling Distribution
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(705)

crashes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/crash-ak.csv",
                    show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(anyone_hurt = injuries > 0)

crashes holds 20,000 Alaska traffic crashes (simulated, but realistic). We only need two columns today: driver_age, and the anyone_hurt column we just built, which is TRUE when at least one person was injured.

crashes |> select(driver_age, injuries, anyone_hurt) |> slice_sample(n = 6)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  driver_age injuries anyone_hurt
       <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>      
1         66        5 TRUE       
2         24        3 TRUE       
3         34        1 TRUE       
4         27        1 TRUE       
5         54        0 FALSE      
6         16        2 TRUE       


For today, pretend these 20,000 crashes are the whole population — every crash there is. That is a fiction, and it is the most useful fiction in statistics, because it lets us check our answers against a truth we can actually see.

title: Lab 4 · Building a Sampling Distribution
text:
Walkthrough
The truth we are allowed to peek at

mean(crashes$driver_age)

[1] 38.5836

sd(crashes$driver_age)

[1] 14.12269


Mean driver age is about 38.6. Remember that number. In real research you never get to run this line.
One sample of 30
Now act like a researcher who can only pull 30 case files:

mean(sample(crashes$driver_age, size = 30))

[1] 35.06667


Not 38.6. Run it again:

mean(sample(crashes$driver_age, size = 30))

[1] 40.8

mean(sample(crashes$driver_age, size = 30))

[1] 40.9


Three samples, three answers, one population. Nothing went wrong. This is sampling error, and it is the whole reason this course exists.
Do it 500 times
replicate() repeats a line of code and keeps the answers:

many_means <- replicate(500, mean(sample(crashes$driver_age, size = 30)))

head(many_means)

[1] 35.33333 35.46667 40.73333 39.56667 39.06667 43.60000


That is one line doing what would take you all night by hand. Now look at the shape of those 500 answers:

tibble(sample_mean = many_means) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(crashes$driver_age),
             color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean age of a 30-crash sample", y = "How often")







That histogram is a sampling distribution: not the distribution of ages, but the distribution of what a study would have concluded. The red line is the truth. Most studies land near it. Some do not.
The standard error
How far off is a typical study? That is just the standard deviation of those 500 answers:

sd(many_means)

[1] 2.654411


And here is the payoff. There is a formula for that number, and you never had to simulate anything:

sd(crashes$driver_age) / sqrt(30)

[1] 2.578439


Close. That is the standard error: the typical distance between a sample mean and the truth. Notice what is on the bottom — \(\sqrt{n}\). Quadruple your sample size and you halve your error. That is why sample size costs money.
Workflow hygiene: scripts and projects
Three habits, thirty seconds, the rest of your life:


Your script is the source of truth, not your console. If you typed it in the console and it worked, paste it into the script. The console is scratch paper.

Use an RStudio Project for this course. File > New Project… once, then always open the course through the .Rproj file. Your working directory is then always the project folder, paths stay relative, and your code runs on any machine — including mine when I grade it.

Never trust the Environment pane. Before you submit anything: Session > Restart R, then run your script top to bottom. If it only works because of something you defined an hour ago and deleted, you want to find that out now, not from me.

title: Lab 6 · One Question, Two Tests
text:
Goal: by the end of this lab you can take one yes/no question about two groups and answer it twice: with a p-value from prop.test(), and with a posterior from bayes_prop_test(). Same four numbers go into both. What changes is the sentence each one lets you say.
How labs work: run the Setup chunk as-is, follow the Walkthrough along with me, then complete the Your Turn tasks in your own script. That script is what you submit to Canvas before you leave.

title: Lab 6 · One Question, Two Tests
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)
source("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/R/bayes.R")

officers <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/officers.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(!is.na(ptsd_screen)) |>
  mutate(ptsd_screen = factor(ptsd_screen, levels = c("Positive", "Negative")))

These are last week’s correctional officers, set up exactly the same way: the eight officers with no PTSD screen on file are dropped (we say so out loud), which leaves 192, and Positive comes first.
One line is new. source() runs an R file from the course website, and that file gives you one new function, bayes_prop_test(). There is nothing to install. If you ever see could not find function "bayes_prop_test", you skipped this line.

title: Lab 6 · One Question, Two Tests
text:
Walkthrough
Count first
Our question: do male and female officers screen positive for PTSD at different rates? Every test today starts from a count, just like last week:

officers |> count(gender, ptsd_screen)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  gender          ptsd_screen     n
  <chr>           <fct>       <int>
1 Female          Positive        8
2 Female          Negative       37
3 Male            Positive       33
4 Male            Negative      111
5 Nonbinary/Other Positive        1
6 Nonbinary/Other Negative        2


Read four numbers off that table, two per group: how many screened positive, out of how many.


Male: 33 positive, out of 33 + 111 = 144


Female: 8 positive, out of 8 + 37 = 45


(Three officers are listed as Nonbinary/Other. Three people is too few to compare with anyone, so we leave that row alone and say so.)

33 / 144

[1] 0.2291667

8 / 45

[1] 0.1777778


About 23% of the men and 18% of the women. A gap of about 5 percentage points. Male goes first all the way through, so every difference reads Male minus Female.
Is a 5-point gap real, or is it the kind of gap you get by luck with only 45 women in the sample?
The frequentist test: prop.test() with two groups
Last week you typed one “how many” and one “out of how many.” With two groups you type two of each, wrapped in c(). Male first, both times:

prop.test(x = c(33, 8), n = c(144, 45))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(33, 8) out of c(144, 45)
X-squared = 0.27341, df = 1, p-value = 0.6011
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.09430734  0.19708512
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.2291667 0.1777778 


Read it from the bottom up.


prop 1 and prop 2 are the two rates, 0.229 and 0.178. Male is prop 1 because we typed it first.

95 percent confidence interval is for the difference, Male minus Female: about -0.09 to +0.20, or 9 points lower to 20 points higher. Zero is inside it. That is last week’s skill.

p-value = 0.6011 is tonight’s new line. If men and women truly screened positive at the same rate, a gap this big or bigger would still turn up about 60% of the time, just from the luck of who landed in the sample.

A p-value of 0.60 is nowhere near 0.05. The verdict is “fail to reject the null.”
Saying it out loud without lying
Here is the sentence I want:

In this sample, 23% of male officers and 18% of female officers screened positive. A gap that size is well within what chance alone produces (p = 0.60), so these data cannot tell us whether the true rates differ.

And here is what not to say:


“There is a 60% chance that men and women have the same rate.” The p-value is about the data, assuming the null is true. It is never the probability that the null is true.

“We proved there is no difference.” Failing to reject is not proving. The interval allows anything from 9 points lower to 20 points higher.

“Men have higher PTSD rates (23% vs 18%).” That is the estimate with the uncertainty deleted.
The Bayesian test: same four numbers
Now hand the same four numbers to bayes_prop_test():

bayes_prop_test(x = c(33, 8), n = c(144, 45))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  33 of 144 (22.9%)
data, group 2:  8 of 45 (17.8%)
prior:          know-nothing (1 yes, 1 no), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  23.3%         16.8% to 30.5%
group 2                  19.1%         9.4% to 31.4%
difference (1 minus 2)   4.2 points    -9.6 to 16.4 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: 0.74 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  0.26 


Read it top to bottom.

The first lines repeat your data back to you, so you can check your typing.

prior says “know-nothing.” We did not tell it what we believed beforehand, so it started from a blank slate.

estimate is the best single guess for each group’s true rate, and each group gets its own credible interval.

difference (1 minus 2) is Male minus Female: about 4 points, with a 95% credible interval of roughly -10 to +16 points.
The last two lines answer the question directly: the probability that the male rate is higher is about 0.74.

Here is the sentence this one lets you say, and it is the sentence we were forbidden to say about a confidence interval last week:

Given these data, there is a 95% probability that the true difference is between 10 points lower and 16 points higher for men, and about a 74% probability that the male rate is the higher one.

Notice the two tests do not disagree. Both intervals run from roughly -10 to somewhere between +16 and +20. One stops at “not significant.” The other tells you how probable each direction is: 74% is better than a coin flip, and a long way from sure.
Adding what you knew beforehand
A Bayesian can bring in earlier knowledge, as long as they say it out loud. Suppose earlier surveys at these facilities found about 1 officer in 5 screening positive, and you trust that about as much as you would trust having already seen 20 officers: 4 positive, 16 negative. That belief is two numbers:

bayes_prop_test(x = c(33, 8), n = c(144, 45), prior = c(4, 16))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  33 of 144 (22.9%)
data, group 2:  8 of 45 (17.8%)
prior:          4 yes, 16 no (about 20%, worth 20 cases), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  22.6%         16.5% to 29.2%
group 2                  18.5%         10.1% to 28.7%
difference (1 minus 2)   4.1 points    -7.6 to 15.0 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: 0.77 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  0.23 


Look at the prior line, then at what changed: almost nothing. The probability moved from 0.74 to 0.77. With 189 real officers in the data, 20 imaginary ones do not carry much weight. A prior matters most when you have very little data.
The p-value was in t.test() the whole time
Last week you ran this line and read the interval. Look one line higher:

t.test(sleep_hours ~ ptsd_screen, data = officers)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  sleep_hours by ptsd_screen
t = 1.0014, df = 60.499, p-value = 0.3206
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Positive and group Negative is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.2568901  0.7721282
sample estimates:
mean in group Positive mean in group Negative 
              6.580952               6.323333 


p-value = 0.3206. If officers who screen positive and negative truly slept the same amount, a gap as big as ours (about 15 minutes) would turn up about a third of the time by luck. Fail to reject. It is the same conclusion the interval gave you last week, because zero was inside it.
