title: Lab 8 · Correlation: Do Two Numbers Move Together?
text:
Goal: by the end of this lab you can take two numeric variables, look at them, put one number on how tightly they move together, test it, and say what it means (and what it does not). Two new functions tonight, cor() and cor.test(), and cor.test() reads a lot like the t.test() output you already know.
How labs work: run the Setup chunk as-is, follow the Walkthrough along with me, then complete the Your Turn tasks in your own script. That script is what you submit to Canvas before you leave.

title: Lab 8 · Correlation: Do Two Numbers Move Together?
text:
The recipe
Same idea as Session 7, with one change: there are no groups. Both variables are numbers.


Question. Name the two numeric variables, and what one row is (a person? a neighborhood?).

Look. A scatterplot, always, before any number.

Number and test. cor() gives r. cor.test() gives r, a confidence interval, and a p-value.

Say it. The honest sentence, how strong in plain words, and one thing a correlation cannot tell you.

title: Lab 8 · Correlation: Do Two Numbers Move Together?
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)

# Walkthrough: Chicago's 77 community areas, 2025
areas <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv",
                  show_col_types = FALSE)

# Your Turn: 500 neighborhoods (the Lab 3 data)
nbhd <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/neighborhoods.csv",
                 show_col_types = FALSE)

# Your Turn: 200 correctional officers (the Lab 5 and 6 data)
officers <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/officers.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE)

Nothing new to install tonight.

title: Lab 8 · Correlation: Do Two Numbers Move Together?
text:
Walkthrough
The data
areas has one row per Chicago community area (77 of them), with 2025 crime rates and Census measures (codebook). One row is one area, not one person. Keep that in mind all night: it decides what your sentences are allowed to claim.
Question
Do community areas with higher unemployment have higher violent-crime rates? Two numeric variables: unemployment_rate (percent) and violent_rate (violent crimes per 1,000 residents).
Look

ggplot(areas, aes(unemployment_rate, violent_rate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)







Read the picture before any number: the dots climb from left to right (positive), they hug the line fairly tightly (strong), the pattern is roughly a straight line, and no single wild point is creating it. Now one number is a fair summary.
Number

cor(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate)

[1] 0.8398579


r = 0.84. Positive, and very strong: r always lands between -1 and +1, and 0.84 is close to the top.
Test

cor.test(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  areas$unemployment_rate and areas$violent_rate
t = 13.4, df = 75, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7585749 0.8954023
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.8398579 


Read it the way you read t.test():


cor at the bottom is r, 0.84

95 percent confidence interval: 0.76 to 0.90. It is an interval for the correlation, not for a difference, so it is in r’s units (between -1 and +1). Zero is far outside it

p-value below 2.2e-16: reject the null of no correlation
Say it
The sentence: across Chicago’s 77 community areas, those with higher unemployment had higher violent-crime rates, r = 0.84 (95% CI 0.76 to 0.90).
How strong, in plain words: a very strong association. Knowing an area’s unemployment rate tells you a lot about where its violent-crime rate sits.
What it cannot tell you:


Cause. Unemployment and violence could both be driven by something else (concentrated poverty, disinvestment). A correlation is a pattern, not a proof.

Anything about individuals. These rows are areas. Nothing here says unemployed people commit violence. Making that jump from areas to people is the ecological fallacy.

title: Lab 8 · Correlation: Do Two Numbers Move Together?
text:
Your Turn
Work in your own script and comment each answer.
Question 1: in the 500 neighborhoods, do neighborhoods with more poverty have more assaults? poverty_rate is the share of residents in poverty (0.25 means 25%) and assaults is the number of assaults recorded there.
1. Look. Make a scatterplot with poverty_rate on the x-axis and assaults on the y-axis, and add geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE). In a comment: which direction do the dots go, and is the pattern straight enough for r to be a fair summary? (The dots sit in rows because assaults is a whole-number count. That is fine.)

# your code here

2. Number. Run cor(nbhd$poverty_rate, nbhd$assaults). In a comment, write r and describe it in words: positive or negative, and weak, moderate, or strong.

# your code here

3. Test. Run cor.test() on the same two variables. In a comment, report the 95% confidence interval and the p-value. Reject or fail to reject the null of no correlation?

# your code here

4. Say it. In a comment, write one sentence about these neighborhoods that a city council member would understand. Then name one thing this correlation cannot tell you. Check your sentence: does it accidentally make a claim about people rather than neighborhoods?

# a comment-only task

Question 2: among the 200 correctional officers, do officers who have been on the job longer have lower (or higher) job satisfaction? tenure_years is years on the job; job_satisfaction is a 0 to 100 score.
5. Run the recipe again: scatterplot (tenure on the x-axis), then cor.test(officers$tenure_years, officers$job_satisfaction). In a comment: r, the confidence interval, and the p-value. Does the interval include zero? Then write the honest sentence. Careful: failing to reject is not the same as proving there is no relationship.

# your code here

6. (Stretch) Spearman on an ordered category. disorder_level is ordered (Low, Moderate, High, Very High), so Pearson’s r does not fit it, but a rank correlation does. Run this, then say in a comment what it shows about disorder and assaults:

nbhd |>
  mutate(disorder_rank = as.numeric(factor(disorder_level,
    levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High", "Very High")))) |>
  with(cor.test(disorder_rank, assaults, method = "spearman"))

When you are done, submit your script to Canvas. The in-class exercise is graded on completing it.

title: Lab 11 · Logistic Regression: Chicago Neighborhoods, Then Alaska Nights
text:
Goal: run the complete logistic-regression workflow from today’s lecture (glm(family = binomial), coefficients → odds ratios, odds ratios → predicted probabilities, and the Bayesian version with brms), first on the Chicago community areas, then on your own model of intoxicated crashes in the Alaska data.
This is the last lab with new statistical content: everything after today is your project. Treat this hour as a dress rehearsal: the workflow you practice here is exactly the workflow Checkpoint 4 asks for if your project outcome is binary.
How labs work: run the Setup chunk as-is, follow the Walkthrough along with me, then complete the Your Turn tasks in your own script. That script is what you submit to Canvas before you leave.

title: Lab 11 · Logistic Regression: Chicago Neighborhoods, Then Alaska Nights
text:
Setup
Open RStudio, start a new R script, and run:

library(tidyverse)
library(brms)

areas   <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv")
crashes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/crash-ak.csv")







brms is the same package you installed for Project Checkpoint 2 and used in Lab 10: nothing new to install. Same reminder as then: the first brm() of a session pauses at Compiling Stan program... for a minute before sampling. It is not frozen.



Two old friends: the 77 Chicago community areas (Homework 2, and the lecture thread ever since), and the 20,000 Alaska crashes (Lab 4, then Homeworks 5 and 6). Today the crash data plays the role of your project dataset: a binary outcome you care about, predictors you have to build yourself.

title: Lab 11 · Logistic Regression: Chicago Neighborhoods, Then Alaska Nights
text:
Walkthrough
Look at the outcome first
Our binary outcome is high_violence: is the area’s violent-crime rate above the citywide median? It ships in the file, but never trust a variable you haven’t checked:

areas |> count(high_violence)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  high_violence     n
  <lgl>         <int>
1 FALSE            39
2 TRUE             38

areas |>
  summarize(median_violent = median(violent_rate), .by = high_violence)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  high_violence median_violent
  <lgl>                  <dbl>
1 FALSE                   14.1
2 TRUE                    43.0


38 areas above the median, 39 at or below (77 is odd, so the split isn’t exactly even). The group medians are wildly different: the flag means what the codebook says it means.
R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0, so a logical column drops straight into glm(): no conversion needed.
One predictor, seen
Before any multi-predictor model, look at the shape of the relationship. This is the lecture’s curved hill, on real data:

ggplot(areas, aes(unemployment_rate, as.numeric(high_violence))) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.04, width = 0, size = 2.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"),
              se = FALSE, color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Probability of high-violence status rises with unemployment",
       x = "Unemployment rate (%)", y = "High-violence area (0/1)")







Low-unemployment areas pile up at 0, high-unemployment areas at 1, and the fitted curve climbs steeply through the middle: most of the action is between roughly 5% and 15% unemployment.
Fit the model
lm() becomes glm() with family = binomial. That one argument is the entire syntax difference:

v_model <- glm(high_violence ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant,
               data = areas, family = binomial)
summary(v_model)


Call:
glm(formula = high_violence ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant, 
    family = binomial, data = areas)

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)        -5.8208     1.3747  -4.234 2.29e-05 ***
unemployment_rate   0.3699     0.1100   3.363 0.000771 ***
pct_vacant          0.2849     0.1428   1.995 0.046007 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 106.73  on 76  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance:  52.06  on 74  degrees of freedom
AIC: 58.06

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6


Both coefficients are positive with small p-values, but they’re in log-odds, and nobody thinks in log-odds.
Exponentiate: log-odds → odds ratios

exp(cbind(OR = coef(v_model), confint(v_model)))

                           OR        2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept)       0.002965276 0.0001115289 0.02846386
unemployment_rate 1.447590364 1.1934960639 1.84714872
pct_vacant        1.329619347 1.0371047252 1.83804694


Reading it out loud (the skill that matters):


Unemployment, OR ≈ 1.45: each additional percentage point of unemployment multiplies the odds of high-violence status by about 1.45 (45% higher odds), holding vacancy constant.

Vacancy, OR ≈ 1.33: each additional point of vacant housing raises the odds by about 33%, holding unemployment constant.
For odds ratios, the no-effect value is 1 (not 0). Both 95% CIs sit entirely above 1.







The classic mistake: “OR = 1.45 means the probability goes up 45%.” No: the odds go up 45%. Odds = p/(1-p). The two only look alike when p is small. Say “odds” when you mean odds, and use predict() when you want probabilities.



Predicted probabilities: from effects to cases
Odds ratios describe effects; decision-makers ask about places. predict(type = "response") answers on the probability scale:

two_areas <- areas |>
  filter(community %in% c("Forest Glen", "West Garfield Park")) |>
  select(community, unemployment_rate, pct_vacant)

two_areas |>
  mutate(p_high_violence = predict(v_model, newdata = two_areas,
                                   type = "response"))

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  community          unemployment_rate pct_vacant p_high_violence
  <chr>                          <dbl>      <dbl>           <dbl>
1 Forest Glen                      4.2        2.6          0.0286
2 West Garfield Park              18.9       20            0.999 


About a 3% predicted probability for Forest Glen; over 99% for West Garfield Park. And the “by hand” version, so the machinery isn’t a mystery: plug the log-odds prediction into plogis() (the inverse of the logit):

b <- coef(v_model)
unname(plogis(b[1] + b[2] * 4.2 + b[3] * 2.6))   # Forest Glen's values, by hand

[1] 0.02856804


The Bayesian version
Same formula, bernoulli() family, and the same sampler settings as Lab 10’s regression:

v_bayes <- brm(high_violence ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant,
               data = areas, family = bernoulli(),
               chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


exp(fixef(v_bayes)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")])

                     Estimate         Q2.5      Q97.5
Intercept         0.001792006 7.756542e-05 0.02117534
unemployment_rate 1.492292997 1.219122e+00 1.92093080
pct_vacant        1.366238869 1.035275e+00 1.87703700


The posterior odds ratios land near the glm() estimates, and both 95% credible intervals exclude 1. The interpretation you’re allowed to say out loud: “Given the data and priors, there’s a 95% probability the unemployment odds ratio lies in this interval.”

title: Lab 11 · Logistic Regression: Chicago Neighborhoods, Then Alaska Nights
text:
Your Turn
Work in your own script. Comment each answer. The question: what predicts whether an Alaska crash involves an intoxicated driver (intox_any)?
1. Build your predictors. No dataset ships with your analysis variables, so build them with lubridate (it loads with the tidyverse): mdy() turns the month/day/year text in date into a real date, hour() pulls the hour out of time, and wday() gives the day of the week:

crashes <- crashes |>
  mutate(
    date    = mdy(date),                         # text month/day/year -> date
    hour    = hour(time),
    weekend = wday(date, week_start = 1) >= 6,   # Mon = 1 … Sat = 6, Sun = 7
    night   = hour >= 22 | hour < 4              # 10 p.m. to 3:59 a.m.
  )
# Sanity checks before modeling, always:
# a) count(crashes, night) and count(crashes, weekend): plausible shares?
# b) mean(crashes$intox_any): what's the baseline rate you're modeling?

2. Fit and translate. Model intox_any from driver_age, night, and weekend; then exponentiate:

# intox_model <- glm(intox_any ~ driver_age + night + weekend,
#                    data = crashes, family = binomial)
# summary(intox_model)
# exp(cbind(OR = coef(intox_model), confint(intox_model)))

In comments: (a) interpret the night odds ratio in one plain sentence: how much higher are the odds of intoxication involvement at night? (b) interpret weekend the same way; (c) what do you conclude about driver_age? Its interval covers 1: practice saying that no evidence is the finding.
3. Predicted probabilities for two drivers. Contrast a 21-year-old driving on a weekend night with a 45-year-old on a weekday afternoon:

# profiles <- tibble(
#   driver_age = c(21, 45),
#   night      = c(TRUE, FALSE),
#   weekend    = c(TRUE, FALSE)
# )
# profiles |> mutate(p_intox = predict(intox_model, newdata = profiles,
#                                      type = "response"))

In a comment: report both probabilities and compare them to the baseline rate from Task 1b. Notice the night OR is ~2 but neither probability is anywhere near “double 50%”: odds ratios multiply odds, and when p is small, doubled odds is roughly doubled probability, but it does not stay that way as p grows.
4. Odds-ratio translation drills. No fitting: just fluency. For each coefficient below (from hypothetical logistic models), write one sentence: the odds ratio, the direction, and the percent change in odds.

# a) beta = 0.30   (body-camera footage available -> case cleared)
# b) beta = -1.00  (defense counsel at first appearance -> pretrial detention)
# c) beta = 0.00   (defendant age -> failure to appear)
# d) A classmate reads (b) as "the probability of detention drops 63%."
#    In a comment: what did they get wrong, and how would you fix the sentence?

5. (Stretch) One more predictor. Add severity to your crash model. Do the night and weekend odds ratios move much? In a comment: why does “holding the other predictors constant” matter when you tell the story?
When you are done, submit your script to Canvas. The in-class exercise is graded on completing it.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different numbers and variables than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, Homework 2 (and the midterm’s descriptives section) will feel routine.
All problems that use data need only:
library(tidyverse)
library(modeest)   # for mfv(); install.packages("modeest") once if needed
officers <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/officers.csv")
nbhd     <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/neighborhoods.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
text:
Problem 1 · Three kinds of typical
Response times (in minutes) for 10 priority calls one Friday night — nine routine, plus one call that sat in the queue through a shift change:
response <- c(4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 42)
Compute the mean, median, and mode. Which of the three would you not want on the department’s public dashboard, and why?






Tip





Solution

response <- c(4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 42)

mean(response)

[1] 9.8

median(response)

[1] 6

mfv(response)

[1] 6


The one 42-minute call drags the mean to 9.8 minutes even though no routine call took longer than 9 — classic central-tendency behavior: the mean chases outliers, while the median (6) and mode (6) stay with the bulk of the data.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
text:
Problem 2 · Same mean, different story
Two detective units both average 30 open cases per detective — but look at the individual caseloads:
unit_a <- c(18, 30, 42)
unit_b <- c(29, 30, 31)
Compute for each unit: the range (with range() and diff()), the deviations from the mean, the sum of squared deviations, and the population variance and SD by hand. Then run var() and sd() — why don’t the built-ins match your hand calculations?






Tip





Solution

unit_a <- c(18, 30, 42)
unit_b <- c(29, 30, 31)

diff(range(unit_a)); diff(range(unit_b))

[1] 24


[1] 2

unit_a - mean(unit_a)

[1] -12   0  12

unit_b - mean(unit_b)

[1] -1  0  1

# Sum of squares
sum((unit_a - mean(unit_a))^2)

[1] 288

sum((unit_b - mean(unit_b))^2)

[1] 2

# Population variance and SD (divide by n)
sum((unit_a - mean(unit_a))^2) / 3; sqrt(sum((unit_a - mean(unit_a))^2) / 3)

[1] 96


[1] 9.797959

sum((unit_b - mean(unit_b))^2) / 3; sqrt(sum((unit_b - mean(unit_b))^2) / 3)

[1] 0.6666667


[1] 0.8164966

# R's built-ins
var(unit_a); sd(unit_a)

[1] 144


[1] 12

var(unit_b); sd(unit_b)

[1] 1


[1] 1


Identical centers, radically different dispersion: unit A’s SD (~9.8 population / 12 sample) says workloads genuinely vary; unit B’s (~1) says everyone carries the same load. The built-ins disagree with your hand math because R divides by n − 1, not n — Session 4 pays off that IOU.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
text:
Problem 3 · Audit the briefing note
A draft briefing memo about Problem 1’s data contains two sentences:


“The typical priority call waited about 10 minutes for an officer.”
“Half of priority calls had an officer on scene within 6 minutes.”


One is defensible, one is misleading. Which is which — and rewrite the misleading one in a single honest sentence.






Tip





Solution

response <- c(4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 42)
c(mean = mean(response), median = median(response))

  mean median 
   9.8    6.0 


Sentence (b) is defensible — it is exactly what the median (6) means. Sentence (a) launders the mean (9.8) into the word “typical,” but nine of ten calls beat 10 minutes; only the queued outlier pushes the average there. An honest rewrite: “Half of priority calls had an officer within 6 minutes; one call held during a shift change took 42.” With skewed data, “typical” belongs to the median — and outliers deserve their own sentence, not a hiding place inside the mean.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
section: Problem 4 · Real data: how much do officers sleep?
text:
Problem 4 · Real data: how much do officers sleep?
Using officers, summarize sleep_hours — mean, median, SD, min, max — and make a histogram (binwidth = 0.5). Is the distribution roughly symmetric or skewed? How do you know from the numbers alone?






Tip





Solution

officers |>
  summarize(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours), median_sleep = median(sleep_hours),
            sd_sleep = sd(sleep_hours), min = min(sleep_hours), max = max(sleep_hours))

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  mean_sleep median_sleep sd_sleep   min   max
       <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1       6.40          6.4     1.40   2.5    10

ggplot(officers, aes(sleep_hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Sleep per night (hours)", y = "Officers")







Mean (6.40) and median (6.4) are essentially identical — the numeric signature of a roughly symmetric distribution, which the histogram confirms. (Compare Problem 1, where mean and median disagreed badly: that gap is the skew detector.)

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
section: Problem 5 · The empirical rule, checked against reality
text:
Problem 5 · The empirical rule, checked against reality
If sleep_hours were perfectly normal, about 68% of officers would fall within ±1 SD of the mean and about 95% within ±2 SD. Compute the actual shares. (Hint: mean(abs(x - m) <= s) — the same mean-of-a-logical move as always.)






Tip





Solution

m <- mean(officers$sleep_hours)
s <- sd(officers$sleep_hours)

mean(abs(officers$sleep_hours - m) <= s)       # within +/- 1 SD

[1] 0.695

mean(abs(officers$sleep_hours - m) <= 2 * s)   # within +/- 2 SD

[1] 0.955


About 69.5% and 95.5% — within a couple points of the empirical rule’s 68/95 benchmarks. That is what “the SD tells you how typical or extreme a value is” means in practice: for bell-shaped data, mean ± 2 SD brackets nearly everyone.

title: Practice Problems · Session 2
section: Problem 6 · A Poisson in the wild
text:
Problem 6 · A Poisson in the wild
Using nbhd (500 neighborhoods), make a bar chart of assaults (last year’s count per neighborhood), then compute its mean and variance. Now simulate 500 draws from a Poisson with the same λ — rpois(500, lambda = mean(nbhd$assaults)) — and compare the two count tables. Does the textbook distribution fit the real one?






Tip





Solution

ggplot(nbhd, aes(assaults)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Assaults last year", y = "Neighborhoods")






nbhd |> summarize(mean_assaults = mean(assaults), var_assaults = var(assaults))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_assaults var_assaults
          <dbl>        <dbl>
1          1.07         1.69

set.seed(705)
table(nbhd$assaults)


  0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7 
219 134  87  32  17   4   5   2 

table(rpois(500, lambda = mean(nbhd$assaults)))


  0   1   2   3   4   5 
148 192 102  45  11   2 


The broad shape matches — right-skewed counts of a rare event, exactly the Poisson’s territory. But look closer: the real data have more zeros (219 vs ~148) and a longer tail (counts up to 7 vs 5), and the variance (1.69) exceeds the mean (1.07), where a true Poisson would have them equal. Real CJ counts are usually messier than the textbook distribution — a mismatch called overdispersion that you’ll meet again later in the course.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different numbers and variables than the homework on purpose — if you can do these cold, Homework 4 (and the midterm’s sampling questions) will feel routine. Your random numbers will differ from the solutions’ unless you run set.seed(705) immediately before each simulation — close is what you’re checking for, not digit-for-digit matches.
All problems that use data need only:
library(tidyverse)
nbhd <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/neighborhoods.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
section: Problem 1 · The long run arrives slowly
text:
Problem 1 · The long run arrives slowly
Suppose 12% of intake drug screens at a jail come back positive. Simulate one week (25 screens), one quarter (250), and one decade (25,000) with sample(), and compute the positive proportion for each. How close does each get to 0.12?






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
mean(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 25,    replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.12, 0.88)))

[1] 0.2

mean(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 250,   replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.12, 0.88)))

[1] 0.156

mean(sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 25000, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.12, 0.88)))

[1] 0.12204


This run: ≈ 0.20, ≈ 0.16, ≈ 0.122. A week of screens can sit far from the truth; a decade practically is the truth — the law of large numbers. The practical warning runs the other way: any rate computed from 25 cases deserves deep suspicion.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
text:
Problem 2 · Build a sampling distribution
Treat the 500 neighborhoods in nbhd as a population, and imagine an analyst who can only audit 40 neighborhoods at a time. Using the tibble() + map_dbl() pattern from the Session 4 slides, draw 1,000 samples of 40 and keep each sample’s mean of assaults. Histogram the 1,000 means and mark the true population mean with a geom_vline(). Where is the distribution centered?






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
sample_means <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(mean_assaults = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(nbhd$assaults, size = 40))))

mean(nbhd$assaults)                 # the truth

[1] 1.072

mean(sample_means$mean_assaults)    # center of the 1,000 sample means

[1] 1.056875

ggplot(sample_means, aes(mean_assaults)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(nbhd$assaults), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean assaults (n = 40)", y = "Number of samples")







The 1,000 means pile up in a bell centered almost exactly on the true mean (≈ 1.06 vs 1.07 this run) — a sampling distribution in action: individual samples wander, but the collection of sample means is centered on the truth.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
section: Problem 3 · The standard error, both ways
text:
Problem 3 · The standard error, both ways
Session 4’s rule: the formula must survive a simulation check. Compute the SD of your 1,000 sample means from Problem 2, then the formula version sd(nbhd$assaults) / sqrt(40). How close?






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
sample_means <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(mean_assaults = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(nbhd$assaults, size = 40))))

sd(sample_means$mean_assaults)     # SE from the simulation

[1] 0.196668

sd(nbhd$assaults) / sqrt(40)       # SE from the formula

[1] 0.2058036


≈ 0.20 simulated vs ≈ 0.21 from the formula — the standard error is just the SD of the sampling distribution, and SD / sqrt(n) predicts it without ever running the simulation. That’s why one sample plus the formula is enough for the inference we start next session.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
text:
Problem 4 · Spot the error
A report on the Problem 2 audit states:

“The standard error of about 0.21 tells us how much individual neighborhoods vary around the citywide average.”

Fix the sentence. Then: if the analyst’s budget grew to n = 160 neighborhoods per audit, what would happen to the SE? Verify with the formula.






Tip





Solution

c(se_40  = sd(nbhd$assaults) / sqrt(40),
  se_160 = sd(nbhd$assaults) / sqrt(160))

    se_40    se_160 
0.2058036 0.1029018 


Wrong quantity: describing how individual neighborhoods vary is the standard deviation’s job (≈ 1.3 here). The standard error describes how much the sample mean would move across repeated audits of 40 — a fix: “If we re-drew the 40-neighborhood audit, the estimated mean would typically shift by about 0.21 assaults.” And quadrupling n to 160 halves the SE (≈ 0.21 → ≈ 0.10) — precision grows with √n, so it gets expensive fast.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
section: Problem 5 · The CLT on a yes/no variable
text:
Problem 5 · The CLT on a yes/no variable
The variable hoa is about as non-normal as data gets — every neighborhood is simply "Yes" or "No". Compute the true population proportion of HOA neighborhoods, then draw 1,000 samples of 60 and keep each sample’s proportion (mean(sample(nbhd$hoa, size = 60) == "Yes")). Histogram the 1,000 proportions. What shape appears, and which theorem predicted it?






Tip





Solution

mean(nbhd$hoa == "Yes")            # true population proportion

[1] 0.354

set.seed(705)
hoa_props <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(prop_hoa = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(nbhd$hoa, size = 60) == "Yes")))

ggplot(hoa_props, aes(prop_hoa)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(nbhd$hoa == "Yes"), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Sample proportion with an HOA (n = 60)", y = "Number of samples")







A two-category population, yet the sample proportions form an approximately normal bell centered on the truth (0.354) — the central limit theorem. It’s the same magic as the homework’s arrest proportions, and it’s why we can attach a standard error to any rate without the raw data ever looking normal.

title: Practice Problems · Session 4
section: Problem 6 · Why n − 1, re-proven on counts
text:
Problem 6 · Why n − 1, re-proven on counts
Session 4 paid the n − 1 IOU with test scores; make it pay again with skewed count data. Draw 2,000 tiny samples of n = 4 from nbhd$assaults and compute each sample’s variance both ways — dividing by n, and with var() (which divides by n − 1). Compare the two averages to the true population variance, mean((x - mean(x))^2). (The slides’ list-column pattern — one map(), then two map_dbl()s — is the move.)






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
var_sims <- tibble(draw = 1:2000) |>
  mutate(
    s           = map(draw, \(d) sample(nbhd$assaults, size = 4)),
    var_div_n   = map_dbl(s, \(x) sum((x - mean(x))^2) / length(x)),
    var_div_nm1 = map_dbl(s, \(x) var(x))
  )

var_sims |>
  summarize(
    true_variance           = mean((nbhd$assaults - mean(nbhd$assaults))^2),
    avg_divide_by_n         = mean(var_div_n),
    avg_divide_by_n_minus_1 = mean(var_div_nm1)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  true_variance avg_divide_by_n avg_divide_by_n_minus_1
          <dbl>           <dbl>                   <dbl>
1          1.69            1.28                    1.71


Dividing by n lands around 1.28 — about 25% below the true variance (≈ 1.69) — while var() averages ≈ 1.7, right on target. Nothing about this trick required bell-shaped data: a sample clusters around its own mean, understating spread, and n − 1 is exactly the correction that makes the estimator unbiased.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different questions and numbers than the homework on purpose — if you can run and read both traditions cold here, Homework 6 will feel routine.
All problems that use data need only:
library(tidyverse)
source("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/R/bayes.R")   # gives you bayes_prop_test()
crimes <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-crimes-2025.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
text:
Problem 1 · What a p-value promises
A study compares case-processing times in two courts and reports p = 0.03. Three readings:


“There is a 3% chance the courts truly process cases at the same speed.”
“If the courts truly processed cases at the same speed, a gap this large or larger would show up in about 3% of studies like this one.”
“There is a 97% chance the courts differ.”


Pick the correct one. Then verify the machinery’s actual promise by simulation: run 5,000 t-tests comparing two groups drawn from the same normal distribution (n = 40 each) and compute how often p < .05.






Tip





Solution

set.seed(705)
null_world_p <- replicate(5000, t.test(rnorm(40), rnorm(40))$p.value)
mean(null_world_p < 0.05)

[1] 0.0552


(b) — and only (b). A p-value is \(P(\text{data this extreme} \mid H_0)\), a statement about data under an assumed null; (a) and (c) both flip it into \(P(H \mid \text{data})\), which frequentism never computes (that flip is Bayes’ job, and it costs a prior). The simulation shows the promise being kept: in a world where the null is true, about 5.5% of our 5,000 tests came up “significant” — right around the advertised 5% false-alarm rate, and no better.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
text:
Problem 2 · Which finding is bigger?
Two studies of body-worn cameras and citizen complaints. Study A (50,000 police stops): 20.8% of stops without a camera drew a complaint vs 20.0% with one, p = 0.03. Study B (40 stops): 70% vs 40%, p = 0.11. A headline writer says A “found an effect” and B “found nothing.” Check both with prop.test() (A: 5,200 of 25,000 vs 5,000 of 25,000; B: 14 of 20 vs 8 of 20), then say what the headline gets wrong.






Tip





Solution

prop.test(x = c(5200, 5000), n = c(25000, 25000))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(5200, 5000) out of c(25000, 25000)
X-squared = 4.8775, df = 1, p-value = 0.02721
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.0008961201 0.0151038799
sample estimates:
prop 1 prop 2 
 0.208  0.200 

prop.test(x = c(14, 8), n = c(20, 20))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(14, 8) out of c(20, 20)
X-squared = 2.5253, df = 1, p-value = 0.112
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.0439946  0.6439946
sample estimates:
prop 1 prop 2 
   0.7    0.4 


Study A’s gap is 0.8 of a percentage point (interval about 0.1 to 1.5 points): real, probably, and tiny. Study B’s gap is 30 points, with an interval from about 4 points lower to 64 points higher: possibly huge, possibly nothing, because 40 stops cannot tell. The p-value measures how detectable a gap is, and detectability is mostly sample size. It never measures how big the gap is. “Significant” is not “large,” and “not significant” is not “nothing.”

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
section: Problem 3 · Both tests, one new question
text:
Problem 3 · Both tests, one new question
Are crimes on the street more likely to end in an arrest than crimes inside a residence? Filter crimes to location_description %in% c("STREET", "RESIDENCE"), count arrests by location, and run both tests with STREET first: prop.test() and bayes_prop_test().






Tip





Solution

crimes |>
  filter(location_description %in% c("STREET", "RESIDENCE")) |>
  count(location_description, arrest)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  location_description arrest     n
  <chr>                <lgl>  <int>
1 RESIDENCE            FALSE   3248
2 RESIDENCE            TRUE     339
3 STREET               FALSE   6533
4 STREET               TRUE    1374

prop.test(x = c(1374, 339), n = c(7907, 3587))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(1374, 339) out of c(7907, 3587)
X-squared = 121.61, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.06635519 0.09216907
sample estimates:
    prop 1     prop 2 
0.17377008 0.09450795 

bayes_prop_test(x = c(1374, 339), n = c(7907, 3587))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  1,374 of 7,907 (17.4%)
data, group 2:  339 of 3,587 (9.5%)
prior:          know-nothing (1 yes, 1 no), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  17.4%         16.6% to 18.2%
group 2                  9.5%          8.5% to 10.5%
difference (1 minus 2)   7.9 points    6.6 to 9.2 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: more than 0.99 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  less than 0.01 


Street: 1,374 arrests out of 1,374 + 6,533 = 7,907 (17.4%). Residence: 339 out of 339 + 3,248 = 3,587 (9.5%). STREET was typed first, so both outputs read STREET minus RESIDENCE. prop.test(): 95% confidence interval about 6.6 to 9.2 points, p-value < 2.2e-16, reject the null. bayes_prop_test(): 95% credible interval about 6.6 to 9.2 points. With more than 11,000 incidents the two traditions return the same range; the data drown out the know-nothing prior.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
section: Problem 4 · How big, in real units
text:
Problem 4 · How big, in real units
Both tests just endorsed the street-vs-residence difference. Before anyone acts on it, say how big it is in words a city council member would follow, with no p-value and no interval. Then say what the tests cannot tell the council.






Tip





Solution
About 17 of every 100 street incidents end in an arrest, against about 10 of every 100 incidents inside a residence: roughly 8 more arrests per 100 incidents. That is the size. Whether 8 per 100 is big enough to matter, and why the gap exists (different crime types happen on the street, officers are already nearby, witnesses are present), no test can say. Both tests tell you the gap is almost surely real. Neither tells you it is important, and neither tells you what causes it.

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
section: Problem 5 · The sentence you’re licensed to say
text:
Problem 5 · The sentence you’re licensed to say
Session 5 forbade “there’s a 95% probability the truth is in this interval.” Using Problem 3’s two outputs, write (1) the honest sentence for the confidence interval and (2) the sentence the credible interval lets you say. The numbers are the same. What is different?






Tip





Solution

Confidence interval: “We estimate the street arrest rate is 7.9 points higher (95% CI: 6.6 to 9.2); the method that built this interval captures the truth 95% of the time.” The 95% belongs to the procedure.
Credible interval: “Given these data, there is a 95% probability that the true difference is between 6.6 and 9.2 points.” The 95% belongs to this interval. That is the sentence everyone wants to say about a confidence interval, and only the Bayesian output licenses it, at the price of a stated prior (here, “know nothing”).

title: Practice Problems · Session 6
text:
Problem 6 · The diversion-program trial
A county pilots a pretrial diversion program to reduce failures to appear (FTA). Historically, about 25% of defendants fail to appear, and the county trusts that figure about as much as having watched 12 defendants: 3 failed to appear, 9 showed up. That is prior = c(3, 9). The pilot randomizes 120 defendants: of 60 diversion clients, 12 fail to appear; of 60 controls, 19 do.

Run the frequentist test, diversion first: prop.test(x = c(12, 19), n = c(60, 60)).
Run bayes_prop_test() with the same numbers and the prior.
Write one sentence for the county board.







Tip





Solution

prop.test(x = c(12, 19), n = c(60, 60))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(12, 19) out of c(60, 60)
X-squared = 1.5658, df = 1, p-value = 0.2108
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.28856877  0.05523544
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.2000000 0.3166667 

bayes_prop_test(x = c(12, 19), n = c(60, 60), prior = c(3, 9))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  12 of 60 (20.0%)
data, group 2:  19 of 60 (31.7%)
prior:          3 yes, 9 no (about 25%, worth 12 cases), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  20.8%         12.3% to 30.9%
group 2                  30.6%         20.5% to 41.6%
difference (1 minus 2)   -9.7 points   -23.7 to 4.4 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: 0.09 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  0.91 


The frequentist verdict: p ≈ 0.21 — an 11.7-point gap like this could plausibly arise if the program did nothing, so “not significant,” and the grant report probably ends there. The Bayesian output tells the board what it actually asked: given prior experience and the pilot data, there is about a 91% probability the diversion program lowers failure-to-appear (credible interval for the difference about −24 to +4 points). One board-ready sentence: “The pilot is too small for a definitive verdict, but the evidence currently runs about 9-to-1 that diversion reduces failures to appear.” Both statements are true of the same data — they answer different questions, and only one of them helps a decision-maker.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
text:
Ungraded self-checks. Work each problem in your own R session before clicking the solution. These use different data and variables than the homework on purpose: if you can do these cold, Homework 10 (and Checkpoint 3’s first regression on your own data) will feel routine.
Problems that use data need only this setup: the same 100 cities as the Session 8 practice bank, where poverty and the violent-crime rate ran r = .61. Correlation said the two travel together; regression asks how much, and what a second predictor changes. One row = one city: every sentence you write stays at that level.
library(tidyverse)
library(brms)   # Problem 5 only: expect the usual compile pause
library(car)    # for vif()

cities <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/cities-wide.csv")

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
section: Problem 1 · One predictor: make the slope speak units
text:
Problem 1 · One predictor: make the slope speak units
Regress vcr_2025 (violent crimes per 100,000 residents) on poverty_rate (percentage points). Interpret the slope with units, say what the intercept means here (and whether any real city lives there), and connect R² to Session 8’s r = .61.






Tip





Solution

city_m1 <- lm(vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate, data = cities)
summary(city_m1)


Call:
lm(formula = vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate, data = cities)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-477.63  -91.04   13.49   94.26  390.25 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   110.298     37.778   2.920  0.00435 ** 
poverty_rate   14.461      1.906   7.586 1.92e-11 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 150.8 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:   0.37, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3635 
F-statistic: 57.54 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 1.92e-11

cor(cities$poverty_rate, cities$vcr_2025)^2

[1] 0.3699531




Slope ≈ 14.5: each additional percentage point of city poverty is associated with about 14.5 more violent crimes per 100,000 residents, in this sample. Units on both ends or the number means nothing.

Intercept ≈ 110: the predicted rate for a city with 0% poverty: no city in the data comes close (the minimum is 4.4%), so it anchors the line rather than describing anywhere real.

R² = .37, which is exactly .61²: with one predictor, R² is Session 8’s correlation squared, so poverty accounts for about 37% of the city-to-city variance in violent-crime rates, leaving 63% to everything else.

A slope is a rate with units (outcome units per predictor unit); R² is the share of outcome variance the model captures: two different questions about the same line.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
section: Problem 2 · A second predictor: does it earn its keep?
text:
Problem 2 · A second predictor: does it earn its keep?
Cities differ in police staffing too. Add police_per_10k (sworn officers per 10,000 residents) to the model. Compare the poverty slope across the two models, interpret the staffing coefficient with its 95% CI, and check what happens to adjusted R². Then write the honest one-sentence conclusion about staffing.






Tip





Solution

city_m2 <- lm(vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate + police_per_10k, data = cities)
summary(city_m2)


Call:
lm(formula = vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate + police_per_10k, data = cities)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-448.76  -91.34    5.14   85.70  379.28 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     179.978     59.917   3.004  0.00339 ** 
poverty_rate     14.592      1.897   7.694 1.19e-11 ***
police_per_10k   -3.232      2.166  -1.492  0.13889    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 149.9 on 97 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3841,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3714 
F-statistic: 30.25 on 2 and 97 DF,  p-value: 6.188e-11

confint(city_m2)

                   2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept)    61.060105 298.896503
poverty_rate   10.828022  18.356175
police_per_10k -7.530335   1.066661

c(adj_m1 = summary(city_m1)$adj.r.squared,
  adj_m2 = summary(city_m2)$adj.r.squared)

   adj_m1    adj_m2 
0.3635241 0.3713927 


The poverty slope barely moves (14.46 → 14.59): poverty and staffing are nearly uncorrelated here (r ≈ .05), so there was almost no shared variance to reapportion. The staffing coefficient is -3.2 violent crimes per 100k per additional officer per 10k residents, 95% CI [-7.5, 1.1], p = .14: the interval spans zero, and adjusted R² ticks up only trivially (.364 → .371). The honest sentence: “Holding poverty constant, police staffing showed no reliable association with the violent-crime rate in these cities.” A new predictor has to earn its coefficient; a CI straddling zero and a flat adjusted R² is the data declining the offer, and saying so is a legitimate finding.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
section: Problem 3 · The lurking third variable, caught in the act
text:
Problem 3 · The lurking third variable, caught in the act
Across 90 towns, an analyst finds that towns with more licensed pawn shops report far more burglaries, and drafts a memo proposing pawn-shop license caps. Simulate the analyst’s data: note what actually generates both variables:

set.seed(705)   # inline seed: keeps this particular draw stable
towns <- tibble(
  population = runif(90, 10, 120),                        # thousands of residents
  pawn_shops = 1 + 0.09 * population + rnorm(90, 0, 1.4),
  burglaries = 30 + 5.5 * population + rnorm(90, 0, 55)   # per year
)


Fit burglaries ~ pawn_shops. How does the coefficient look, and does anything in the output warn you it’s misleading?
Now add population. What happens to the pawn-shop coefficient, and what does that tell the memo’s author?







Tip





Solution

lm(burglaries ~ pawn_shops, data = towns) |> summary() |> coef() |> round(3)

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   63.323     25.188   2.514    0.014
pawn_shops    48.350      3.217  15.031    0.000

lm(burglaries ~ pawn_shops + population, data = towns) |> summary() |> coef() |> round(3)

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   37.007     12.830   2.884    0.005
pawn_shops     1.365      3.347   0.408    0.684
population     5.290      0.329  16.056    0.000



About 48 more burglaries per additional pawn shop, p < .001 by a mile, and nothing in the output warns you. The model can only see the variables you gave it.
Holding population constant, the pawn-shop coefficient collapses to ≈ 1.4 with p ≈ .68 (nothing), while population comes in at ≈ 5.3 burglaries per additional thousand residents. Bigger towns simply have more of both. That collapse is “holding constant” doing real work: comparing towns of the same size, pawn-shop counts tell you nothing about burglary. And the sobering corollary: regression can only hold constant the lurkers you measured and included; the ones you didn’t are still at large.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
section: Problem 4 · Diagnostics: the residual plot and VIF
text:
Problem 4 · Diagnostics: the residual plot and VIF
Back to the real model, city_m2 from Problem 2. Make the residuals-vs-fitted plot and run vif(). For each: what is it checking, and what does it show here?






Tip





Solution

tibble(fitted = fitted(city_m2), residual = resid(city_m2)) |>
  ggplot(aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, color = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Fitted violent-crime rate", y = "Residual")






vif(city_m2)

  poverty_rate police_per_10k 
      1.002158       1.002158 


The residual plot checks whether the model’s misses are patternless: no curve (the straight-line shape isn’t visibly wrong) and roughly even spread across the fitted range. This one is what healthy looks like: a shapeless band centered on zero, no bend, no widening, with the biggest misses (reaching roughly ±400) scattered across the range rather than piling up at one end. Compare Lab 10’s Chicago plot, where the spread visibly widened at high fitted values; that’s the kind of pattern this plot exists to catch.
VIF checks a different disease: predictor redundancy. Both values sit at ≈ 1.00 (poverty and staffing share almost nothing, r ≈ .05), so each coefficient is estimated on its own information. The residual plot audits the misses; VIF audits the predictors: one model, two separate health checks.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
section: Problem 5 · Both traditions, one sentence each
text:
Problem 5 · Both traditions, one sentence each
Fit the Bayesian twin of city_m2 with brm() (expect the Compiling Stan program… pause: normal, not frozen), look at the posterior summaries, and then write the pair of reporting sentences: one frequentist (estimate, CI, p) and one Bayesian (the credible-interval sentence you’re allowed to say) about the poverty coefficient.






Tip





Solution

city_bayes <- brm(vcr_2025 ~ poverty_rate + police_per_10k, data = cities,
                  chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


fixef(city_bayes) |> round(2)

               Estimate Est.Error  Q2.5  Q97.5
Intercept        178.32     60.45 62.08 294.22
poverty_rate      14.65      1.97 10.71  18.35
police_per_10k    -3.18      2.20 -7.46   1.01


The posterior lands almost exactly on lm()’s estimates, as expected with brms default priors (say so when you report: “brms default priors, 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705”) and 100 cities of data.

Frequentist: “Holding police staffing constant, each additional percentage point of poverty was associated with about 14.6 more violent crimes per 100,000 residents (b = 14.59, 95% CI [10.8, 18.4], p < .001).”


Bayesian: “Given the data and priors, there is a 95% probability the poverty coefficient lies between roughly 10.9 and 18.3: zero is not a credible value.”

Same formula, nearly identical numbers: what changes is the sentence each tradition licenses, and the Bayesian one makes the direct probability statement the confidence interval never could.

title: Practice Problems · Session 10
text:
Problem 6 · The sentence audit
Four sentences drafted from the Problem 2 model. Two are defensible; two are not. Sort them, and fix the broken ones.


“Holding police staffing constant, each additional percentage point of poverty was associated with about 14.6 more violent crimes per 100,000 residents (95% CI [10.8, 18.4]).”
“Poverty drives up violent crime in American cities.”
“R² = .38, so the model correctly predicts 38% of cities.”
“Police staffing showed no reliable association with the violent-crime rate in these cities (b = -3.2, 95% CI [-7.5, 1.1]).”








Tip





Solution

confint(city_m2) |> round(1)

               2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept)     61.1  298.9
poverty_rate    10.8   18.4
police_per_10k  -7.5    1.1

summary(city_m2)$r.squared

[1] 0.3840918


Defensible: (a) and (d). Both state an adjusted association, with magnitude, units, uncertainty, and the holding-constant clause, and (d) shows that “no reliable association” is a reportable result, not a failure.
(b) fails twice: “drives up” is a causal verb no cross-sectional model earns (lurkers we never measured are still at large: Problem 3’s lesson), and “American cities” generalizes a 100-city sample to a population the data can’t speak for. Fix: “In these 100 cities, higher poverty was associated with higher violent-crime rates, holding staffing constant.”
(c) misreads R²: .38 is the share of variance in the outcome the model accounts for, not an accuracy rate, and not a count of cities predicted “correctly.” Fix: “The two predictors together account for about 38% of the city-to-city variance in violent-crime rates.” The audit habit: check every regression sentence for causal verbs, level of analysis, units, and what R² actually is.

title: Final-Project Data Options
text: Your final project needs a real criminal justice dataset. This page is a menu: eight datasets that are ready to use, each loadable with one line of R, plus a few places to look if none of them fits your question. Explore at least two this week (that is Homework 7), then choose one.

title: Final-Project Data Options
section: Two ways to load a dataset
text:
Two ways to load a dataset
Every dataset below has a course copy you load the way you have loaded everything this semester. Run library(tidyverse) first, once per session:
library(tidyverse)
arrests <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/toronto-arrests.csv")
Several also live in an R package, which is where the course copy came from. That route needs a one-time install:
install.packages("carData")   # once, typed in the console, not in your script
library(carData)
data(Arrests)                 # now there is an object called Arrests
Same data either way. The course copy is simpler, so it is what the examples below use.

title: Final-Project Data Options
section: How to size up a dataset in five minutes
text:
How to size up a dataset in five minutes

What is one row? A person? An arrest? A stop? A state?
How many rows? Hundreds is plenty; millions is a headache
What are the variables? glimpse(your_data) gives every name and type
Anything strange? summary(your_data) shows impossible values (999s, negative ages) and NAs
Could it answer a question you care about? Name the two groups and the outcome, or the variables you would relate

“Limited” means most of the variables are categories rather than numbers, so a regression is possible (logistic, with categories as predictors) but you will have fewer choices. Ask me before you commit to one of those.

Rossi reentry experiment
432 men released from Maryland state prisons in the 1970s, followed for one year. Half were randomly assigned to receive financial aid. We used it in Session 7 (aid vs. no aid).

Key variables: arrest (1 = arrested within the year), week (week of first arrest; 52 if never), fin (financial aid), age, prio (number of prior convictions), wexp (work experience before prison), mar (married), paro (released on parole), educ (education level, coded 2 to 6), race
Numbers for regression: age, prio, week, educ
Starter question: were men released on parole re-arrested less often than men released without it?
Quirks: the original has 52 weekly employment columns (emp1 to emp52); the course copy leaves them out. educ is a code, not years: 2 = 6th grade or less, 3 = 7th to 9th, 4 = 10th to 11th, 5 = 12th, 6 = some college.

rossi <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/rossi.csv")
Original: carData package, data(Rossi). Rossi, Berk & Lenihan (1980), Money, Work, and Crime.


Toronto arrests
5,226 arrests by Toronto police for possession of small amounts of marijuana, 1997 to 2002, from a Toronto Star investigation. We used it in Session 7 (employed vs. not).

Key variables: released (released with a summons instead of held for a bail hearing), employed, citizen, sex, age, year, checks (how many of six police databases, such as prior arrests or parole, had the person’s name), colour
Numbers for regression: age, checks, year
Starter question: were citizens released with a summons more often than non-citizens?

arrests <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/toronto-arrests.csv")
Original: carData package, data(Arrests).


Minneapolis police stops
Nearly every stop the Minneapolis Police Department made in 2017. We used it in Lab 7 (searches in suspicious-person vs. traffic stops).

Key variables: problem (suspicious or traffic), citationIssued, personSearch, vehicleSearch, gender, policePrecinct (1 to 5), neighborhood, date, MDC, race, preRace
Numbers for regression: almost none (location and date). Outcomes are yes/no, so this one points toward logistic regression with categorical predictors
Starter question: among people stopped, were men searched more often than women?
Quirks: personSearch, vehicleSearch, and gender were recorded only for stops entered from a squad car’s computer (MDC), so the 8,221 stops by officers on foot, bike, or horseback show NA for them. citationIssued is missing for about 63% of all stops, so be careful building a question on it. NA means “not recorded,” not “no.”

stops <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/mpls-stops.csv")
Original: carData package, data(MplsStops); the Minneapolis open data portal has more years.


Fatal police shootings
The Washington Post’s database of every person shot and killed by an on-duty police officer in the United States, 2015 through 2024. We used it in Session 7 and Lab 7.

Key variables: date, state, city, armed_with, threat_type, flee_status, was_mental_illness_related, body_camera, age, gender, race
Numbers for regression: age only, at the level of the person. (Counting shootings by state or year opens more doors, but that takes skills we have not covered yet.)
Starter question: was a body camera reported more often when the person was in a mental health crisis?
Quirks: each row is a person who died, and the file includes names. Treat it with care, and leave names out of anything you show. This one is not copied to the course site; it is read straight from the Post.

shootings <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/washingtonpost/data-police-shootings/master/v2/fatal-police-shootings-data.csv")
Source: github.com/washingtonpost/data-police-shootings. License CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.


COMPAS risk scores
People arrested in Broward County, Florida, in 2013 and 2014, scored by the COMPAS pretrial risk-assessment tool, then followed for two years by ProPublica. We used it in Lab 7 (High vs. Low labels).

Key variables: two_year_recid (1 = arrested again within two years), score_text (Low, Medium, High), age, sex, priors_count...15 (number of prior offenses), juv_fel_count, juv_misd_count, c_charge_degree (F = felony, M = misdemeanor), race
Numbers for regression: several: age, the prior-count columns, the juvenile counts, the decile score
Starter question: were people charged with a felony re-arrested more often than people charged with a misdemeanor?
Quirks: 53 columns, many of them dates and case numbers you will not need. The file has two columns named decile_score and two named priors_count, so R renames them (the New names: message). The file includes names; leave them out of anything you show. Read straight from ProPublica.

compas <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/propublica/compas-analysis/master/compas-scores-two-years.csv")
Source: github.com/propublica/compas-analysis and ProPublica’s 2016 article “Machine Bias.”


GSS 2024: crime and justice attitudes
The General Social Survey, a national survey of U.S. adults run since 1972. The course copy keeps the 2024 respondents and the questions about crime, courts, guns, and police, plus basic background questions.

Key variables:

fear: afraid to walk alone at night in your neighborhood?
cappun: death penalty for murder
gunlaw: require a police permit to buy a gun
owngun: gun in the home
courts: courts too harsh or not harsh enough
grass: legalize marijuana
natcrime: spending on halting rising crime
polhitok, polabuse, polattak: when is it OK for police to strike a citizen
background: sex, degree, region, partyid, polviews

Numbers for regression: age, educ (years of school), coninc (family income in constant dollars)
Starter question: are women more likely than men to be afraid to walk alone at night in their neighborhood?
Quirks: the GSS asks each question of only part of the sample (a “split ballot”), so most questions have NA for somewhere between a third and three-quarters of people. NA means “not asked” or “no answer,” not “no.” Ages 89 and older are all coded 89.

gss <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/gss-2024-cj.csv")
Source: NORC at the University of Chicago, gss.norc.org. The full 2024 file has 813 variables, if you want to look for more.


U.S. states, 1960
A classic criminology dataset on crime and punishment across 47 states in 1960 (Ehrlich, 1973).

Key variables: y (crime rate), So (1 = Southern state), Prob (probability of imprisonment), Time (average time served), Po1 (police spending), Ed (schooling), U1, U2 (unemployment), Ineq (income inequality), GDP, M (share of young men)
Numbers for regression: nearly everything; this one was built for regression
Starter question: did Southern states have higher crime rates than the rest?
Quirks: only 47 rows, and several columns were rescaled to convenient numbers (for example, Ed is years of schooling times 10). Read ?MASS::UScrime before you interpret a number.

uscrime <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/uscrime.csv")
Original: the MASS package, which comes with R (nothing to install): MASS::UScrime.


U.S. arrest rates, 1973
Arrests per 100,000 residents for murder, assault, and rape in each of the 50 states in 1973, plus the percent of each state’s population living in cities.

Key variables: state, Murder, Assault, Rape, UrbanPop
Numbers for regression: all four, but only 50 rows and four variables
Starter question: do more urban states have higher assault arrest rates? (Split UrbanPop into two groups now; in Session 8 you will be able to use it as a number.)
Quirks: small and old. Fine for learning, thin for a whole project unless you pair it with a clear question.

usarrests <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/usarrests.csv")
Original: built into R, no package needed: USArrests.

title: Final-Project Data Options
text:
Finding your own
If your question needs something else, these are good places to look. Check with me before you commit, and prefer a single CSV that downloads directly.

City open data portals. Chicago, New York, Los Angeles, Dallas, and dozens of other cities post crime incidents, arrests, stops, and use-of-force reports. Search “[city name] open data police.”
The Stanford Open Policing Project (openpolicing.stanford.edu): traffic stops from dozens of states and cities. The files are large; pick one city.
NACJD at ICPSR (icpsr.umich.edu/web/NACJD): the national archive of criminal justice research data. Excellent, but many files come in SPSS or Stata formats and need a free account.
The Bureau of Justice Statistics (bjs.ojp.gov): national statistics on jails, prisons, victimization, and courts, mostly as summary tables.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
This Week
Topic: Descriptive statistics and statistical vocabulary

Measures of central tendency
Measures of dispersion
Distributions and their shapes

Learning goals: define in your own words — mean, median, mode, variance, standard deviation, histogram, normal distribution, Poisson distribution — and use R to describe a small dataset and plot a distribution.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Two Threads, One Course
Starting today, every week builds two things at once — watch for this slide each session:


Statistics thread — lecture + homework
Stanton Ch. 1 → describing data: center, spread, and distribution shapes

Wrangling thread — lab
R4DS Ch. 1–2 → ggplot2: histograms, bar charts, boxplots

Two threads on purpose: the stats thread makes you a careful consumer of evidence; the wrangling thread is why your final project won’t hurt. They merge at the Session 7 workshop.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Three Ways to Say “Typical”



Measure
Meaning




Mean
the average


Median
the halfway point


Mode
the most frequently occurring value



Measures of central tendency summarize a vector of data by locating the typical, the middle, or the most common point.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Mean

rainfall <- c(0, 0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 4)   # rain each day this week

# The hard way:
sum(rainfall) / length(rainfall)

[1] 1.142857




# The easy way:
mean(rainfall)

[1] 1.142857

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Median

rainfall

[1] 0 0 0 2 1 1 4

sort(rainfall)   # middle value of the sorted data?

[1] 0 0 0 1 1 2 4




median(rainfall)

[1] 1

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — The Mode

rainfall          # which value appears most often?

[1] 0 0 0 2 1 1 4

library(modeest)  # install.packages("modeest") once, library() every session
mfv(rainfall)     # mfv = "most frequent value"

[1] 0

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
What Do These Look Like?

stats <- tibble(
  measure = c("Mean", "Median", "Mode"),
  value = c(mean(rainfall), median(rainfall), mfv(rainfall))
)
ggplot(tibble(rainfall), aes(rainfall)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "lightblue", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(data = stats, aes(xintercept = value, color = measure),
             linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Rainfall with Mean, Median, and Mode",
       x = "Rainfall (inches)", y = "Frequency", color = NULL)

title: Descriptive Statistics
text: What Do These Look Like?

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Why We Care in CJ: Sentencing
text:
Why We Care in CJ: Sentencing

# Sentence lengths for 10 people convicted of robbery (years)
sentences <- c(2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 30)   # note the outlier!

mean(sentences)

[1] 6.1

median(sentences)

[1] 3.5

mfv(sentences)

[1] 3


One 30-year sentence drags the mean to 6.1 — nobody in the data actually got a “typical” 6-year sentence.

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Why We Care in CJ: Sentencing
text: Why We Care in CJ: Sentencing

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Thoughts?

Why do these three values (mean = 6.1, median = 3.5, mode = 3) give such different impressions of “typical” sentence length?
Which one might be most fair to use when describing a sentencing policy to the public?
When might the mean be misleading?

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: The Same Thing in Real Data
text:
The Same Thing in Real Data
Community-level crime rates in Chicago, 2025:

areas |>
  summarize(
    mean_rate   = mean(crime_rate),
    median_rate = median(crime_rate),
    max_rate    = max(crime_rate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_rate median_rate max_rate
      <dbl>       <dbl>    <dbl>
1      96.9          82     292.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Who’s Dragging the Mean?

areas |> slice_max(crime_rate, n = 3) |> select(community, crime_rate)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  community          crime_rate
  <chr>                   <dbl>
1 Fuller Park              292.
2 West Garfield Park       220.
3 Englewood                214.


Fuller Park’s rate — nearly 300 crimes per 1,000 residents, inflated by its tiny residential population — pulls the mean above the median: same lesson as the 30-year sentence, in live data. (Rates with small denominators are a recurring CJ trap; we’ll meet it again.)

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: The Same Thing in Real Data
text: The Same Thing in Real Data

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Central Tendency Isn’t the Whole Story
text:
Central Tendency Isn’t the Whole Story
Three people run for city council; only the top two vote-getters win:


Scenario 1

A = 200 votes
B = 300 votes
C = 400 votes


Scenario 2

X = 299 votes
Y = 300 votes
Z = 301 votes


In both cases the average is 300. But scenario 1 has much greater spread in support; scenario 2 is tightly clustered — it’s hard to say who’s truly “preferred.”
→ We need measures of dispersion: range, deviations, variance, standard deviation.

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Seeing the Machinery — Step 1: Raw Votes
text: Seeing the Machinery — Step 1: Raw Votes

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Range

votes1 <- c(200, 300, 400)   # wide spread
votes2 <- c(299, 300, 301)   # tight cluster

mean(votes1); mean(votes2)   # identical means

[1] 300


[1] 300




range(votes1); diff(range(votes1))

[1] 200 400


[1] 200

range(votes2); diff(range(votes2))

[1] 299 301


[1] 2

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Seeing the Machinery — Step 2: Deviations

(Notice the Tight Cluster panel: deviations of −1, 0, +1 are barely visible on the same scale.)

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Deviations from the Mean

votes1 - mean(votes1)

[1] -100    0  100

votes2 - mean(votes2)

[1] -1  0  1



Why can’t we just sum the deviations?

sum(votes1 - mean(votes1))   # they always cancel to zero!

[1] 0

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Seeing the Machinery — Step 3: Squared Deviations
text:
Seeing the Machinery — Step 3: Squared Deviations

Average these and you have the variance; take the square root and you’re back in vote units — the SD.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Sum of Squares
Squaring makes every deviation positive (and emphasizes big misses):

sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2)

[1] 20000

sum((votes2 - mean(votes2))^2)

[1] 2

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Variance

# Variance = mean squared deviation (population formula)
sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2) / length(votes1)

[1] 6666.667

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Standard Deviation, in Words
The standard deviation measures how spread out the data are around the mean.

“On average, how far is each value from the mean?”

We square the deviations (to make them positive and emphasize larger differences), average them (that’s the variance), then take the square root (back to the original units).

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Practice — Standard Deviation

# Standard deviation = square root of variance (back to vote units!)
sqrt(sum((votes1 - mean(votes1))^2) / length(votes1))

[1] 81.64966




var(votes1); sd(votes1)   # R's built-ins use the SAMPLE formula (divide by n-1)

[1] 10000


[1] 100

var(votes2); sd(votes2)   # more on WHY in Session 4

[1] 1


[1] 1

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Why the Standard Deviation?

Same units as the data — variance is in squared units; SD is interpretable
Works with the normal distribution — SD tells us how typical or extreme a value is
The basis for many tools — confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, z-scores, regression all rely on it
Lets you compare variability across datasets with similar scales

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
In CJ Scenarios
Response times for patrol officers:

Low SD → officers respond in consistently similar times
High SD → sometimes fast, sometimes slow — inconsistency that matters for policy, supervision, training

Sentence lengths for the same crime:

High SD might suggest inconsistency — or bias — in sentencing

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Real Data: Consistency Across Communities

# Violent-crime rates: how much do Chicago communities differ?
areas |>
  summarize(
    mean_violent = mean(violent_rate),
    sd_violent   = sd(violent_rate),
    min_violent  = min(violent_rate),
    max_violent  = max(violent_rate)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  mean_violent sd_violent min_violent max_violent
         <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1         30.7       22.5           4        111.


The SD is nearly as large as the mean — Chicago communities differ enormously in violence exposure. That inequality is a finding, and it took exactly one line of dispersion statistics to see it.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
What Is a Distribution?
A distribution shows how many observations fall at different values — the shape of the data.
It answers:

“Where do most of the values fall?”
“How spread out are they?”
“Are some values rare or common?”

We visualize distributions with a histogram.

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Normal Distribution

sims <- tibble(x = rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 100, sd = 10))
ggplot(sims, aes(x)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey80", color = "white")


Symmetrical, bell-shaped; defined by two numbers — the mean (center) and SD (spread). Try different values!

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: SD and the Normal: the Empirical Rule
text:
SD and the Normal: the Empirical Rule


pct_within <- function(k) 100 * (pnorm(k) - pnorm(-k))
tibble(k = 1:3, pct_within = round(pct_within(1:3), 2))

# A tibble: 3 × 2
      k pct_within
  <int>      <dbl>
1     1       68.3
2     2       95.4
3     3       99.7

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Poisson Distribution

pois_sims <- tibble(x = rpois(n = 1000, lambda = 1))
ggplot(pois_sims, aes(x)) + geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["navy"])


Often skewed, especially when λ is low. Models counts of rare events: 911 calls per hour, crimes per day, cars per minute. One parameter: λ = expected number of events. Try different values!

title: Descriptive Statistics
text:
The Poisson Is Not Hypothetical
Daily robbery counts in our Chicago sample, all of 2025:

daily_robberies <- crimes |>
  filter(primary_type == "ROBBERY") |>
  count(date)

ggplot(daily_robberies, aes(n)) +
  geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  labs(x = "Robberies per day", y = "Number of days",
       title = "Real crime counts look Poisson")

title: Descriptive Statistics
section: Why We Care About Distributions in CJ
text:
Why We Care About Distributions in CJ

The normal distribution helps us understand common variation (response times, test scores)
The Poisson distribution models event counts, especially rare ones — crimes, incidents — and underlies many forecasting tools
Recognizing the shape of your data is the first step in choosing the right analysis — a theme for the whole semester
