text:
Today’s Lab & Homework

Lab 2: your first ggplots — histograms, boxplots, and bar charts with real corrections data (lab page)
Homework 2: descriptive statistics in R (posted on the Session 2 page)
Read before Session 3: Stanton Ch. 2 · R4DS Ch. 3 (Data transformation) & Ch. 4 (Code style)

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
This Week
Topic: probabilities in the long run and sampling distributions — taught by simulation. We won’t derive anything today; we’ll draw thousands of samples in R and watch the theory appear on screen.
Learning goals: explain in your own words — law of large numbers, sampling distribution, standard error, central limit theorem — and say why R’s var() and sd() divide by n − 1 (Session 2’s IOU gets paid today).

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 2: describing data — center, spread, and the shapes distributions take
Session 3: probability as the long run; conditioning as shrink the world, re-proportion; and Bayes’ theorem — the base rate is never optional
Today: what happens to statistics themselves — means, proportions — when sampling repeats. This is the engine under every inference we make for the rest of the course

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
How Today Works


The lecture — concepts
Stanton Ch. 3 → sampling distributions, the standard error, and the CLT. I run the simulations on screen; you watch and argue with me.

The in-class exercise — code
You write it, together, one idea at a time. Simple code, no rush.

Everything I run today is written up in the demo walkthrough, so nothing on screen is something you have to capture in real time.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
A Question to Start

If I told you the chance of being selected for a jury was 10%, and you weren’t selected after 10 tries, would that surprise you? Why or why not?


Two kinds of probability:

Theoretical probability — based on mathematical reasoning (a fair coin is 50/50 by definition)
Empirical probability — observed through repetition (flip it and count)

Today’s whole session is about the gap between these two — and how it shrinks.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Theoretical vs. Empirical Probability
Flip a fair coin 10 times:

flips_10 <- sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10, replace = TRUE)
table(flips_10) / 10

flips_10
heads tails 
  0.6   0.4 



Now 10,000 times:

flips_10k <- sample(c("heads", "tails"), size = 10000, replace = TRUE)
table(flips_10k) / 10000

flips_10k
 heads  tails 
0.5055 0.4945 


Empirical results fluctuate in small samples but converge toward the theoretical probability — the law of large numbers.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Watching the Long Run Arrive

lln <- tibble(
  flip = 1:10000,
  heads = sample(c(0, 1), size = 10000, replace = TRUE)
) |>
  mutate(running_prop = cumsum(heads) / flip)
ggplot(lln, aes(flip, running_prop)) +
  geom_line(color = crju_colors["navy"]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Proportion of heads in coin flips",
       x = "Number of flips", y = "Proportion heads")


Concept: in the long run, empirical ≈ theoretical. But “long run” might be longer than we think — look how wild the first few hundred flips are.

title: Sampling Distributions
text: Watching the Long Run Arrive

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Simulating Probabilities in CJ (1)
Roadside drug tests. A field test for illegal drugs flags 5% of the drivers who are carrying nothing at all (a 5% false-positive rate). Simulate 100 tests of drivers who are clean:

tests <- sample(c("false positive", "correct"), size = 100,
                replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.95))
table(tests)

tests
       correct false positive 
            91              9 



Discussion: even with a low false positive rate, false positives occur regularly in practice. What do we think about this? Does it matter?

title: Sampling Distributions
section: What Does a Positive Test Mean?
text:
What Does a Positive Test Mean?
Session 3 ran this with a disease screen. Same trap, new setting: 1,000 drivers stopped at a checkpoint, field-tested for illegal drugs.

2% are actually carrying: 20 carriers, 980 with nothing on them
The 5% false-positive rate hits those 980 → ~49 false alarms
Let the test catch all 20 carriers: 69 positives, only 20 real → \(P(\text{carrying} \mid +) = 20/69 \approx 29\%\)
The 5% is \(P(+ \mid \text{clean})\); the stop needs \(P(\text{carrying} \mid +)\). Never confuse the direction — at its best this test is wrong about 7 of every 10 drivers it flags

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Simulating Probabilities in CJ (2)
Stop & frisk outcomes. Suppose 8% of stops yield contraband. What happens over 1,000 stops?

stop_outcomes <- sample(c("found", "nothing"), size = 1000,
                        replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.08, 0.92))
table(stop_outcomes)

stop_outcomes
  found nothing 
     69     931 



Discussion: is that hit rate too low? What if each find were an illegal gun that would have been used in a violent crime? Simulation makes the long-run consequences of a policy concrete.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Random Does Not Mean Balanced
Two runs of 100 dice rolls — same die, same code:

dice <- tibble(
  run  = rep(c("Run 1", "Run 2"), each = 100),
  roll = c(sample(1:6, size = 100, replace = TRUE),
           sample(1:6, size = 100, replace = TRUE))
)
ggplot(dice, aes(x = factor(roll))) +
  geom_bar(fill = crju_colors["garnet"]) +
  facet_wrap(~run) +
  labs(title = "Dice roll frequencies — two runs of 100",
       x = "Face", y = "Count")


Does either look fair? Both are. Random does not mean balanced in small samples — remember this every time you see a “streak” in real data.

title: Sampling Distributions
text: Random Does Not Mean Balanced

title: Sampling Distributions
section: A Population We Can Actually See
text:
A Population We Can Actually See
population-data.csv — 10,000 test scores. In real research we never see the whole population; today we get to cheat:

pop |>
  summarize(mean = mean(score), median = median(score),
            sd = sd(score), n = n())

# A tibble: 1 × 4
   mean median    sd     n
  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1  100.   100.  15.0 10000

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
One Sample of 30

samp <- sample(pop$score, size = 30)
mean(samp)

[1] 100.3389

sd(samp)

[1] 13.16761


Close to the truth (mean ≈ 100, SD ≈ 15) — but not exact. That gap is sampling error, and it is not a mistake; it’s a fact of life.

The question that drives the rest of the semester: how wrong can one sample be?

title: Sampling Distributions
section: What If We Sampled From the Tail?
text:
What If We Sampled From the Tail?
Draw 10 scores from the bottom 5% of the population — and look at them in context:

tail_scores <- pop |> filter(score < quantile(score, 0.05))
tail_sample <- sample(tail_scores$score, size = 10)
mean(tail_sample)

[1] 70.02723

title: Sampling Distributions
section: …And What If We Didn’t Know It?
text:
…And What If We Didn’t Know It?
Now pretend that sample is all we ever get to see:

If this were your dataset, you’d report a “typical” score near 70 — and you’d be badly wrong. How often does that actually happen with a random sample? Let’s find out.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Do It a Thousand Times
The key move of this whole session — instead of drawing one sample, draw 1,000 samples of 30 and keep each sample’s mean:

sample_means <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(mean_score = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(pop$score, size = 30))))

sample_means

# A tibble: 1,000 × 2
   draw mean_score
  <int>      <dbl>
1     1       99.7
2     2       97.4
3     3       97.5
4     4       99.6
5     5      105. 
6     6      104. 
# ℹ 994 more rows




map_dbl(draw, \(d) …) reads as “for each draw, do this and return one number” — Session 3’s replicate(), tibble-flavored. See the simulation verbs reference.

title: Sampling Distributions
section: The Sampling Distribution of the Mean
text:
The Sampling Distribution of the Mean

ggplot(sample_means, aes(mean_score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = crju_colors["blue"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(pop$score), color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "1,000 sample means (n = 30 each)",
       x = "Sample mean", y = "Number of samples")


This histogram of means is a sampling distribution. It’s centered on the true population mean — and it’s much narrower than the population itself.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Two Distributions, Side by Side

Same center. Radically different spread. Individual scores wander all over; averages of 30 stay close to home.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
The Standard Error
The SD of the sampling distribution has its own name: the standard error. And it has a formula — which our simulation can check:

sd(sample_means$mean_score)   # SE from the simulation

[1] 2.648695

sd(pop$score) / sqrt(30)      # SE from the formula: SD / sqrt(n)

[1] 2.733584




The standard error answers: “if I re-ran my study, how much would my estimate typically move?”

That single number is the foundation of confidence intervals and hypothesis tests — the rest of this course.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Sample Size Buys Precision

many_ns <- expand_grid(n = c(5, 30, 100), draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(mean_score = map_dbl(n, \(k) mean(sample(pop$score, size = k))))
ggplot(many_ns, aes(mean_score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = crju_colors["navy"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(pop$score), color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~n, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean", y = "Count")



many_ns |>
  summarize(simulated_se = sd(mean_score), formula_se = sd(pop$score) / sqrt(first(n)),
            .by = n)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
      n simulated_se formula_se
  <dbl>        <dbl>      <dbl>
1     5         6.84       6.70
2    30         2.77       2.73
3   100         1.49       1.50


The SE shrinks like 1/√n: to halve your uncertainty you need four times the data.

title: Sampling Distributions
text: Sample Size Buys Precision

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
The Least Normal Variable Imaginable
Back to our 30,000 real Chicago incidents. Whether an incident ended in arrest is as far from a bell curve as data gets — every value is TRUE or FALSE:

crimes |> count(arrest) |> mutate(prop = n / sum(n))

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  arrest     n  prop
  <lgl>  <int> <dbl>
1 FALSE  25176 0.839
2 TRUE    4824 0.161



Treat these 30,000 incidents as the population. True arrest proportion: 0.161.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Sample 100 Incidents. Repeat 1,000 Times.
Imagine an analyst who can only pull 100 case files at a time:

arrest_props <- tibble(draw = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(prop_arrest = map_dbl(draw, \(d) mean(sample(crimes$arrest, size = 100))))


ggplot(arrest_props, aes(prop_arrest)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01, fill = crju_colors["blue"], color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(crimes$arrest), color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "1,000 sample arrest proportions (n = 100 incidents each)",
       x = "Proportion of sampled incidents with an arrest", y = "Samples")

title: Sampling Distributions
section: A Bell Curve Out of TRUE/FALSE Data
text:
A Bell Curve Out of TRUE/FALSE Data
That’s the central limit theorem:

Whatever shape the population has — even a two-bar TRUE/FALSE stack — the sampling distribution of a mean (or proportion) becomes approximately normal as n grows, centered on the true value.


It’s why polls of ~1,000 people work for a country of 330 million
It’s why we can attach a standard error to an arrest rate, a clearance rate, a recidivism rate — without ever seeing the full population
It’s why the normal distribution keeps showing up even though raw CJ data almost never look normal

title: Sampling Distributions
section: The CLT Also Obeys the √n Rule
text:
The CLT Also Obeys the √n Rule

At n = 25 a sample could easily tell you the arrest rate is 8% or 28%. At n = 400 you’re rarely off by more than a couple of points.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Session 2’s IOU
In Session 2 we noticed var() and sd() divide by n − 1, not n, and I promised you’d see why. Simulation pays the debt. Draw 5,000 tiny samples (n = 5) and compute the variance both ways:

var_pop <- mean((pop$score - mean(pop$score))^2)   # true population variance

variance_sims <- tibble(draw = 1:5000) |>
  mutate(
    s            = map(draw, \(d) sample(pop$score, size = 5)),
    var_div_n    = map_dbl(s, \(x) sum((x - mean(x))^2) / length(x)),
    var_div_nm1  = map_dbl(s, \(x) var(x))          # R's built-in: n - 1
  )



map() builds a list column — each row’s s holds an entire 5-value sample; map_dbl() then computes one number per sample. Don’t worry about the list-column mechanics — watch the two averages on the next slide.

title: Sampling Distributions
section: Divide by n, and You’re Biased
text:
Divide by n, and You’re Biased

variance_sims |>
  summarize(
    true_variance   = var_pop,
    avg_divide_by_n = mean(var_div_n),
    avg_divide_by_n_minus_1 = mean(var_div_nm1)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  true_variance avg_divide_by_n avg_divide_by_n_minus_1
          <dbl>           <dbl>                   <dbl>
1          224.            179.                    224.

title: Sampling Distributions
section: Divide by n, and You’re Biased (cont.)
text:
Divide by n, and You’re Biased (cont.)

Dividing by n systematically underestimates the population variance — across 5,000 samples, not occasionally
Why? A sample clusters around its own mean, which is always closer to the sample’s values than the true mean is — so measured spread comes up short
Dividing by n − 1 inflates each estimate just enough to land, on average, on the truth. That’s all “unbiased estimator” means

title: Sampling Distributions
section: What If the Population Is Unknown?
text:
What If the Population Is Unknown?
In real life you never get the left-hand panel. One draw from a mystery population:

unknown_population <- rnorm(1000, mean = 100, sd = 50)   # don't peek!
mystery_sample <- sample(unknown_population, size = 30)
mean(mystery_sample)

[1] 95.44168



Based on 30 points, you might assume normality — or skew, or outliers — and be wrong. Sampling-distribution logic is what lets us say how wrong we’re likely to be.

title: Sampling Distributions
text:
Why This Matters in CJ

Almost every number in CJ research is a sample statistic: a survey of officers, a sample of case files, one year of one city’s incidents
Every one of those statistics has a sampling distribution — it would come out differently if the study were re-run
The standard error turns “it would come out differently” into a number
Starting next session: use the SE to build confidence intervals — a range of values the truth is likely to be in

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 3: Bayes’ theorem: beliefs update by evidence; ignore the base rate and “90% accurate” becomes a 15% answer
Session 4: sampling distributions: sample statistics fluctuate in predictable ways
Session 5: confidence intervals: an honest range around an estimate, and one sentence we were not allowed to say about it
Today: the formal machinery for “is there a difference?”, then a second tradition answering the question you meant to ask

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Tonight’s Question
Among violent crimes in our Chicago sample: are the domestic ones more likely to end in an arrest?

violent <- crimes |> filter(crime_category == "Violent")

violent |> count(domestic, arrest)

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  domestic arrest     n
  <lgl>    <lgl>  <int>
1 FALSE    FALSE   4685
2 FALSE    TRUE     714
3 TRUE     FALSE   3009
4 TRUE     TRUE     740

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Reading the Table




Arrests
Out of
Arrest rate




Domestic
740
740 + 3,009 = 3,749
19.7%


Not domestic
714
714 + 4,685 = 5,399
13.2%




A gap of about 6.5 percentage points. All night the difference reads one way: Domestic minus Not domestic.


But this is a sample of Chicago’s 2025 incidents. Session 4 taught us that sample numbers bounce around. Could a gap like this be nothing but bounce?

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Let’s Pretend We Sampled Repeatedly
Session 4’s move, applied to both groups at once: draw 10,000 repeated samples of each group and compute the arrest rate every time.

The two piles do not even touch.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Difference and Its 95% Interval
Subtract, pair by pair, and the difference gets its own pile:

The middle 95% runs from about 5 to 8.1 points. Zero is nowhere near it.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: What If There Were No Real Difference?
text:
What If There Were No Real Difference?
Build the boring world on purpose: give both groups the same arrest rate (the overall 15.9%), and run the same machinery.

Chance alone makes gaps of a point or two. It made a gap as big as ours in 0 of 10,000 tries. That count is the whole idea of a p-value.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Null Hypothesis Significance Test

State the null, \(H_0\): the two arrest rates are the same (difference = 0). The boring world.
State the alternative, \(H_1\): some difference. Note how little we commit to.
Compute a test statistic: the observed gap, measured against how much gaps bounce by chance.
Ask: how often would a gap this large appear by luck in the boring world? The p-value.
Verdict: \(p < \alpha\) (usually .05) → “reject \(H_0\).” Otherwise → “fail to reject.”
Note: the machine only weighs evidence against the null: \(H_1\) never gets scored.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: Watch the p-Value Do Its Job
text:
Watch the p-Value Do Its Job


As the true difference grows, the overlap shrinks and p falls. Black = null · green = one alternative · orange = overlap · blue dashes = the α = .05 cutoffs.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: What a p-Value Is, and Is Not
text:
What a p-Value Is, and Is Not
It is: the probability of data this extreme or more, if the null is true and the model is right.

It is not:

the probability the null hypothesis is true: that’s \(P(H_0 \mid \text{data})\), which frequentism never computes
the probability the result “is due to chance”: same confusion, folksier outfit
1 - the probability the alternative is true
a measure of how big or important the effect is: with enough data, microscopic effects earn microscopic p-values (hold that thought)

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
prop.test() on the Real Question
Lab 5’s function, now with two groups: how many, out of how many, for each. Domestic first.

prop.test(x = c(740, 714), n = c(3749, 5399))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(740, 714) out of c(3749, 5399)
X-squared = 69.744, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.04929331 0.08098520
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.1973860 0.1322467

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Reading the Verdict

prop 1 and prop 2 at the bottom: 19.7% and 13.2%. Domestic is first because we typed it first
95 percent confidence interval: about 4.9 to 8.1 points, Domestic minus Not domestic. Last week’s skill
p-value < 2.2e-16: R’s way of writing a decimal point followed by fifteen zeros. In the boring world, a gap like ours essentially never happens


\(p < .05\): “statistically significant.” Reject the null.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: The Same Line Lives in t.test()
text:
The Same Line Lives in t.test()
Last week’s homework, comparing two means. The p-value sat right above the interval the whole time:

t.test(injuries ~ intox, data = crashes)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  injuries by intox
t = 12.489, df = 1732.6, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Intoxicated and group Sober is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.3259893 0.4474533
sample estimates:
mean in group Intoxicated       mean in group Sober 
                1.1300971                 0.7433758 


Same reading: if both kinds of crash truly injured the same number of people, a gap this big would essentially never appear.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Assumption 1 · The Null Stands Alone

We computed how surprising the data are under the null, and never once said what the alternative world looks like.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
…But the Alternative Could Be Anywhere

“Reject the null” tells you where you aren’t. It never tells you where you are.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Assumption 2 · The Shape Itself

The p-value came from this specific curve, which assumes large-enough samples, independent observations, and a model that fits the data.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: …And Many Shapes Fit the Same Data
text:
…And Many Shapes Fit the Same Data

How often do researchers test those assumptions before trusting the p-value? Less often than you’d hope.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Bayes’ Theorem: Recap from Session 3
\[
P(H \mid \text{data}) = P(\text{data} \mid H) \times P(H) \,/\, P(\text{data})
\qquad \small{\text{posterior} = \text{likelihood} \times \text{prior} / \text{evidence}}
\]

Session 3’s move: conditioning is shrink the world, re-proportion; Bayes’ theorem reverses the direction. Ianfluenza: prior 1% + “90% accurate” → posterior ≈ 15%
New today: look where the p-value lives: entirely in the likelihood, \(P(\text{data} \mid H_0)\). It never becomes \(P(H_0 \mid \text{data})\)
Bayesian testing finishes the flip: \(P(H \mid \text{data})\), the question your chief, judge, or city council actually asked, at the price of a stated prior

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: The Two Traditions, Side by Side
text:
The Two Traditions, Side by Side









Frequentist
Bayesian




Asks
How surprising are these data if \(H_0\) is true?
How probable is each hypothesis, given the data?


Probability attaches to
Data, over imagined repeated samples
Hypotheses and parameters directly


Prior knowledge
None used
Explicit, stated up front


Output
p-value, confidence interval
Posterior distribution, credible interval


“95%” means
The procedure captures the truth in 95% of replications
95% probability the parameter lies in this interval

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Setup

Context: typical recidivism runs about 60%: that’s what we believed going in
Design: randomized trial of a reentry program: 100 treated, 100 control
Outcomes: treatment 40/100 reoffend · control 50/100 reoffend
Question: did the program reduce recidivism?


Ten percentage points, exactly the kind of effect a city would fund. Both traditions, go.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Frequentist Answer
Treatment first, so the difference reads Treatment minus Control:

prop.test(x = c(40, 50), n = c(100, 100))


    2-sample test for equality of proportions with continuity correction

data:  c(40, 50) out of c(100, 100)
X-squared = 1.6364, df = 1, p-value = 0.2008
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.24719748  0.04719748
sample estimates:
prop 1 prop 2 
   0.4    0.5

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Frequentist Answer, Read Aloud

\(p = 0.20\): not statistically significant
The interval, about -25 to +5 points, has zero inside it
Honest reading: a 10-point gap like this could plausibly occur even if the program did nothing
The grant report writes itself (“no significant effect”), and the program probably dies there

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: What We Knew Before the Trial
text:
What We Knew Before the Trial
A Bayesian has to say, out loud, what they believed before seeing the data. That is the prior.

We said it already: recidivism typically runs about 60%
How firmly do we believe that? Let’s say: about as firmly as if we had already watched 10 people: 6 reoffended, 4 did not
In R, that whole belief is two numbers: prior = c(6, 4)
Then the trial’s 200 real people get added to our 10 imaginary ones. That adding-up is the posterior: what we believe after the data

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Bayesian Answer
Same two numbers per group as prop.test(), plus the prior:

bayes_prop_test(x = c(40, 50), n = c(100, 100), prior = c(6, 4))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  40 of 100 (40.0%)
data, group 2:  50 of 100 (50.0%)
prior:          6 yes, 4 no (about 60%, worth 10 cases), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  41.8%         32.8% to 51.1%
group 2                  50.9%         41.6% to 60.2%
difference (1 minus 2)   -9.1 points   -22.0 to 4.0 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: 0.09 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  0.91

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Reading It

estimate: our best single guess for each group’s true rate, after the data
95% credible interval for the difference: about -22 to +4 points, Treatment minus Control
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2: 0.91: given the prior and the data, about a 91% probability the program reduces recidivism


And the sentence Session 5 forbade is now legal: “There is a 95% probability the true difference lies between -22 and +4 points.” That is exactly what a credible interval means.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text: The Posteriors, Seen

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Same Data, Different Questions









Frequentist
Bayesian




Verdict
\(p = 0.20\): cannot reject “no effect”
Probability the program works ≈ 0.91


Plain English
“This gap could plausibly be luck”
“About 9-to-1 odds the program works”




Both statements are true of the same data. Neither is a trick
A policymaker deciding whether to fund the program next year: which sentence actually helps?
Your homework asks you to sit with exactly this discomfort

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Does the Prior Matter Here?
Leave prior = out and the function starts from “I know nothing”:

bayes_prop_test(x = c(40, 50), n = c(100, 100))


Probability the program works: 0.92 instead of 0.91. It barely moved
Why? 200 real people outweigh 10 imaginary ones. Data overwhelm a modest prior
A prior matters most when data are scarce, which is exactly when you most need to say it out loud

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: The Bayesian Answer to Tonight’s Question
text:
The Bayesian Answer to Tonight’s Question
We have no strong belief going in, so no prior =:

bayes_prop_test(x = c(740, 714), n = c(3749, 5399))


    Bayesian test of two proportions 

data, group 1:  740 of 3,749 (19.7%)
data, group 2:  714 of 5,399 (13.2%)
prior:          know-nothing (1 yes, 1 no), same for both groups

                         estimate      95% credible interval
group 1                  19.8%         18.5% to 21.0%
group 2                  13.2%         12.3% to 14.2%
difference (1 minus 2)   6.5 points    5.0 to 8.1 points

Probability group 1 is higher than group 2: more than 0.99 
Probability group 1 is lower than group 2:  less than 0.01

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Big Sample, Small Sample









Chicago arrests (9,148 cases)
Reentry trial (200 people)




prop.test()
95% CI: 4.9 to 8.1 points · \(p < .001\)
95% CI: -25 to +5 points · \(p = 0.20\)


bayes_prop_test()
95% credible: 5 to 8.1 points
95% credible: -22 to +4 points · P(works) ≈ 0.91




With thousands of cases the two traditions hand you nearly the same range. The data drown out everything else
With 100 per group, both ranges still include zero, but one tradition stops at “not significant,” and the other tells you how probable the effect is
Neither is wrong. They answer different questions

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The p-Value and Sample Size
Fix a trivial true effect (Δ = 0.1) and just keep collecting data:

The effect never grows, only n does, and p still dives below .05. Given enough data, everything is “significant.”

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Bayes and Sample Size
Same trivial effect, Bayesian glasses: watch the posterior for the difference as n grows:

More data doesn’t flip a verdict: it sharpens the estimate, which visibly converges on “about 0.1, i.e., almost nothing.” The tininess stays in view.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
So Always Ask: How Big?

“Significant” only means detectable. With enough cases, a gap of a single percentage point would earn a tiny p-value too
So after either test, say the size in real units: arrest rates about 6.5 points apart (19.7% vs 13.2%)
Then ask the question no test can answer for you: is a gap that size big enough to matter?

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
What We Learned Today

NHST: standardized and everywhere, but it only asks how surprising are the data under the null?, never scores the alternative, and rewards sheer n
p-values are not the probability any hypothesis is true, and are silent about size
Bayes answers \(P(H \mid \text{data})\) at the price of a stated prior: tonight, in one line of R
The same trial gave \(p = 0.20\) and a 91% probability the program works. Both true; different questions
Whatever tradition you use: say how big the difference is, in units a human cares about

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
The Ugly Denominator
Not on any exam: this is the machinery behind the Bayesian models we start fitting in Session 10, for the curious.
\[
P(H \mid \text{data}) = \frac{P(\text{data} \mid H)\,P(H)}{\color{#73000A}{P(\text{data})}}
\]
That innocent-looking denominator is the probability of the data under every possible hypothesis, weighted by its prior:
\[
\color{#73000A}{P(\text{data}) = \int P(\text{data} \mid \theta)\, P(\theta)\, d\theta}
\]

For realistic models this integral is intractable: for most of the 20th century, Bayes was philosophically beautiful and practically unusable.

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
Enter MCMC
How Markov chain Monte Carlo “measures the curve” without solving the integral:

We don’t know the whole posterior curve, but we do know its formula up to a constant (likelihood × prior)
A sampler evaluates that formula at its current spot and at a proposed spot
Compare the two values: if the new spot is higher → accept; if lower → accept with that probability
The impossible constant appears in both numerator and denominator: it cancels in the ratio. We never need to know it

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
text:
MCMC, Watched Live
A Metropolis sampler exploring a distribution (left) while its samples pile up into that very shape (right):

title: Hypothesis Testing: Frequentist and Bayesian
section: We End Up With the Probability Distribution
text:
We End Up With the Probability Distribution

The pile of accepted samples is the posterior: to any precision you like, just run longer
Think back to Session 4: we approximated sampling distributions by drawing samples and stacking them. MCMC plays exactly the same trick on the posterior
This is why modern Bayes is possible at all, and it is what brms will do for us starting in Session 10. (Tonight’s bayes_prop_test() did not need it: for a simple proportion, the posterior has an exact formula.)

The outcome is…

Sessions 5 to 7 were all about groups. Tonight every row has two numbers: do they rise and fall together? This is the doorway to regression (Sessions 10 and 11).

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
What Does Correlation Tell Us?
When two variables move together, how can we describe that relationship?

One goes up when the other goes up: positive correlation
One goes up when the other goes down: negative correlation
Changes in one don’t track changes in the other: no correlation


Direction is only half the story. The strength of the relationship tells how tightly the changes are linked. That’s the number we build today.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Which Is Which?
Positive, negative, or nothing? Make your call for each panel:

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Which Is Which? Revealed


The lines make it obvious, and the r values put a number on what your eye already knew.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Real-World Examples

Positive: hours studied ↑, exam scores ↑
Negative: officers on shift ↑, response times ↓
Near zero: shoe size and GPA


Your turn: give me a CJ example of each, and one pair you suspect people believe is correlated but isn’t.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Correlation Does NOT Mean Causation

Correlation shows association, not cause and effect
Ice cream sales and violent crime rise together every year. Does ice cream cause violence?
Two variables can move together because of a third variable (summer heat drives both), or by pure coincidence
When you see a correlation, ask: does X cause Y? Y cause X? Does something else drive both? Or is it luck?
Correlation is a pattern, not proof of cause. Beware the lurking third variable!

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
section: Covariance: Moving Together, in Raw Units
text:
Covariance: Moving Together, in Raw Units
Row by row: do x and y sit on the same side of their averages?
\[\text{cov}(x, y) \;=\; \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{n - 1}\]

Both above average (or both below): positive products, positive covariance. Opposite sides: negative covariance
The sign is trustworthy: covariance tells you whether two variables move together
The size is not. Watch what happens on real data

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
The Units Problem
Two covariances with violent crime, from Chicago’s 77 community areas:

cov(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate)

[1] 107.7543

cov(areas$median_income,     areas$violent_rate)

[1] -482660.1



Is -482,660 a “stronger” relationship than 108? No idea. The first number is in dollars times crimes per 1,000; the second in percentage points times crimes per 1,000. Covariance is glued to its units, so you can’t compare across pairs.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Correlation Rescales It
Divide the covariance by both standard deviations and the units cancel:
\[r \;=\; \frac{\text{cov}(x, y)}{s_x \, s_y}\]

cov(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate) /
  (sd(areas$unemployment_rate) * sd(areas$violent_rate))

[1] 0.8398579

cor(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate)   # same thing, one function

[1] 0.8398579



Always between -1 and +1, no units, comparable. Income runs r = -0.71 with violence, so unemployment (0.84) tracks violence more tightly than income does, direction aside.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Reading r








r (either sign)
Strength
What the scatterplot looks like




0.8 to 1.0
Very strong
Dots hug a line


0.4 to 0.7
Moderate
A clear trend, with plenty of scatter


0.1 to 0.3
Weak
A slight tilt you might not see without the line


about 0
None (no straight-line pattern)
A shapeless cloud




The sign gives the direction: + means both rise together; - means one rises as the other falls. These bands are conventions, not laws: in messy social-science data, a “moderate” r can be a major finding.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Calibrate Your Eye

By 0.5 (either sign) the trend is visible; below 0.2 your eye mostly sees noise, and it’s right.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Anscombe’s Quartet: Four Identical Summaries

anscombe_long <- anscombe |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c(".value", "set"), names_pattern = "(.)(.)")

anscombe_long |>
  summarize(mean_x = mean(x), mean_y = mean(y), r = cor(x, y), .by = set)

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  set   mean_x mean_y     r
  <chr>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 1          9   7.50 0.816
2 2          9   7.50 0.816
3 3          9   7.5  0.816
4 4          9   7.50 0.817



Four little datasets that ship with R (Anscombe, 1973). Same averages, same r = 0.82. Statistically interchangeable. Right?

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Anscombe’s Quartet, Seen

Only Set 1 is what you picture when someone says “r = 0.82.” Always plot before you correlate.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
section: Limitation 1: r Only Sees Straight Lines
text:
Limitation 1: r Only Sees Straight Lines

Think stress and performance: an upside-down U. r near 0 means no straight-line relationship, not no relationship.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
section: Limitation 2: One Point Can Manufacture a Correlation
text: Limitation 2: One Point Can Manufacture a Correlation

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
What Just Happened

Twenty points of pure noise happened to give r = -0.28. Small samples produce correlations out of nothing; that’s why we test, not just compute
Adding one extreme point swung r to +0.42: it flipped the sign and manufactured a “moderate positive” correlation
Neither number describes a real relationship
Outliers can also work the other way, hiding a real correlation
Defenses: plot first (you’d catch this instantly), and a correlation that doesn’t care about wild values…

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
A Rank-Based Backup: Spearman’s rho
Replace each value with its rank (1st, 2nd, 3rd…), then correlate the ranks. Spearman asks only: is the relationship consistently up, or consistently down?

c(pearson  = cor(outlier_data$x, outlier_data$y),
  spearman = cor(outlier_data$x, outlier_data$y, method = "spearman"))

   pearson   spearman 
 0.4235804 -0.1142857 



To Spearman, the wild point is just “rank 21”: rho drifts from -0.29 to -0.11, still weak, while Pearson flipped sign. When data are skewed or have wild values, check Spearman alongside Pearson.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
From Incidents to Areas
The anchor data’s second level (codebook): all 237,472 of 2025’s incidents, added up to the 77 community areas and joined with Census measures:

areas |>
  select(community, violent_rate, unemployment_rate, median_income, pct_vacant) |>
  head(3)

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  community   violent_rate unemployment_rate median_income pct_vacant
  <chr>              <dbl>             <dbl>         <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Rogers Park         21.7               7.1         60916        9.5
2 West Ridge          12.2               7.3         70823        7.7
3 Uptown              22.8               4.7         70067        9.1



A classic question about places: which features of a neighborhood track its violence? Correlation is the right first tool.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Look First: Unemployment and Violence

One dot = one community area. This is about as strong as area-level associations get in criminology.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
section: The Full Menu, in One Dataset
text:
The Full Menu, in One Dataset

Strong positive, moderate positive, strong negative, and one genuine nothing (median age). Real data span the whole menu.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
These Are Areas, Not People
Our r = 0.84 says: community areas with higher unemployment rates record more violent crime per 1,000 residents.






The ecological fallacy: using an association between groups (areas, states, cities) to make claims about individuals. Our data contain no individuals. Nothing here says unemployed people commit violence.




The classic example (Robinson, 1950): across U.S. states, more immigrants went with higher literacy. Across individuals, immigrants had lower literacy. Immigrants had settled in states with high literacy. Adding people up into areas can weaken, exaggerate, or even flip a relationship.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Saying It Out Loud (Area Data)
✅ Defensible:

“Community areas with higher unemployment rates recorded higher violent-crime rates (r = 0.84).”

❌ Not defensible:

“Unemployed residents commit more violent crime.” (A claim about individuals. These data can’t see individuals.)


“Unemployment drives up violence.” (A claim about cause. Concentrated poverty, disinvestment, and policing patterns all lurk behind both variables.)

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
From Description to a Test
We can see r = 0.84. The same question as every test since Session 6:

Null hypothesis: the true correlation is 0. No straight-line association in the process that produced these data
If it were 0, how surprising would an r like ours be, with 77 areas?
One wrinkle: these 77 areas are all of Chicago, not a sample. Read the null as a claim about the process that produces neighborhood outcomes, not about a bigger population we sampled from

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
cor.test()

cor.test(areas$unemployment_rate, areas$violent_rate)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  areas$unemployment_rate and areas$violent_rate
t = 13.4, df = 75, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7585749 0.8954023
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.8398579

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Reading It

cor = 0.84 at the bottom: that’s r
95% confidence interval: 0.76 to 0.90. An interval for the correlation, so it lives between -1 and +1. Where is zero? Far outside it
p-value < 2.2e-16: reject the null. A world with no correlation essentially never lines up 77 areas this tightly
With 77 areas, any r above about 0.22 (either sign) clears p < 0.05. Passing the test is a low bar; the strength is the story
Nothing in this output turns association into cause, or areas into individuals

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
When the Answer Is “Nothing Here”
Median age and violence, from the menu slide:

cor.test(areas$median_age, areas$violent_rate)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  areas$median_age and areas$violent_rate
t = -0.1336, df = 75, p-value = 0.8941
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.2385791  0.2092774
sample estimates:
        cor 
-0.01542445 



Interval -0.24 to +0.21: zero is inside. Fail to reject. Say no evidence of a straight-line association, which is not proof there is none.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
Several Pairs at Once
Real analyses rarely stop at one pair. cor() takes every numeric column you give it:

areas |>
  select(violent_rate, unemployment_rate, median_income, pct_vacant) |>
  cor() |>
  round(2)

                  violent_rate unemployment_rate median_income pct_vacant
violent_rate              1.00              0.84         -0.71       0.81
unemployment_rate         0.84              1.00         -0.81       0.67
median_income            -0.71             -0.81          1.00      -0.55
pct_vacant                0.81              0.67         -0.55       1.00



Read it like a mileage chart: each pair appears twice, and the 1s down the diagonal are each variable with itself. Handy for a first look at your project variables. Then plot and cor.test() the pairs that matter.

title: Correlation, Then Midterm Review
text:
How to Report It

“Across Chicago’s 77 community areas, unemployment was strongly associated with the violent-crime rate, r = 0.84, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.90, p < 0.001. This is an area-level association; it does not speak to individuals.”

Direction, strength, uncertainty, and the level of analysis. Every time.

Your Turn (5 Minutes)
pct_no_hs_diploma is the share of an area’s adults without a high-school diploma. Before you compute anything: write down your guess for the sign and rough size of its correlation with violent_rate.
areas <- read_csv("https://smourtgos.github.io/crju705/data/chicago-areas.csv")

ggplot(areas, aes(pct_no_hs_diploma, violent_rate)) + geom_point()

Most people guess a strong positive. The data: r = 0.17, p = 0.13, no evidence of an association. Yet pct_bachelors runs -0.45. Sensible-sounding measures can fail, and related measures tangle together. Untangling them is exactly what regression does in Session 10.

This Week

Why lm() breaks when the outcome is 0/1
Odds, log-odds, and the odds ratio: the currency of logistic regression
glm(family = binomial), predicted probabilities, and the Bayesian version with brms

Also today: the course pays off a promise it made in Session 1.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Where We’ve Been

Session 8: correlation: how two continuous variables move together
Session 10: multiple regression: a plane through a 3D cloud of points, minimizing squared error, each coefficient’s effect holding the others constant (and lurking variables like the ice-cream/drowning lurker handled by putting them in the model)
Every model so far predicted a number: a crime rate, an incident hour, an exam score
Today: what happens when the outcome only has two values: arrest or no arrest, reoffend or desist, hit again or not?

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
section: Criminal Justice Runs on Binary Outcomes
text:
Criminal Justice Runs on Binary Outcomes

Was an arrest made?
Does the defendant fail to appear?
Is the parolee re-arrested within three years?
Did the crash involve an intoxicated driver?
Is this neighborhood a high-violence area?


Linear regression predicts continuous outcomes (crime rates, response times). Logistic regression predicts binary outcomes: its currency is probability (0 to 1), expressed along the way as odds and log-odds.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Session 1 Made You a Promise
Remember the opening case study? 40 bank robberies, five zones, one question: where will they hit next?

We built future_hit = 1 if the same zone was hit again within 10 days, 0 otherwise
We fit a model, showed you a coefficient table nobody could read yet, and sent the patrol cars to the West Zone: where the robber was caught
That slide said: “Don’t worry about the machinery today: logistic regression is Session 11.”


Today is Session 11. Let’s reopen the machinery.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Machinery, Reopened
The exact model from Session 1: one function, one family argument:

robbery_model <- glm(
  future_hit ~ 0 + scale(day_of_year) + prior_robberies_in_zone + zone,
  data = robberies, family = binomial
)


glm() = generalized linear model: regression’s family business
family = binomial is the switch that makes it logistic: predict a 0/1 outcome
Everything else looks exactly like the lm() formulas from Session 10



Two formula details you can safely skim: 0 + drops the global intercept so each zone gets its own baseline, and scale() puts day-of-year on a standard scale. Read the table, not the formula: today is about the family switch.

Reading It With Today’s Eyes

The estimate column is in log-odds: that’s why it looked like gibberish in August; by the end of today it won’t

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
section: Logistic vs. Linear: The Road and the Hill
text:
Logistic vs. Linear: The Road and the Hill
Linear regression is a straight road: it keeps going forever in both directions. Logistic regression is a curved hill that flattens at 0 and 1, because probabilities can’t go below 0 or above 1.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Watch Linear Regression Fail
Predicting graduated the academy (yes/no) from study hours:

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
What Went Wrong

The linear model happily predicts values like 1.2 and -0.3: probabilities that cannot exist
Inside the middle of the data the two lines nearly agree; the damage is at the edges: exactly where predictions get used (“what about a recruit who studies a lot?”)
The fix is the logit transformation: instead of modeling the probability directly, model something built from it that a straight line can live on
(The full derivation is Ph.D.-stats material: what you need is the ladder on the next slides)

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Model You Already Know
\[Y = b_0 + b_1 X_1 + b_2 X_2 + \varepsilon\]

\(Y\): outcome (dependent variable)
\(b_0\): intercept (value of \(Y\) when all X’s are zero)
\(b_1, b_2\): slope coefficients (effect of each X, holding the others constant)
\(\varepsilon\): error term (what’s left unexplained)


The right-hand side is an unbounded straight line. Probability is trapped in [0, 1]. Something has to give.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Step 1: Probability to Odds
Suppose 3 out of 4 parolees complete supervision: \(p = 0.75\).
\[\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p} = \frac{0.75}{0.25} = 3 \quad \text{("three to one")}\]



Probability
Odds
Log-odds




0.25
0.33
-1.10


0.50
1.00
0.00


0.75
3.00
+1.10



Step 2, odds to log-odds: odds run 0 to ∞; log-odds run -∞ to +∞. That’s a scale a straight line can live on.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Logistic Model
Just treat logit(\(p\)), the log-odds, as your Y. Then…
\[\text{logit}(p) = \ln\!\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = b_0 + b_1 X_1 + b_2 X_2\]

Same intercept, same slopes, same “holding the others constant”
The line now predicts log-odds, which convert back to a probability that politely stays between 0 and 1: the curved hill








But the coefficients are log-odds!!! Nobody thinks in log-odds. So what do we do with them?

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
section: What Do We Do With Log-Odds?
text:
What Do We Do With Log-Odds?


EXPONENTIATE!


exp(coefficient) = the odds ratio: multiply the odds of the outcome by this much for each one-unit increase in X, holding the other predictors constant.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Two Traditions, Same Curve








Approach
What it estimates
Interpretation




Frequentist
Point estimates and confidence intervals
“If we repeated this 100 times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true β.”


Bayesian
Posterior distributions for each β
“Given our data and priors, there’s a 95% probability β lies in this range.”



Exactly the split you know from Sessions 6 and 10: nothing new, just a new model underneath it.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Frequentist Version
Toy data first: 32 cars from a 1974 Motor Trend issue, predicting manual transmission (1) vs. automatic (0) from horsepower and weight. Small enough to check every number; real CJ data in a few minutes.

data(mtcars)
cars_df <- mtcars |>
  rownames_to_column("car") |>
  mutate(am = as.factor(am))   # 0 = automatic, 1 = manual

model_freq <- glm(am ~ hp + wt, data = cars_df, family = binomial)
summary(model_freq)

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Frequentist Version


Call:
glm(formula = am ~ hp + wt, family = binomial, data = cars_df)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
(Intercept) 18.86630    7.44356   2.535  0.01126 * 
hp           0.03626    0.01773   2.044  0.04091 * 
wt          -8.08348    3.06868  -2.634  0.00843 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 43.230  on 31  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 10.059  on 29  degrees of freedom
AIC: 16.059

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 8

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Reading the Output: Exponentiate

exp(coef(model_freq))

         (Intercept)                   hp                   wt 
156145483.5063250661         1.0369208455         0.0003085967 



hp: log-odds 0.036 → odds ratio 1.037; each additional horsepower multiplies the odds of a manual transmission by about 1.04 (+3.7%), holding weight constant
wt: log-odds -8.08 → odds ratio 0.0003; each additional 1,000 lbs cuts the odds by ~99.97%, holding horsepower constant
Wildly different sizes partly because the units differ: one horsepower is a nudge; a thousand pounds is a different car

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
From Effects to Cases: predict()
Odds ratios describe effects. For an actual case, ask for the probability directly:

two_cars <- cars_df |>
  filter(car %in% c("Honda Civic", "Cadillac Fleetwood")) |>
  select(car, hp, wt)

two_cars |>
  mutate(p_manual = predict(model_freq, newdata = two_cars, type = "response"))

                 car  hp    wt         p_manual
1 Cadillac Fleetwood 205 5.250 0.00000009787752
2        Honda Civic  52 1.615 0.99954591741880



type = "response" returns probabilities: the light Civic is a near-certain manual (99.95%); the 5,250-lb Fleetwood, near-certain automatic. Report both: odds ratios for effects, predicted probabilities for cases.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Session 10’s Plane, Bent

Last session: two predictors + linear regression = a flat plane floating through the 3D cloud
Same two predictors + logistic regression = a curved sheet: a plateau near probability 1, a floor near 0, and an S-shaped cliff between them
The surface is the model: its height at any (hp, wt) combination is the predicted probability of a manual transmission there
Let’s build it from nothing but predict()

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Building the Surface
Ask the model for a prediction at every combination of horsepower and weight: a 40 × 40 grid, 1,600 predictions:

hp_seq <- seq(min(cars_df$hp), max(cars_df$hp), length.out = 40)
wt_seq <- seq(min(cars_df$wt), max(cars_df$wt), length.out = 40)
grid   <- expand.grid(hp = hp_seq, wt = wt_seq)

grid$prob <- predict(model_freq, newdata = grid, type = "response")

# Reshape the 1,600 predictions into a grid; t() puts rows on the
# wt (y) axis and columns on the hp (x) axis, which is what plotly expects
z_matrix <- t(matrix(grid$prob, nrow = length(hp_seq), ncol = length(wt_seq)))

The observed cars sit at height 0 (automatic) or 1 (manual); the surface passes between them.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The 3D Logistic Surface

data_points <- cars_df |>
  mutate(prob = as.numeric(as.character(am)))   # 0 = auto, 1 = manual

plot_ly(width = 950, height = 520) |>
  add_markers(data = data_points,
              x = ~hp, y = ~wt, z = ~prob,
              color = ~am, colors = c("steelblue", "firebrick"),
              symbol = I("circle"), size = I(50),
              name = "Observed Data") |>
  add_surface(x = hp_seq, y = wt_seq, z = z_matrix,
              colorscale = list(c(0, 'lightblue'), c(1, 'firebrick')),
              opacity = 0.6,
              name = "Predicted Probability Surface") |>
  layout(
    title = "Logistic Regression: Curved Probability Surface",
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "Horsepower (hp)"),
      yaxis = list(title = "Weight (1000 lbs)"),
      zaxis = list(title = "Probability (Manual Transmission)")
    )
  )

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Same Formula, Bayesian Machinery

model_bayes <- brm(am ~ hp + wt, data = cars_df,
                   family = bernoulli(),
                   chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


family = bernoulli() is brms’s name for a 0/1 outcome: the switch that family = binomial flips in glm()
Everything else is Session 10’s brm() pattern, compile pause included
The prior: none stated → brms defaults again. Your project’s model will use these too, so say so in your methods: “brms default priors, 2 chains × 2,000 iterations, seed 705”
A full posterior distribution for each log-odds coefficient

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Posterior Odds Ratios
Exponentiate the posterior summaries: dropping the intercept row, whose posterior is astronomically wide with only 32 cars:

exp(fixef(model_bayes)[-1, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")])

        Estimate               Q2.5       Q97.5
hp 1.05233926370 1.0168277428244001 1.120707968
wt 0.00001855298 0.0000000008757284 0.006666486



Same story as glm(): horsepower nudges the odds of a manual up; weight crushes them
The payoff is the sentence you’re allowed to say: “Given the data and priors, there’s a 95% probability the true odds ratio lies in this interval”, and with 32 cars, those honest intervals are huge. Watch them tighten on real data next.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Question
What separates Chicago’s high-violence community areas from the rest?

areas |> count(high_violence)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  high_violence     n
  <lgl>         <int>
1 FALSE            39
2 TRUE             38



high_violence ships in the file (it’s in the codebook): is the area’s violent-crime rate above the citywide median? 38 above, 39 at or below.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Making a Binary Outcome
The line that built it:
areas |> mutate(high_violence = violent_rate > median(violent_rate))

R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0, so a logical column drops straight into glm()
If your project outcome isn’t binary yet, it may be one mutate() away too
One caution: cutting a continuous variable in half throws away information; defensible when the yes/no version is the question you actually care about

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Look First (Always)
One predictor at a time before the model: unemployment against the outcome, with the fitted logistic curve:

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Fit It
Two predictors: unemployment and vacant housing, both plausible markers of concentrated disadvantage:

v_model <- glm(high_violence ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant,
               data = areas, family = binomial)
summary(v_model)

    family = binomial, data = areas)

(Intercept)        -5.8208     1.3747  -4.234 0.0000229 ***
unemployment_rate   0.3699     0.1100   3.363  0.000771 ***
pct_vacant          0.2849     0.1428   1.995  0.046007 *

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Coefficients, Translated

exp(cbind(OR = coef(v_model), confint(v_model)))

                           OR        2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept)       0.002965276 0.0001115289 0.02846386
unemployment_rate 1.447590364 1.1934960639 1.84714872
pct_vacant        1.329619347 1.0371047252 1.83804694



Unemployment: OR 1.45 [1.19, 1.85]; each additional point of unemployment multiplies an area’s odds of high-violence status by ~1.45 (+45%), holding vacancy constant
Vacancy: OR 1.33 [1.04, 1.84]; +33% odds per point, holding unemployment constant
For a ratio, no effect = 1, not 0: both intervals exclude it. And these are associations, not causes: nobody randomly assigned unemployment to neighborhoods

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
The Bayesian Version, Real Data

v_bayes <- brm(high_violence ~ unemployment_rate + pct_vacant,
               data = areas, family = bernoulli(),
               chains = 2, iter = 2000, seed = 705, refresh = 0)


exp(fixef(v_bayes)[, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")])

                     Estimate          Q2.5      Q97.5
Intercept         0.001792006 0.00007756542 0.02117534
unemployment_rate 1.492292997 1.21912215721 1.92093080
pct_vacant        1.366238869 1.03527533301 1.87703700



Both traditions land in the same place: posterior odds ratios near the glm() estimates, credible intervals excluding 1. With 77 areas instead of 32 cars, the intervals are usably tight.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
How to Report It: Frequentist

“Each one-point increase in the unemployment rate was associated with 45% higher odds of being a high-violence area (OR = 1.45, 95% CI [1.19, 1.85]), holding vacancy constant. Predicted probabilities ranged from about 3% for the least-disadvantaged areas to over 99% for the most.”


The effect (as an odds ratio), the uncertainty, and a probability a reader can feel: all three, every time.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
How to Report It: Bayesian

“Given the data and priors, each one-point increase in unemployment multiplied the odds of high-violence status by about 1.5 (posterior mean OR 1.49, 95% credible interval [1.22, 1.92]).”


Same three ingredients, and this one gets to make a direct probability statement about the odds ratio itself.

title: Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
section: Your Turn (3 minutes, with a neighbor)
text:
Your Turn (3 minutes, with a neighbor)

A reentry study models re-arrest within 12 months and reports two log-odds coefficients: risk score (per point): 0.7 · completed programming: -0.5

Convert both to odds ratios (Rosetta Stone, or exp() in R)
Say each in a sentence a police chief would understand
Audit your neighbor: did they say odds, or slip into probability?



exp(0.7) ≈ 2.0: each risk point roughly doubles the odds. exp(-0.5) ≈ 0.61: about 39% lower odds. Neither is a statement about probability.

In Session 1 we predicted a robber’s next move with a table you couldn’t read. You’ve now earned the tool the course opened with: that table is just log-odds, and log-odds are just exp() away from sense

text:

Session 2 taught you to describe what data are; this week asks what data are likely to be — the first step toward inference. Probability gets taught the course’s way: don’t take a claim on faith, simulate it and watch it happen. Along the way you plant the seed the whole second half of the course grows from — conditional probability, and Bayes’ theorem for reversing it — harvested in Session 6, when the two great traditions of inference meet on the same question. In lab, dplyr hands you the verbs every later analysis will use.

text:
📽️ Slides: The Logic of Inference: Confidence Intervals · 🧪 Lab 5: Putting an Interval On It · 📝 Homework 5 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Session 4 showed that sample statistics fluctuate in predictable ways; this week cashes that in. If we know how estimates behave, we can attach an honest statement of uncertainty to a single sample’s number — a confidence interval. The hard part isn’t computing the interval (R does that); it’s saying what it means out loud without lying, and reporting size along with direction — detectable ≠ dramatic. That habit is your vaccination for Session 6, where “significant” enters the vocabulary.

title: Session 8 · Correlation + Midterm Review
text:
📽️ Slides: Correlation, Then Midterm Review · 🧪 Lab 8: Correlation · 📝 Homework 8 + Project Checkpoint 1 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Until now, every test had the same shape: two groups and one outcome. Tonight there are no groups. Both variables are numbers, and the question is whether two measures move together. Pearson’s r puts one number on it, cor.test() tests it, and Chicago’s 77 community areas force the semester’s standing warning into the open: a correlation between areas says nothing about people (the ecological fallacy). Correlation is the doorway to regression in Sessions 10 and 11, where your final project lives. The second half of the night is review for next week’s midterm.

title: Session 8 · Correlation + Midterm Review
text:
In class

Correlation (first half):

A new kind of question: both variables are numbers, no groups
Association is not causation: ice cream, violent crime, and the lurking third variable
From covariance (the right idea, stuck in its units) to Pearson’s r (always between -1 and +1)
What r cannot see: Anscombe’s quartet, curved relationships, one outlier creating a correlation out of noise, and Spearman’s rho as the backup
Chicago’s 77 community areas: unemployment tracks violent-crime rates at r = 0.84; median age gives a genuine zero
The ecological fallacy: area-level patterns license no claims about individuals
cor.test(): r, a confidence interval, and a p-value. Where is zero?

Lab 8: the recipe yourself, on neighborhoods (poverty and assaults) and correctional officers (time on the job and job satisfaction). You submit your Your Turn script
Midterm review (second half): the exam’s format and six parts, and one practice problem for each part

Missed class? The demo walkthrough reproduces tonight’s correlation lecture step by step. The review slides are at the end of the slides.

title: Session 11 · Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
📽️ Slides: Logistic Regression · 🧪 Lab 11: Logistic Regression: Chicago Neighborhoods, Then Alaska Nights · 📝 Homework 11 + Project Checkpoint 4 · 🎬 Demo walkthrough · ✍️ Practice
Every model so far predicted a number; this week the outcome is yes or no (arrest or not, reoffend or desist), which is the form most criminal-justice questions actually take. A straight line can’t live on a 0/1 outcome, so probability climbs the ladder to odds and log-odds, and lm() becomes glm(family = binomial). It’s also the week the course pays off its opening promise: the Session 1 bank-robbery model you couldn’t read gets re-fit and finally read, line by line. This is the last session of new statistical content: the toolbox is complete, and Checkpoint 4 (the final one) fits your actual project model.

title: Session 11 · Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of this week you can:

explain why lm() fails on a 0/1 outcome, and how the probability → odds → log-odds ladder fixes it
fit a logistic regression in both traditions: glm(family = binomial) and brm(family = bernoulli())
translate coefficients into odds ratios and predicted probabilities, and keep the two straight
say logistic results in plain language a police chief could act on, without confusing odds with probability

title: Session 11 · Logistic Regression: Yes/No Outcomes
text:
In class

Why criminal justice runs on binary outcomes (arrest, failure to appear, re-arrest, intoxicated or not), and why lm() predicts impossible probabilities when you feed it one
Closing the loop on Session 1: the bank-robbery case study that opened the course was a logistic regression: we re-fit the exact model and finally read its table (coefficients are log-odds; exp() them into odds ratios; West Zone’s odds ratio is why the cars went west)
The ladder: probability → odds → log-odds, and why a straight line can only live on the last rung
glm(family = binomial), one argument away from lm(), and the two interpretation moves: odds ratios for effects, predicted probabilities for cases
The 3D logistic surface: Session 10’s flat plane, bent into an S-shaped probability sheet: built live from predict() on a 40 × 40 grid, plus the recorded guided tour
The Bayesian version: brm(family = bernoulli()) with the same settings as Session 10’s regression, posterior odds ratios, and the credible-interval sentence you’re allowed to say
Real-data thread: which Chicago community areas are high-violence? Unemployment (OR ≈ 1.45 per point) and vacant housing (OR ≈ 1.33 per point) both raise the odds; predicted probabilities run from ~3% (Forest Glen) to over 99% (West Garfield Park). Associations, not causes, and we say so.
Lab 11: the whole workflow yourself: Chicago walkthrough, then intoxicated-crash odds in the Alaska data with lubridate-built night/weekend flags, plus odds-ratio translation drills
Code clinic (final half hour): open floor for your project: live debugging, interpretation workshopping, and the presentation order draw. Bring a runnable draft and your two hardest problems: Checkpoint 4 is due Sunday, November 22, so the clinic is where you get unstuck before you finish it.
